topics.title: Algebraic Expressions
learningObjectives: Apply the index laws to positive, negative, fractional and zero indices, and manipulate surds including rationalising denominators (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.1/2.2, AQA 7357 B1-B2, OCR A H640 2.01
Expand single and double brackets, recognising and deploying the difference of two squares and perfect square expansions (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.1, AQA 7357 B3
Factorise quadratics with a = 1 and a is not 1 using the AC method, and factorise expressions by grouping (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B3
Simplify, multiply, divide, add and subtract algebraic fractions by factorising and cancelling whole factors only (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B8

Divide polynomials by linear expressions using long division or the remainder theorem, and use the factor theorem to extract linear factors and unknown coefficients (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B4
Combine these skills fluently to prove simple statements and simplify harder expressions under timed exam conditions (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Collect like terms: only terms with identical variables and powers combine - 3x^2y and 3xy^2 are not like terms.
Index laws: x^a x x^b = x^(a+b), x^a / x^b = x^(a-b), (x^a)^b = x^(ab), x^0 = 1, x^(-a) = 1/x^a.
Difference of two squares a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); perfect squares a^2 +/- 2ab + b^2 = (a +/- b)^2.
In algebraic fractions, factorise numerator and denominator fully, then cancel common FACTORS only - never terms joined by + or -.
Factor theorem: f(a) = 0 means (x - a) is a factor; remainder theorem: remainder on division by (x - a) is f(a).
topics.exampleQuestion: Simplify fully (2x^2 + 3x - 2)/(x + 2) - (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2), and state the values of x for which the original expression is undefined. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 5 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Factorise both numerators: 2x^2 + 3x - 2 = (2x - 1)(x + 2) (M1: correct factorisation, AC method), and x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2) (M1: difference of two squares). The first fraction becomes (2x - 1)(x + 2)/(x + 2) = 2x - 1 and the second becomes (x - 2)(x + 2)/(x - 2) = x + 2 (M1: cancelling whole factors only). Subtracting: (2x - 1) - (x + 2) = x - 3 (A1: correct simplified form). The original expression is undefined at x = -2 and x = 2, where a denominator is zero - cancelling hides these restrictions, so state them (A1: restrictions identified).
practiceQuestions: Expand and simplify (3x - 2)(x + 4) - (x - 1)^2.
Factorise completely 6x^2 + 13x + 6, and hence simplify (6x^2 + 13x + 6)/(2x + 3).
Simplify (x^3 - 8)/(x^2 - 4).
Divide 2x^3 - 5x^2 + 3x - 1 by (x - 2), giving the quotient and remainder, and verify the remainder using the remainder theorem.
Given f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6, show that (x - 1) is a factor and factorise f(x) completely.
Simplify (2x^2 y^(-3))^3 / (4x^(-1) y^2)^2, giving your answer with positive indices.

topics.title: Quadratic Equations
learningObjectives: Solve quadratic equations by factorising, including when the coefficient of x^2 is not 1 (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3
Complete the square for a = 1 and a is not 1, and use the completed square form to find exact roots and turning points (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3
Use the quadratic formula to solve any quadratic, leaving answers in exact surd form (AO1)
Interpret the discriminant to determine the number and nature of roots, including unknown-coefficient problems (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3
Use the relationships between roots and coefficients: alpha + beta = -b/a and alpha beta = c/a (AO2)
Solve quadratic inequalities graphically and algebraically, giving answers in correct set notation (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.4, AQA 7357 B3
Solve hidden quadratic equations by substitution, back-substituting with the range of the substituted variable checked (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Standard form: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a is not 0; factorising when a = 1 uses two numbers with product c and sum b; when a is not 1, use the AC method.
Completing the square: x^2 + bx = (x + b/2)^2 - (b/2)^2; for a is not 1, factor a out first.
Quadratic formula: x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/2a; always works, required for surd-form answers.
Discriminant b^2 - 4ac: > 0 two distinct real roots; = 0 one repeated root (tangency); < 0 no real roots. Sum of roots -b/a, product c/a.
Hidden quadratics: substitute u = x^2, u = sin(theta), u = e^x and solve in u, then back-substitute and CHECK the range of the substituted variable.
topics.exampleQuestion: Solve 2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0, and hence solve 2sin^2(theta) - 5sin(theta) - 3 = 0 for 0 <= theta < 2pi. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Factorise: ac = -6, so 2x^2 - 6x + x - 3 = 2x(x - 3) + 1(x - 3) = (2x + 1)(x - 3) = 0 (M1 A1), giving x = -1/2 or x = 3 (A1). Substituting u = sin(theta) (M1): sin(theta) = -1/2 or sin(theta) = 3. Since -1 <= sin(theta) <= 1, sin(theta) = 3 is impossible and is rejected (B1: range check). For sin(theta) = -1/2, the reference angle is pi/6, and sine is negative in quadrants 3 and 4 (M1), giving theta = pi + pi/6 = 7pi/6 and theta = 2pi - pi/6 = 11pi/6 (A1 A1).
practiceQuestions: Solve 3x^2 + 10x - 8 = 0 by factorising.
Solve x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0 by completing the square, giving exact surd answers.
Use the quadratic formula to solve 5x^2 - 3x - 1 = 0, leaving your answers in surd form.
Find the set of values of k for which kx^2 + 4x + k = 0 has real roots.
Solve the inequality x^2 - 5x + 6 > 0, giving your answer in set notation.
A rectangle has area 24 cm^2 and perimeter 20 cm. Find its dimensions.

topics.title: Coordinate Geometry
learningObjectives: Find the equation of a line from a gradient and point or from two points, in y = mx + c or ax + by + c = 0 form (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1, AQA 7357 C1
Calculate distances and midpoints, and use the parallel (m1 = m2) and perpendicular (m1 m2 = -1) conditions (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1, AQA 7357 C1
Find the equation of a circle from its centre and radius, and recover centre and radius by completing the square from the expanded form (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.6, AQA 7357 C2
Use circle properties: the radius is perpendicular to the tangent, and the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.6, AQA 7357 C2
Find intersections of lines with lines and lines with circles, interpreting a zero discriminant as tangency and deriving exact chord lengths (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1/3.6
Determine loci of points satisfying distance conditions and prove geometric facts using gradients and distances (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1); line through (x1, y1): y - y1 = m(x - x1).
Distance d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2); midpoint M = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2).
Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular lines have gradients multiplying to -1 (m1 x m2 = -1).
Circle: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 with centre (a, b), radius r; radius is perpendicular to the tangent; the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre.
Line-circle intersection: substitute and examine the resulting quadratic - discriminant zero means tangency; chord length follows from the two roots.
topics.exampleQuestion: Find the equation of the circle with diameter endpoints A(1, 2) and B(5, 6), and find the equation of the tangent at A. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Centre = midpoint of AB = ((1 + 5)/2, (2 + 6)/2) = (3, 4) (M1). AB = sqrt((5 - 1)^2 + (6 - 2)^2) = sqrt(32), so r^2 = 32/4 = 8 (M1 A1). Circle: (x - 3)^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 8 (A1). Gradient of the radius from (3, 4) to A(1, 2) is (2 - 4)/(1 - 3) = 1 (M1), so the tangent gradient is -1 (perpendicular to radius). Tangent at A: y - 2 = -1(x - 1), i.e. y = -x + 3 (A1).
practiceQuestions: Find the equation of the line through (-2, 3) perpendicular to 2x + 3y = 6, in the form ax + by + c = 0.
Find the intersection of y = 2x - 1 and 3x + y = 7.
Find the tangent to the circle (x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 25 at the point (5, 3).
Points A(1, 1), B(2, 2) and C(4, 0). Show that triangle ABC is right-angled, stating the right angle.
Show that the line 3x + 4y = 25 is a tangent to the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25 and find the point of contact.
The line y = 2x + 1 intersects the circle (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 10 at A and B. Find the exact length AB.

topics.title: Trigonometry
learningObjectives: Work in radians and degrees, using s = r(theta) and A = 1/2 r^2 (theta) for arcs and sectors, and recall exact values for 0, pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, pi/2 (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.1-5.2, AQA 7357 E1
Sketch sin, cos and tan graphs and their transformations y = a sin(bx + c) + d, stating amplitude, period and phase (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.1, AQA 7357 E1
Use the core identities sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 and tan = sin/cos to solve equations and prove identities (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.4, AQA 7357 E4
Apply compound angle, double angle and R-formula results, including expressing a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) as R sin(theta + alpha) (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.5, AQA 7357 E6
Solve trigonometric equations in a given interval, using the CAST diagram or graphs and rejecting impossible solutions (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.4, AQA 7357 E4
Apply the sine rule (including the ambiguous case), cosine rule and area = 1/2 ab sin C to triangles (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.3, AQA 7357 E3
Use inverse trigonometric functions with their domains and ranges, and small-angle approximations (AO1/AO2)
keyPoints: Exact values: sin: 0, 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2, 1; cos: 1, sqrt(3)/2, sqrt(2)/2, 1/2, 0 for pi/6 steps from 0 to pi/2; tan = sin/cos.
Core identity: sin^2(theta) + cos^2(theta) = 1; tan(theta) = sin(theta)/cos(theta) when cos(theta) is not 0.
Compound angles: sin(A +/- B) = sin A cos B +/- cos A sin B; cos(A +/- B) = cos A cos B -/+ sin A sin B; double angle: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A, cos 2A in three forms.
R-formula: a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) = R sin(theta + alpha), R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), tan(alpha) = b/a; maximum R, minimum -R.
Sine rule a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C (ambiguous case SSA); cosine rule a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A; area = 1/2 ab sin C.
topics.exampleQuestion: Solve 2sin(2theta) = sqrt(3)cos(theta) for 0 <= theta < 2pi. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 6 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Expand sin(2theta) = 2sin(theta)cos(theta): 2(2sin(theta)cos(theta)) = sqrt(3)cos(theta) (M1: double angle). Rearrange and factorise: 4sin(theta)cos(theta) - sqrt(3)cos(theta) = 0, so cos(theta)(4sin(theta) - sqrt(3)) = 0 (M1: factorise rather than divide, preserving all solutions). Case 1: cos(theta) = 0 gives theta = pi/2 and theta = 3pi/2 (A1). Case 2: sin(theta) = sqrt(3)/4 = 0.4330 (M1: reference angle), giving theta = arcsin(0.4330) = 0.448 and theta = pi - 0.448 = 2.694 (A1 A1). All four solutions lie in the interval.
practiceQuestions: Prove that tan(2theta) = 2tan(theta)/(1 - tan^2(theta)).
Solve 3cos(2theta) + sin(theta) = 1 for 0 <= theta < 360 degrees.
Express 3sin(theta) + 4cos(theta) in the form R sin(theta + alpha), R > 0, and state the minimum value.
In triangle ABC, a = 7, b = 9 and angle C = 60 degrees. Find c and the area of the triangle.
Sketch y = 2cos(2x - pi/3) for 0 <= x <= 2pi, stating the amplitude, period and the x-coordinate of the first maximum.
Find the exact value of sin(arcsin(3/5) + arccos(4/5)).

topics.title: Differentiation
learningObjectives: Differentiate x^n from first principles for positive integer n and understand the first principles definition of the derivative (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.1, AQA 7357 G1
Apply the power rule to polynomials and to negative and fractional powers (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.2, AQA 7357 G2
Apply the sum, product, quotient and chain rules, including to e^x, ln x, sin x, cos x and tan x (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.5, AQA 7357 G2
Find equations of tangents and normals, using the perpendicular condition for the normal (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.3, AQA 7357 G3
Find and classify stationary points using the second derivative, including points of inflection (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.4, AQA 7357 G3
Solve optimisation problems, justifying maxima and minima, and use implicit differentiation and connected rates of change (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.6-7.7, AQA 7357 G3-G4
keyPoints: Power rule: d/dx(x^n) = n x^(n-1) for all real n; sum and difference differentiate term by term.
Product rule: d/dx(fg) = f'g + fg'; quotient rule: d/dx(f/g) = (f'g - fg')/g^2; chain rule: d/dx(f(g(x))) = f'(g(x)) x g'(x).
Standard derivatives: e^x, ln x = 1/x, sin x = cos x, cos x = -sin x, tan x = sec^2 x.
Stationary points: f'(x) = 0. Second derivative test: f'' < 0 maximum, f'' > 0 minimum; inflection requires f'' = 0 with sign change of f'.
Tangent gradient f'(x1); normal gradient -1/f'(x1). Implicit: differentiate term by term, y-terms get dy/dx factors. Connected rates: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt).
topics.exampleQuestion: Find the stationary points of y = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 and determine the nature of each. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: dy/dx = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 3(x - 3)(x + 1) (M1: differentiation, M1: factorisation). Stationary points where dy/dx = 0: x = 3 and x = -1 (A1). Second derivative: d^2y/dx^2 = 6x - 6 (M1). At x = 3: d^2y/dx^2 = 12 > 0, so a minimum (A1). At x = -1: d^2y/dx^2 = -12 < 0, so a maximum (A1). Coordinates: y(3) = -22 and y(-1) = 10, so minimum at (3, -22) and maximum at (-1, 10) (B1: coordinates stated).
practiceQuestions: Differentiate x sqrt(x + 2) using the product rule, simplifying your answer.
Find the equation of the normal to y = x^2 - 4x + 3 at the point where x = 2.
The radius of a sphere increases at 0.5 cm/s. Find the rate of increase of the volume when r = 10 cm.
For the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25, find dy/dx when x = 3 (y > 0).
Differentiate y = e^(3x) sin(2x), simplifying your answer.
Differentiate f(x) = 1/x from first principles.

topics.title: Integration
learningObjectives: Integrate polynomials and negative powers with the power rule, and recall the standard results for 1/x, e^x and basic trigonometric functions (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.1, AQA 7357 H1
Integrate composite functions using the reverse chain rule and substitution, changing limits correctly in definite integrals (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.2/8.5, AQA 7357 H2
Apply integration by parts, choosing u sensibly and repeating where needed (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.5, AQA 7357 H3
Evaluate definite integrals and find areas under and between curves, splitting where the curve crosses the axis (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.3, AQA 7357 H4
Calculate volumes of revolution about the x-axis and y-axis (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.4, AQA 7357 H4
Form and solve differential equations by separation of variables, finding particular solutions from initial conditions (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.6, AQA 7357 H5
keyPoints: Power rule: the integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not -1; special: 1/x gives ln|x| + C, e^x gives e^x + C.
Trig: the integral of sin x dx = -cos x + C; cos x dx = sin x + C; sec^2 x dx = tan x + C - always check the sign on sine.
Reverse chain rule: the integral of f'(x)[f(x)]^n dx = [f(x)]^(n+1)/(n+1) + C; the integral of f'(x)e^(f(x)) dx = e^(f(x)) + C.
Substitution: u = f(x), dx = du/f'(x), and CHANGE the limits for definite integrals. By parts: the integral of u dv = uv - the integral of v du; choose u by LIATE.

Definite integral F(b) - F(a) measures signed area: split where f crosses the axis. Area between curves: the integral of (top - bottom) dx. Volumes: V = (pi) times the integral of y^2 dx (x-axis) or (pi) times the integral of x^2 dy (y-axis).
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the integral from 0 to 2 of x sqrt(4 - x^2) dx using the substitution u = 4 - x^2. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 5 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: u = 4 - x^2, so du/dx = -2x and x dx = -du/2 (M1: substitution and differential). Change the limits: x = 0 gives u = 4, and x = 2 gives u = 0 (B1: limits changed). The integral becomes the integral from 4 to 0 of u^(1/2) (-1/2) du = (1/2) times the integral from 0 to 4 of u^(1/2) du (M1: rewritten, flipped). Evaluating: (1/2)[(2/3)u^(3/2)] from 0 to 4 = (1/3)(4^(3/2)) = (1/3)(8) = 8/3 (A1: exact answer).
practiceQuestions: Find the integral of (3x^2 - 2x + 5)e^(x^3 - x^2 + 5x) dx.
Use integration by parts to find the integral of x cos x dx.
Evaluate the integral from 0 to 1 of x/(1 + x^2)^2 dx.
Find the area of the region bounded by y = x^2 and y = 2x - x^2.
The curve y = sqrt(x) from x = 0 to x = 4 is rotated a full turn about the x-axis. Find the exact volume formed.
Use integration by parts twice to find the integral of x^2 e^x dx.

topics.title: Vectors
learningObjectives: Represent vectors in 2D and 3D using components and unit vectors, and calculate magnitudes and direction angles (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 Section J, OCR A H640 14.01
Add, subtract and scalar-multiply vectors, and use position vectors to find displacements, midpoints and collinear points (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J1-J2

Calculate the scalar (dot) product in component and magnitude form, and determine angles between vectors and conditions for perpendicularity and parallelism (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J2-J3
Find the vector and Cartesian equations of a line in 2D and 3D, and determine whether lines are parallel, intersecting or skew (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J3
Solve geometric problems using vectors, proving properties such as right angles, parallelograms and collinearity (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, OCR A H640 14.01
Connect vectors to kinematics (velocity and displacement as vector quantities) and understand scalar triple product contexts as a Further Mathematics extension (AO2)
keyPoints: Magnitude: |a| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) in 2D and sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) in 3D; unit vector in the direction of a: a/|a|.
Displacement from A to B: AB = b - a (subtract position vectors: end minus start).
Scalar product: a . b = |a||b|cos(theta) = x1x2 + y1y2 + z1z2; perpendicular exactly when a . b = 0; parallel when components are in the same ratio.
Vector equation of a line: r = a + t d (or r = a + t(b - a) through two points); Cartesian form (x - x1)/l = (y - y1)/m = (z - z1)/n.
In 3D, intersecting lines: solve two equations for t and s, then CHECK the third equation - failure means the lines are skew.
topics.exampleQuestion: The points A and B have position vectors a = (2, 1, 3) and b = (5, 3, 7). Find the vector AB, the distance AB, and a unit vector in the direction of AB. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 6 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AB = b - a = (5 - 2, 3 - 1, 7 - 3) = (3, 2, 4) (M1: subtract position vectors, A1). Distance: |AB| = sqrt(3^2 + 2^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 4 + 16) = sqrt(29) (M1 A1). Unit vector: AB/|AB| = (1/sqrt(29))(3, 2, 4), i.e. (3/sqrt(29), 2/sqrt(29), 4/sqrt(29)) (A1 A1: direction preserved, magnitude 1).
practiceQuestions: Find the angle between a = (1, 2, 2) and b = (2, 1, 0), in degrees to 1 d.p.
Find the value of x for which a = (2, -1, 3) and b = (1, x, -2) are perpendicular.
Find the vector equation of the line through A(1, 2, 0) with direction (2, -1, 4), and its Cartesian form.
Show that the points P(1, 2), Q(3, 4) and R(5, 6) are collinear.
Lines L1: r = (1, 2, 2) + t(1, 1, 0) and L2: r = (1, 5, 1) + s(2, -1, 1). Determine whether they intersect, and if so find the point.
A(1, 1), B(4, 2) and C(6, 5) are three vertices of parallelogram ABCD. Find the position vector of D.

topics.title: Algebraic Methods and Proof
learningObjectives: Understand and use the structure of mathematical proof, proceeding from given assumptions through a chain of valid logical steps to the conclusion (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 1, AQA 7357 A1, OCR A H640 1.01
Prove statements by deduction and by exhaustion, and prove algebraic identities using the equivalence sign (AO2) - AQA 7357 A1, Edexcel 9MA0 1.1-1.2
Disprove a statement by counter-example, selecting one value satisfying the conditions for which the claim fails (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 1.3, AQA 7357 A1

Carry out proofs by contradiction, including the irrationality of sqrt(2) and the infinitude of the primes (AO2) - AQA 7357 A1, OCR A H640 1.01; Edexcel tests contradiction-style arguments in past papers
Decompose proper rational functions into partial fractions with distinct and repeated linear factors, dividing improper fractions first (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B8
Select and justify the correct proof technique and write arguments in full sentences showing every logical step (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Deduction chains known facts into the conclusion; exhaustion proves every case in a finite split; a single counter-example disproves a general claim.
Contradiction: assume the statement false, derive an impossible consequence, conclude the original statement is true.
Identities use the equivalence sign and hold for all values of the variable; manipulate each side independently.
Partial fraction forms: A/(ax+b) + B/(cx+d) for distinct linear factors; A/(ax+b) + B/(ax+b)^2 for a repeated factor; divide improper fractions first.
Proofs are marked on structure: state the assumption or case split, show every logical step, state the contradiction or conclusion explicitly.
topics.exampleQuestion: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many prime numbers. (AQA 7357-style, 5 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Assume, for contradiction, that there are finitely many primes, listed p_1, p_2, ..., p_n (M1: assumption stated). Let N = p_1 p_2 ... p_n + 1 (M1: construction). When N is divided by any listed prime p_i, the remainder is 1, so no p_i divides N (A1: valid deduction). Therefore N is either prime itself or has a prime factor that is not in the list - in both cases a prime exists outside the assumed complete list (A1: contradiction identified). This contradicts the assumption that the list contained all primes, so there must be infinitely many primes (A1: conclusion stated in words).
practiceQuestions: Prove by contradiction that sqrt(2) is irrational.
Disprove by counter-example the statement: for all real x, x^2 > x.
Prove that n^3 - n is divisible by 3 for all positive integers n.
Express (3x^2 + 7x - 2)/((x - 1)(x + 2)^2) in partial fractions.
Express (2x^2 + 3x + 5)/(x + 1)^2 in partial fractions.
Prove by exhaustion that every perfect square ends in the digit 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.

topics.title: Probability and Distributions
learningObjectives: Use Venn diagrams, tree diagrams and the addition and multiplication laws, including conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 13, AQA 7357 M1-M3
Determine whether two events are independent (P(A and B) = P(A)P(B)) or mutually exclusive, and use these conditions in problems (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 13, AQA 7357 M3
Model a situation with the binomial distribution B(n, p), checking the four conditions, and calculate probabilities and E(X) = np, Var(X) = np(1 - p) (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 14, AQA 7357 N1-N2
Model with the normal distribution N(mu, sigma^2), standardising with Z = (X - mu)/sigma, and solve forward and inverse problems (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 14, AQA 7357 N3
Conduct hypothesis tests on a binomial model: state H0 and H1, find the critical region or p-value, and conclude in context (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 15, AQA 7357 O1-O2
Select an appropriate distribution for a context and justify the choice; understand the central limit theorem idea for large samples (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 14, AQA 7357 N1
keyPoints: Addition law: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); mutually exclusive events simplify it to P(A) + P(B).
Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B); independence: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B), equivalently P(A|B) = P(A).
Binomial X ~ B(n, p): P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n-r); E(X) = np, Var(X) = np(1 - p); conditions: fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independent trials.
Normal X ~ N(mu, sigma^2): standardise Z = (X - mu)/sigma; the 68-95-99.7 rule: about 68.3% within 1 sigma, 95.4% within 2 sigma, 99.7% within 3 sigma.
Hypothesis test: H0 (no change) against H1 (one- or two-tailed); reject H0 when the test statistic falls in the critical region or the p-value is below the significance level; conclude in context.
topics.exampleQuestion: A coin is tossed 20 times and 15 heads are observed. Test, at the 5% level of significance, whether the coin is biased. State your hypotheses clearly and conclude in context. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Let p be the probability of heads. H0: p = 0.5 (the coin is fair); H1: p is not 0.5 (the coin is biased) (B1 M1: hypotheses with the parameter). Two-tailed test, so the significance is 2.5% in each tail (B1: tail split stated). Under H0, X ~ B(20, 0.5), where X is the number of heads (B1: model stated). P(X >= 15) = 1 - P(X <= 14) = 0.0207 (M1 A1: p-value from tables or calculator). Since 0.0207 < 0.025, the result falls in the critical region, so reject H0 (A1: comparison and decision). There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the coin is biased towards heads (A1: conclusion in context).
practiceQuestions: State the four conditions required for a binomial model, and give a situation where one fails.
X ~ N(mu, sigma^2). Given that P(X < 60) = 0.2119 and mu = 70, find the value of sigma.

Machine A produces 60% of items with a 2% defect rate; machine B produces 40% with a 5% defect rate. An item is chosen at random. Find the probability it is defective, and the probability it came from A given that it is defective.
Of 100 students, 60 study maths, 45 study physics and 20 study both. Find P(maths or physics), P(neither) and P(maths | physics).

topics.title: The Large Data Set
learningObjectives: Know the prescribed large data set for your board - its context, variables and structure - and use it to interpret statistical results in context (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topics 11-12, AQA 7357 K1-L1
Select and justify an appropriate sampling method, and criticise unsuitable methods for bias (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 11, AQA 7357 K1-K2
Take a random, systematic, stratified, quota or opportunity sample from a large data set using a sampling frame (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 11, AQA 7357 K2
Clean data: handle n/a entries, trace values and outliers using the 1.5 x IQR rule, justifying decisions (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 12, AQA 7357 L1
Compare two distributions from the data set in context, commenting on location, dispersion and skewness (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 12, AQA 7357 L1-L2
Calculate summary statistics from data set samples and interpret them in the context of the data (AO1/AO2)
keyPoints: Edexcel LDS: weather data from 8 stations - 5 UK (Heathrow, Hurn, Leeming, Leuchars, Camborne) and 3 overseas (Beijing, Jacksonville, Perth) - for 1987 (May to October) and 2015 (full year).
Edexcel variables: daily mean temperature, total rainfall, total sunshine, mean windspeed and direction (Beaufort), mean cloud cover (oktas), mean pressure (hPa), mean gust.
AQA LDS: vehicles registered in Great Britain - make, engine size, fuel type, engine power and CO2 emissions among the recorded variables.
Data cleaning: tr means trace rainfall (below 0.05 mm); n/a means not available; outliers flagged by the 1.5 x IQR rule.
Sampling: census (all), simple random (random numbers), systematic (every kth after a random start), stratified (proportional), quota and opportunity (non-random, prone to bias).
topics.exampleQuestion: The Edexcel large data set contains daily mean temperature data for Heathrow in 1987 and 2015. A student compares the mean of all the 1987 data with the mean of all the 2015 data and concludes that the climate at Heathrow cooled between the two years. Give two reasons why this comparison may be misleading, and suggest how a fairer comparison could be made. (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 4 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: The 1987 data covers only May to October, while the 2015 data covers the full calendar year, so the two means are not based on the same months - the seasonal structure differs (B1: unlike-for-like comparison identified). A single year is weather rather than climate, so one year's mean against another's does not establish a trend (B1: interpretation). A fairer comparison restricts both years to the same months - for example comparing May to October 1987 with May to October 2015 - or takes samples of the same size in the same way from both years (B1 B1: fairer comparison described).
practiceQuestions: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a census compared with a sample.
Describe how to take a systematic sample of 31 days from the 365 days of 2015 Heathrow data.
A school of 800 students has 300 in Year 12 and 500 in Year 13. A stratified sample of 40 students is taken. How many from each year group?
A 31-day sample of daily total sunshine has Q1 = 1.1 h, median = 3.4 h and Q3 = 6.2 h. Use the 1.5 x IQR rule to test whether 14.9 h is an outlier.
In the Edexcel weather data, what does a daily total rainfall recorded as tr mean, and how should it be treated when calculating statistics?

A sample of 30 days gives Heathrow a mean daily temperature of 11.2 degrees C with standard deviation 5.6, and Hurn a mean of 10.4 degrees C with standard deviation 4.9. Compare the two distributions.

topics.title: Mechanics: Dynamics and Kinematics
learningObjectives: Use the five constant-acceleration (SUVAT) formulae, choosing the right one and stating when they are valid (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 17, AQA 7357 Q1-Q2
Interpret velocity-time graphs: gradient as acceleration and area as displacement (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 17, AQA 7357 Q2

Use calculus kinematics: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt, and s = integral of v dt, v = integral of a dt with initial conditions, distinguishing displacement from distance (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 17, AQA 7357 Q3
Apply Newton's second law (F = ma) to single particles and connected systems, and use Newton's third law for tensions (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 18, AQA 7357 R1-R3
Model friction with F = mu R and resolve forces on inclined planes (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 18, AQA 7357 R4-R5
Model projectile motion: constant horizontal velocity, vertical acceleration -g, maximum height and range (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 17, AQA 7357 Q4
State and use modelling assumptions (smooth, light, inextensible, no air resistance) in mechanics problems (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: SUVAT (constant acceleration only): v = u + at, s = ut + 1/2 at^2, s = 1/2 (u + v)t, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, s = vt - 1/2 at^2 - pick the equation missing the quantity you do not need.
Calculus kinematics: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt; backwards: s = integral of v dt, v = integral of a dt, with initial conditions fixing constants. Distance = integral of |v| dt.
Newton's second law: resultant force F = ma; weight = mg; resolve perpendicular and parallel to slopes (R = mg cos(theta), weight component mg sin(theta)).
Friction: at most F = mu R, opposing motion; reaches the maximum in limiting equilibrium. Connected particles: F = ma for each mass, solve simultaneously.
Projectiles: horizontal velocity u cos(theta) constant; vertical u sin(theta) with acceleration -g; at maximum height vertical velocity is 0.
topics.exampleQuestion: A mass of 4 kg slides down a slope inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the mass and the slope is 0.2. Find the acceleration of the mass down the slope. (g = 9.8 m/s^2) (Edexcel 9MA0-style, 7 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Resolve perpendicular to the slope: R = mg cos(30 degrees) = 4(9.8)(sqrt(3)/2) = 33.9 N (M1 A1: normal reaction). Friction opposes the motion (up the slope) with maximum value F = mu R = 0.2 x 33.9 = 6.79 N (M1 A1: friction model). Weight component down the slope: mg sin(30 degrees) = 4(9.8)(0.5) = 19.6 N (B1). Applying Newton's second law along the slope: 19.6 - 6.79 = 4a, so the resultant is 12.8 N (M1). a = 12.8/4 = 3.20 m/s^2 down the slope (A1).
practiceQuestions: A particle moves with velocity v(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 m/s. Find its displacement and the distance travelled from t = 0 to t = 3.
Particles of mass 3 kg and 5 kg hang from a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley. Find the acceleration and the tension (g = 9.8 m/s^2).
A car travelling at 25 m/s brakes uniformly and comes to rest in 50 m. Find the deceleration and the braking time.
A ball is projected from ground level at 20 m/s and 30 degrees above the horizontal. Find the maximum height and the range (g = 9.8 m/s^2).
A particle starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s^2 for 6 s. Find its final velocity and displacement.
A particle moves from rest at the origin with acceleration a = 6t - 12 m/s^2. Find v(t) and s(t), and the times when it is at rest.

topics.title: Shakespeare
learningObjectives: Analyse dramatic techniques - soliloquy, aside, dramatic irony, foil, subplot - and argue their effect on an audience, not just spot them (AO2)
Interpret Shakespearean language: blank verse, prose shifts, imagery clusters and wordplay, linking method to meaning (AO2)
Evaluate staging: set, lighting, costume, movement and directorial choices, including how performance reshapes character (AO2)
Explore themes of power, ambition, love, betrayal and appearance versus reality through a thesis-led argument (AO1)
Understand Elizabethan/Jacobean context and theatrical conventions, and weave them into analysis (AO3)
Deploy critical readings (feminist, Marxist, psychoanalytic; Bradley versus Leavis) as AO5 debate within your own argument
keyPoints: Soliloquy: character alone, reveals inner thoughts; aside: to audience, others do not hear
Dramatic irony: audience knows more than characters; creates tension - Iago's soliloquies versus 'honest Iago'
Blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter (nobles); prose: lower status, madness, intimacy
Shakespearean imagery clusters: clothing, blood, disease, nature, light/dark - track one per play
Stagecraft: minimal sets, emphasis on language in the early modern playhouse; modern productions: lighting, sound, multimedia
Tragedy: hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis, catharsis; comedy: marriage, mistaken identity, restoration of community
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA B (7717) Paper 1 style (25 marks): 'Othello's tragedy is caused by Iago's manipulation rather than any flaw in Othello himself.' In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents Othello.
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic: AO1 consistent argument (thesis + judgement), AO2 dramatic methods with effects, AO3 context woven, AO5 alternative readings weighed. Thesis (AO1): Iago is the proximate cause, but Shakespeare engineers the tragedy so that Iago's poison lands on soil Othello has already prepared - jealousy and insecurity are Othello's hamartia, fertilised by a racist society. AO2 paragraph 1: Iago's soliloquies and asides build the plot ('Thus do I ever make my fool my purse', 1.3), and dramatic irony makes every 'honest Iago' agonising - but note that Iago never lies outright; he arranges truths (the handkerchief, Cassio's exit) for Othello to misread, so credulity is Othello's contribution. AO2 paragraph 2: the temptation scene's staged two-hander (3.3) shows manipulation as technique - Iago's hesitant 'Ha! I like not that' plants suspicion while appearing reluctant; Othello's own diction then degrades ('Damn her, lewd minx!'), and his verse collapses into broken prose in the fit of 4.1 - method proving internal collapse, not merely external pressure. AO2 paragraph 3: animal and poison imagery - once Iago's 'old black ram' and 'pestilence' enter Othello's speech, we watch a mind colonised: the imagery tracks the transfer of fault between villain and hero. AO3: Venice needs Othello's soldiering but makes his status conditional; a Jacobean audience primed by racialised stereotypes of Moors makes 'credulity' partly a social product - woven, one sentence. AO5: Bradley's noble hero (tragedy of manipulation) versus Leavis's self-dramatising egotist (tragedy of vanity); a feminist counter-view centres Desdemona and Emilia - the real tragedy is that women's testimony is structurally unheard. Judgement: Iago supplies the mechanism, Othello the flaw, Venice the conditions - a three-cause thesis that answers 'to what extent' with a proportion, which is what the top band requires.
practiceQuestions: How does Shakespeare use dramatic irony in 'Othello' to heighten tension?
Compare the effects of Shakespeare's use of verse and prose in 'Hamlet'.
'The tragic hero's downfall is caused by external forces rather than his own hamartia.' To what extent do you agree with reference to 'Macbeth'?
Analyse the significance of the Gloucester subplot in 'King Lear'.
Evaluate a feminist reading of Desdemona's role in 'Othello'.
How does the dagger soliloquy (Macbeth 2.1) reveal Macbeth's state of mind?

topics.title: Poetry: Pre-1900 and Post-1900 Anthologies
learningObjectives: Analyse how form, metre, rhyme and imagery shape meaning in the pre-1900 (Donne, Marvell, Hardy, Keats) and post-1900 (Heaney, Duffy, Larkin) anthologies (AO2).
Compare two anthology poems, or an anthology poem with your prose text, via linked topic sentences naming method and idea (AO1/AO4).
Apply a timed unseen-poetry method to the compulsory two-poem question (AQA A Paper 1 Section B, 25 marks).
Weave in context: courtly love, metaphysical wit, carpe diem, Victorian double standards, confessional poetry (AO3).
Evaluate alternative readings of poems and reach a supported judgement (AO5).
keyPoints: AQA A (7712): you study ONE anthology - pre-1900 (14 poems, Wyatt to Dowson) or post-1900 (15 poems, Millay to Cope) - examined open book in Paper 1 Section C with your prose text.
Paper 1 Section B is two UNSEEN poems (25 marks) - a reusable timed method is non-negotiable.
AQA A-level AO weightings: AO1 28%, AO2 24%, AO3 24%, AO4 12%, AO5 12%.
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA A (7712) Paper 1 Section C style (25 marks, open book): 'In love poetry the beloved is always a fiction the lover constructs.' Compare how poets from your anthology and the author of your prose text present the gap between desire and the person desired.
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic: AO1 (28%) coherent comparative thesis with sustained judgement; AO2 (24%) methods and effects in every paragraph across both texts; AO3 (24%) contexts woven, not bolted; AO5 (12%) readings weighed. Thesis (AO1): pre-1900 poets construct the beloved through inherited convention - Wyatt's deer and Donne's flea are arguments, not people - while post-1900 poetry exposes the construction: Heaney's speaker admits the bog woman exists chiefly as his projection. Paragraphs (AO2) isolate one method each - conceit, monologue, free verse, voice - and apply it to both texts. Conclusion (AO5): weigh whether modern texts demystify the beloved or install a new fiction; commit.
practiceQuestions: Paper 1 Section B style (25 marks): compare two unseen poems on lost love, focusing on how voice and structure present grief.
'The argument of The Flea is comic bravado rather than coercive pressure.' In the light of this view, consider how Donne presents seduction.
Compare how Hardy's At an Inn and Larkin's Talking in Bed present emotional distance in love.
'Heaney's Punishment is an apology that becomes another judgement.' How far do you agree?

topics.title: Prose: Modern Novel and Set Texts
learningObjectives: Analyse narrative voice and focalisation: Nick's retrospective ambivalence, Frankenstein's framed narrators, Offred's present-tense fragmentation, Briony's metafictional control (AO2).
Track symbol patterns (green light, light and fire, colour coding, the Tallis vase) and structural devices across whole texts (AO2).
Situate novels in context - Jazz Age American Dream, Romanticism and galvanism, 1980s New Right, WW2 and postmodernism - woven into analysis (AO3).
Deploy critical readings (Trilling, Moers, Atwood) as interpretations to weigh, not quotations to drop (AO5).
Structure 25-mark essays with thesis, method-first paragraphs and evaluative or comparative judgement (AO1/AO4).
keyPoints: Boards: Gatsby (AQA B tragedy prose; AQA A Paper 1), Atonement (AQA A prose; AQA B crime), Frankenstein + The Handmaid's Tale (Edexcel 9ET0 Paper 2 'Science and society', one text pre-1900), The Handmaid's Tale also on AQA A Modern times and AQA B protest.
Edexcel Paper 2 is comparative: two prose texts, one pre-1900, integrated comparison throughout.
AQA essays are 25 marks: AO1 28%, AO2 24%, AO3 24%, AO4 12%, AO5 12% across the A-level.
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA B (7717) Paper 1 Section C style (25 marks): 'Gatsby is destroyed by his own idealism rather than by the carelessness of others.' In the light of this view, consider how Fitzgerald presents Gatsby's tragedy.
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic: AO1 coherent thesis with judgement; AO2 methods (narrative voice, symbol, structure) with effects; AO3 Jazz Age context woven; AO5 alternative readings weighed. Thesis (AO1): idealism and carelessness are complicit - Gatsby's 'extraordinary gift for hope' is genuine, but it is spent on a world built by careless wealth, so Fitzgerald makes the Dream itself tragic. Paragraphs (AO2): the green light as idealism made visible; Nick's elegiac narration as the vehicle of tragedy; Daisy's voice 'full of money' as the object idealism mistakes for love; the valley of ashes and Myrtle's death as carelessness. AO3: prohibition-era aspiration and inherited class barriers. AO5: weigh idealism as ennobling ('worth the whole rotten bunch') against enabling; conclude that Fitzgerald refuses to separate the two - the tragedy is the fit between them.
practiceQuestions: 'The Creature is more sinned against than sinning.' Discuss (Edexcel 9ET0 style, Frankenstein).
'Offred's narrative is an act of resistance, not merely of survival.' How far do you agree? (25 marks)
'Briony's coda redeems neither the novel nor herself.' Evaluate this view of Atonement.
'Nick's narration betrays more than it reveals.' Discuss narrative voice in The Great Gatsby.

topics.title: Drama: Modern and Set Plays
learningObjectives: Analyse dramatic methods: staging, props, lighting, sound, dialogue registers, dramatic irony, asides and soliloquy (AO2).
Evaluate genre debates - modern tragedy, problem play, revenge tragedy, 'plastic theatre' - as AO5 arguments with a committed judgement.
Situate plays in contexts of production and reception: Jacobean court, 1879 Norway, post-war America (AO3).
Adapt planning between passage-based and whole-text questions, using stage directions as evidence (AO1/AO2).
Weigh critical readings (Eliot on Webster, Shaw on Ibsen, Williams on his own craft) and reach a supported view (AO5).
keyPoints: Boards: Streetcar (AQA A Modern times core text; Edexcel 9ET0 post-1900 drama), A Doll's House (AQA B Option 2B political and social protest writing; OCR pre-1900 drama), The Duchess of Malfi (OCR Component 01 pre-1900 drama).
Write about staging as AO2 evidence: props, light, sound and exits are authorial choices, not scene-setting.
AQA essays are 25 marks; genre debate ('aspects of tragedy', 'elements of protest') must be explicit, not implied.
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA B (7717) Paper 2, Option 2B style (25 marks): 'Nora's rebellion is justified by the society that has made her powerless.' In the light of this view, discuss how Ibsen presents Nora in A Doll's House.
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic: AO1 - thesis with sustained judgement; AO2 - dramatic methods (props, register, staging) with effects; AO3 - context of production and reception woven in; AO5 - protest-writing lens weighed against other readings. Thesis (AO1): Ibsen engineers the play so Nora's rebellion reads as the only rational response to legal and emotional infantilisation - justification is structural, not personal. Paragraphs (AO2): the macaroons and forgery as staged transgressions against her 'doll' status; the tarantella as performance of the performance; the shift from 'little lark' diction to legal prose as liberation made audible; the door slam as the argument's final clause. AO3: 1879 Norwegian marriage law, the German alternative ending Ibsen called a 'barbaric outrage', Shaw's reading. AO5: weigh 'elements of political and social protest writing' (oppression, power, rebellion) against readings that stress family tragedy; conclude that Ibsen stages both - and makes the social reading win on the evidence.
practiceQuestions: 'Blanche is destroyed by her own illusions rather than by Stanley's brutality.' In the light of this view, discuss how Williams presents Blanche (Edexcel 9ET0 style).
'The Duchess is destroyed by her own transgression rather than her brothers' cruelty.' How far do you agree? (OCR H472 style).
How does Williams use staging and sound to present Blanche's inner life in A Streetcar Named Desire?
'The play's ending is a victory, not a tragedy.' In the light of this view, discuss how Ibsen presents Nora's exit.

topics.title: Comparative and Critical Reading
learningObjectives: Structure integrated comparative essays - one point of contact per paragraph across both texts, never text-then-text (AO1/AO4).
Apply critical lenses (feminist, Marxist, historicist, psychoanalytic) to textual evidence and weigh the readings produced (AO5).
Use AQA critical anthologies (7712 NEA; 7717 Theory and independence) as springboards for readings, not substitutes for evidence.
Execute a timed unseen-prose method for contextual linking questions (AQA A Paper 2 Section B, 25 marks).
Recall AO weightings and per-question AO emphasis across boards, and direct revision accordingly.
keyPoints: AQA A-level AO weightings (same AOs set by Ofqual for all boards): AO1 28%, AO2 24%, AO3 24%, AO4 12%, AO5 12%.

AQA A NEA (Independent critical study, texts across time): 2,500 words + bibliography, two texts, at least one pre-1900, 50 marks - AO1 7, AO2 6, AO3 6, AO4 3, AO5 3; interpretations over time required on at least one text.
AQA B Paper 2 is open book: set-text essay, unseen passage, and an essay linking two texts - comparison is the core skill.
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA B (7717) Paper 2, Option 2B style (25 marks, open book): 'Texts of protest make power visible by staging powerlessness.' Compare how two of your set texts present power and powerlessness.
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic: AO1 - comparative thesis with tension and judgement; AO2 - methods (narrative voice, props, colour coding, form) with effects in both texts per paragraph; AO3 - contexts of oppression woven in; AO5 - critical lenses weighed. Thesis (AO1): both texts stage powerlessness to indict the power that produces it - Atwood's colour-coded castes make powerlessness visible as uniform, while Ibsen's props (letterbox, locked door) make Nora's powerlessness domestic and legal. Paragraphs (AO2) take one point of contact each: bodies as property (Offred's 'two-legged wombs'; Nora's forgery prosecuted), language as control (Offred's permitted vocabulary; Torvald's pet names), escape as performance (Offred's narration; Nora's tarantella). AO3: 1980s authoritarianism; 1879 Norwegian marriage law. AO5: weigh feminist and Marxist lenses, then judge which text indicts power more completely - and commit.
practiceQuestions: Plan an AQA A NEA-style comparative critical essay (feminist lens) on The Handmaid's Tale and The Duchess of Malfi.
Apply a Marxist lens to The Great Gatsby and A Doll's House in a comparative essay (25 marks).
How should you approach the unseen prose extract in AQA A Paper 2 Section B? Give a worked method.
Apply a psychoanalytic reading to Blanche (A Streetcar Named Desire) and the Creature (Frankenstein) comparatively.
'Interpretations of A Doll's House have changed more than the play.' Discuss with reference to reception over time.

topics.title: Textual Variations and Representations
learningObjectives: Apply systematic methods from all language levels (lexis/semantics, grammar, pragmatics, discourse, phonology/prosodics, graphology) to unseen spoken, written and electronic texts (AO1).
Analyse how mode, register, genre, audience and purpose shape meanings in a text, evidencing each with a linguistic choice (AO1/AO3).
Construct precise representation claims - 'the text represents X as...' - and advance them through every paragraph (AO1/AO3).
Select relevant contextual factors (mode, era, audience, production) rather than listing context indiscriminately (AO3).
Compare two texts through integrated points of similarity and difference instead of parallel text-by-text analysis (AQA Q3 / OCR H470/01 Section C).
Meet top-band descriptors (AQA Level 5; OCR 'confident' band) within exam timing: roughly 25 minutes per AQA text question and 20 for the comparison.
keyPoints: AQA Paper 1 Section A = 70 marks: Q1 Text A 25, Q2 Text B 25, Q3 comparison 20; Section B (children's language development) = 30 marks.
OCR H470/01 = 80 marks: Language under the microscope (2 x 10), Writing about a topical language issue (24), Comparing and contrasting texts (36).
Register = field + tenor + mode (Halliday & Hasan 1976): evidence each element with a linguistic choice.
A representation statement is a thesis: every paragraph must advance it - description without representation caps the mark.
Comparison must be integrated: point of comparison, then Text A evidence, then Text B evidence, then an explicit link.
AQA pairs texts from different modes and eras (June 2023: BBC News online, 2019 + The Bystander, 1928) - mode and context are the fastest AO3 route.
topics.exampleQuestion: Analyse how Text A uses language to create meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1, June 2023, Question 01 - Text A: a BBC News online article, March 2019)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AO1 + AO3, Level 5 requirements):

AO1 - conceptualised, systematic analysis: an opening thesis naming what Text A represents and through which genre/audience/purpose; then 4-6 paragraphs organised by representational angle, each applying methods from at least two language levels - lexis/semantics (e.g. connotative or emotive lexis building a semantic field), grammar (agency, transitivity, modality, nominalisation showing who acts and who is acted upon), pragmatics (presupposition, synthetic personalisation addressing the reader as 'you'), discourse (headline/standfirst structure, foregrounding, anecdote placement) and graphology (image, typography, hyperlink placement for the scrolling online reader). Every claim must be anchored in a precise quotation with accurate terminology and fluent written expression.

AO3 - relevant, woven context: the electronic mode of a 2019 online news article (immediacy, scannable short paragraphs, hyperlinks, searchable permanence, primary plus secondary search-driven audiences); news genre conventions (inverted pyramid, attributed sources); audience and purpose shaping choice. Context must be used to explain language, not listed.

What the top band adds: perceptive interpretation of the representation (what the text makes salient and why), consistent close analysis rather than feature-spotting, and a conclusion that returns to the representation thesis. The same logic applies to Question 02 on Text B.

For Question 03 (20 marks, comparison): integrated paragraphs organised by points of similarity and difference - e.g. shared covert purpose despite different modes; bolder, shorter syntax in the online text; historical lexis and longer syntax in the 1928 magazine - with differences explicitly attributed to mode, era and audience, and comparative connectives throughout.
practiceQuestions: Giving careful consideration to the context of the text, identify and analyse patterns of lexical and semantic use in Text A. [10 marks] (OCR H470/01, Section A, Question 1(a) - June 2023 wording)
Analyse how Text B uses language to create meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1, June 2023, Question 02 - Text B: a magazine article from The Bystander, April 1928)

Explore the similarities and differences in the ways these two texts use language: Text A is a company's email newsletter to customers; Text B is a transcript of the same company's customer-service live chat. [20 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Question 03 style)
Explain how electronic mode shapes the language of online texts. Illustrate with examples from two different online genres. [10 marks] (OCR ExamBuilder-style synthesis question)
Analyse how language in this radio phone-in transcript creates meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Section A style - spoken text)

topics.title: Language Frameworks and Methods
learningObjectives: Classify word classes (open vs closed), phrase, clause and sentence types, and mood, and justify why each choice matters in an unseen text (AO1).
Apply semantic concepts - connotation, semantic fields, figurative language - to build representation claims rather than label devices (AO1/AO2).
Use Grice's maxims, speech act theory and face/politeness to explain inferred meanings and interpersonal stance (AO1/AO2).
Analyse phonemic, prosodic and graphological/multimodal features appropriate to the mode of the text (AO1/AO3).
Push every point through the chain quotation - terminology - effect - context, selecting features rather than listing them (AO1/AO3).

Evaluate frameworks critically: name the theorist, apply the concept, then judge its explanatory power for the text (AO2 - AQA 'critical understanding'; OCR 'critical understanding of concepts and issues').
keyPoints: AQA 7702 examines frameworks through Paper 1 Section A (70 marks: Q1 25, Q2 25, Q3 20) and Paper 2 Q3 (40 marks, two-text discourses analysis); OCR's most direct framework test is H470/01 Section A 'Language under the microscope' (2 x 10 marks).
AO1 (both boards) = apply appropriate methods with associated terminology and coherent expression: feature-spotting without effect caps the mark.
AO2 = critical understanding of concepts and issues: name the framework (Grice, Austin/Searle, Brown & Levinson, Halliday, Kress & van Leeuwen), apply it, then evaluate its explanatory power.

AO3 = analyse and evaluate how contextual factors and language features construct meaning: mode determines which levels matter - prosodics for speech, graphology for print and electronic, multimodality for screen texts.
Selection beats coverage: four features pushed deep through quotation, terminology, effect and context outscore twelve named and dropped.
topics.exampleQuestion: Analyse how language in Text A creates meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Question 1 or 2 style; OCR equivalent: H470/01 Section C, 36 marks). Shorter-form version: using appropriate linguistic terminology, analyse the lexis, grammar and graphology of this short charity appeal. [10 marks] (OCR H470/01 Section A, 'Language under the microscope' style)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AO1 + AO2 + AO3, per the AQA 7702/1 levels-based mark scheme; OCR rewards the same through 'appropriate linguistic concepts and methods'):

Opening: a thesis - what the text represents (e.g. the crisis as urgent but solvable; the donor as the hero) and through which genre, audience and purpose (charity appeal; sympathetic mass audience; to persuade and collect).

AO1 - systematic methods (the analysis engine): (1) Lexis/semantics: a semantic field of need ('struggling', 'crisis') set against a field of hope ('change', 'future'); connotation carrying the representation; euphemism or dysphemism framing the cause. (2) Grammar: second-person pronouns and synthetic personalisation (Fairclough, 1989); imperative calls to action ('Donate now'); modal auxiliaries ('can', 'will') building epistemic confidence; transitivity casting the donor in material processes and the beneficiary in relational ones. (3) Pragmatics: presupposition that donation is expected ('your gift will...'); flouted quantity via statistics performing authority; indirect speech acts softening the ask. (4) Graphology/multimodality: bold totals, captioned images, white space and salience directing the eye to the ask (Kress & van Leeuwen's information value and salience).

AO2 - critical understanding: frameworks named and evaluated - e.g. Grice's maxims assumed then commercially exploited; Brown & Levinson's positive politeness ('you, together with us') building solidarity before the FTA of the request.

AO3 - context woven: the promotional mode, the mass/non-specialist audience constraining jargon, and the purpose (influence, not just inform) driving every choice - woven through, never listed.

Top band: perceptive, conceptualised analysis where every claim runs quotation → terminology → effect → context, and the representation thesis is advanced in every paragraph.
practiceQuestions: Using appropriate linguistic terminology, analyse the lexis and semantics of this short advertising copy. [10 marks] (OCR H470/01 Section A, 'Language under the microscope' style)
Analyse how language in this transcript of a doctor-patient consultation creates meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1 style - spoken text)
Explore the similarities and differences in the ways that Text A and Text B use language to represent the same event. [20 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Q3 style)
Evaluate the idea that some language levels are more useful than others when analysing written texts. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A evaluation style)

Using appropriate linguistic concepts, analyse how graphological and multimodal features construct meanings in this social media post. [10 marks] (OCR H470/01 Section A, 'Language under the microscope' style)

topics.title: Language and Gender
learningObjectives: Outline and evaluate the deficit model (Jespersen; Lakoff 1975) with its criticisms of evidence and scope (AO2).
Evaluate dominance research - Zimmerman & West (1975), Fishman (1983) - including the interruption/overlap distinction and O'Barr & Atkins' (1980) 'powerless language' critique (AO2).
Assess the difference model (Tannen 1990) against diversity and dynamic approaches - Cameron (2007), Butler's (1990) performativity, Eckert & McConnell-Ginet's communities of practice (AO2).
Analyse how unseen media texts represent women and men through marked lexis, semantic derogation, agency and multimodal choices (AO1/AO3).
Deploy two or three theorists woven into an argument rather than listed, matching the AQA AO2 'evaluate the idea' essay demands (AO1/AO2).
Explain how contextual factors - era, domain (public/private), publication - shape gendered language use (AO3).
keyPoints: Lakoff (1975) 'women's language': hedges, tag questions, empty adjectives, intensifiers, superpolite forms, hypercorrect grammar, rising intonation on declaratives.
O'Barr & Atkins (1980): courtroom 'powerless language' correlates with social status, not sex - the standard AO2 critique of the deficit model.
Zimmerman & West (1975): men made almost all recorded interruptions in cross-sex conversations; Fishman (1983): women do the 'housework' of talk - topic-raising, questions, minimal responses.
Tannen (1990): report talk vs rapport talk; difference is cultural mismatch, not domination.
Cameron (2007): differences are small, within-gender variation exceeds between-gender; the difference model is a 'zombie' statistic recycled by publishers.
Butler (1990): gender is performed through repeated stylistic acts; Eckert & McConnell-Ginet: styles emerge in communities of practice.

AQA 7702/2 Section A = one 'Evaluate the idea that...' essay, 30 marks; OCR H470/02 Section B (Language in the media) = investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings, 24 marks.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the idea that a person's language use is completely determined by the social groups they belong to. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2017, Question 01)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AO1 + AO2 + AO3, 30 marks):

AO1: fluent, coherent essay with accurate terminology (hedges, tag questions, interruptions, report/rapport talk, communities of practice) and a clear argumentative line sustained from thesis to verdict.

AO2 - evaluating the idea (the core of the essay): the idea must be tested, not merely illustrated.
(1) Evidence for group influence: Lakoff's (1975) 'women's language' features as socialisation into tentativeness; Zimmerman & West's (1975) cross-sex interruption findings and Fishman's (1983) conversational 'housework' showing gendered patterns of talk; occupational and regional varieties conditioning registers.
(2) Evidence against complete determination: O'Barr & Atkins (1980) - 'powerless language' tracks status, not sex, so groups do not fix style; Cameron (2007) - within-gender variation exceeds between-gender; Hyde (2005) - gender similarities on most variables; Butler (1990) and Eckert & McConnell-Ginet - gender is performed and built in communities of practice, so speakers exceed their categories.
(3) Refined verdict: social groups shape access to registers and constrain style (deficit/dominance data are real), but 'completely determined' fails against within-group variation and contextual style-shifting - language use is conditioned, not determined.

AO3: contexts decide the case - public vs private domains (broadcast phone-ins vs Fishman's domestic data), era of research (1970s samples predate contemporary audiences), medium (interruption in face-to-face talk vs online chat), and the ideological context in which the deficit model was produced. Context woven through the evaluation, not appended.

Top-band marker: an explicit, defended verdict plus theorists used as evidence and critique (two or three, integrated), with awareness that the models themselves carry ideological baggage.
practiceQuestions: Evaluate the idea that women's language is deficient. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A style)

Using your understanding of relevant ideas and concepts, investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings in this magazine article about women in the workplace. [24 marks] (OCR H470/02, Section B - Language in the media, June 2023 wording)
Evaluate Tannen's difference model of language and gender. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A style)
Evaluate the claim that interruptions signal male dominance in conversation. [25 marks] (AQA-style AO2/AO3 essay)
Explain how semantic derogation supports the male-as-norm view of language. Illustrate with examples. [10 marks] (OCR ExamBuilder-style AO2/AO1 question)

topics.title: Language and Power and Technology
learningObjectives: Distinguish power in discourse from power behind discourse (Fairclough 1989) and instrumental from influential power, with textual evidence for each (AO1/AO2).
Apply Goffman's (1967) face and Brown & Levinson's (1987) politeness theory - positive/negative face, FTAs, mitigation strategies - to transcripts and media texts (AO1/AO3).
Analyse occupational power using Wareing (1999): vertical vs horizontal power, jargon as gatekeeping, and workplace discourse features (AO1/AO2).
Use the CDA three-dimensional method (description, interpretation, explanation) to link textual features to ideology and institutional power (AO1/AO3).
Analyse electronic language: multimodality (Kress & van Leeuwen 2006), CMC features (synchronicity, permanence, interactivity) and power online (AO1/AO3).
Deploy politeness and power concepts in directed writing for electronic and specialist audiences (AQA 7702/2 Q4; OCR H470/01 Section B) (AO1/AO2).
keyPoints: Fairclough (1989): power in discourse (visible in the encounter) vs power behind discourse (institutions setting conventions); instrumental vs influential power.
CDA method: description (text) - interpretation (discursive practice) - explanation (social practice/ideology).
Brown & Levinson (1987): positive face (approval) vs negative face (autonomy); FTAs mitigated by bald on-record, positive politeness, negative politeness, off-record, or avoidance.
Goffman (1967): face = the positive social value claimed in interaction; face-work maintains it.
Wareing (1999): vertical (hierarchical) vs horizontal (peer) occupational power; jargon gatekeeps; Koester (2004): phatic talk builds workplace solidarity.
Sinclair & Coulthard (1975): IRF/IRE - the teacher controls classroom turns and topics.
Crystal (2001): e-language as a third mode blending speech and writing; synchronous vs asynchronous CMC.
Electronic power: gatekeeping lowered (anyone can publish) but re-concentrated in platforms, algorithms and moderation; synthetic personalisation scales online.
AQA 7702/2 Section A = one 'Evaluate the idea...' essay (30); Q3 analyse discourses (40); Q4 directed writing (30). OCR H470/02 Section B Language in the media (24).
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the idea that it is an advantage to be able to switch between different varieties of language. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 01)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AO1 + AO2 + AO3, 30 marks):

AO1: fluent, coherent argument with accurate terminology (code-switching, register, instrumental/influential power, positive/negative face, jargon, CMC affordances) sustained from thesis to verdict.

AO2 - evaluating the idea: test the claim, don't illustrate it.
(1) Evidence for the advantage: switching between registers gives access to instrumental and influential power - standard English and jargon unlock institutional gatekeeping (Wareing 1999); switching politeness strategies manages face across power distances (Brown & Levinson 1987); e-language demands a further switch (synchronous chat vs asynchronous email vs formal writing). O'Barr & Atkins (1980): high-status speakers command the powerful varieties - repertoire is a resource.
(2) Complexities and counters: switching is not equally available to all - repertoire reflects education and class, so the 'advantage' is unevenly distributed (a critical-linguistics point: Fairclough 1989 - unequal access to discourse power); value judgements attach to varieties, so switching can be read as 'selling out' or as insufficiently 'authentic'; Butler's (1990) performativity reframes switching as identity work, not mere advantage.
(3) Refined verdict: switching is an advantage where power is at stake - occupational, institutional, media - but it is a resource whose distribution is socially patterned, not a free good.

AO3: contexts decide - occupational settings (jargon gatekeeping), media and electronic settings (register shifts for platform audiences), public vs private domains, and the ideological context in which some varieties are ranked as standard.

Top-band marker: an explicit, defended verdict plus theorists used as evidence and critique, with awareness that the 'advantage' framing itself carries ideological weight.
practiceQuestions: Evaluate the idea that a person's language use is completely determined by the social groups they belong to. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2017, Question 01 - occupation/power focus)
Analyse how language in this hospital consultation transcript creates meanings and representations. [25 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Section A style - unequal encounter)

Using your understanding of relevant ideas and concepts, investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings in this online news article about workplace surveillance. [24 marks] (OCR H470/02, Section B - Language in the media, June 2023 wording)
Evaluate the claim that politeness strategies always signal social power. [25 marks] (AQA-style AO2/AO3 essay)
Explain how electronic mode shapes politeness in computer-mediated communication. Illustrate with examples. [10 marks] (OCR ExamBuilder-style synthesis question)

topics.title: Child Language Acquisition
learningObjectives: Sequence the stages of spoken development - pre-verbal, holophrastic, two-word, telegraphic, post-telegraphic - and label the stage in unseen data from linguistic evidence, not from age alone (AO1).
Analyse phonological development (substitution, deletion, assimilation, cluster reduction) and link phonological processes to lexical and grammatical growth (AO1).
Categorise virtuous errors - overextension, underextension, overgeneralisation - and explain why they evidence rule formation rather than failed imitation (AO1/AO2).
Evaluate theories critically: Chomsky's LAD and its critiques, Skinner's behaviourism, Piaget's cognitive model, Vygotsky's ZPD, Bruner's LASS and Halliday's functions (AO2).
Analyse reading and writing development (emergent literacy, Kroll's phases, Britton's modes) and compare spoken and written trajectories (AO1/AO2).
Apply the data-analysis method for AQA 7702/1 Section B (30 marks, AO1 15 + AO2 15) and OCR H470/02 Section A (20 marks, AO1 10 + AO2 10) within exam timing.
keyPoints: AQA 7702/1 Section B = 30 marks: a discursive essay, choice of two questions, data may be spoken, written or multimodal (June 2024: a child transcript and children's writing).
The June 2024 mark scheme splits Section B as AO1 15 + AO2 15: half data analysis, half critical evaluation of theories and the given statement - theory description alone cannot pass.
OCR H470/02 Section A = 20 marks (AO1 10 + AO2 10): the language development stage of a child aged 0-7, analysing phonology, grammar and meaning, with the IPA provided in the paper.
Label stages from evidence - utterance length, grammatical completeness, phonological processes - never from the child's age; mixed-stage data is normal and expected.
Theories work best in evaluation pairs: nature (Chomsky) vs nurture (Skinner); cognition-first (Piaget) vs interaction-first (Vygotsky/Bruner); functions (Halliday) cut across all four.
Virtuous errors are the single strongest classroom argument: systematic, rule-governed errors absent from adult input cannot be products of imitation alone.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Adults play the most important role in children's language development.' Referring to Data Set 1 in detail, and to relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children's language development. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/1, June 2024, Question 4 - Section B)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AQA 7702/1 Section B: 30 marks = AO1 15 + AO2 15, per the June 2024 mark scheme):

AO1 - analysis of the data (15): open by identifying the stage(s) evidenced in Data Set 1 from linguistic evidence - utterance length, grammatical completeness, phonological processes - not from age alone. Then analyse systematically: phonology (substitutions, deletions, cluster reduction read against the transcription key - what the child can and cannot produce), lexis/semantics (Nelson's categories, overextension/underextension, concrete nominals dominant), grammar (negatives and questions against Bellugi's stages, missing auxiliaries and articles, overgeneralisation such as 'goed'), pragmatics (turn-taking, Halliday's functions, caregiver recasts and expansions visible in the data). Every point anchored in a precise quotation from the data set.

AO2 - critical evaluation of the view (15): evaluate the statement, don't describe it. Support: child-directed speech and scaffolding - Vygotsky's ZPD and the more knowledgeable other, Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976), Bruner's LASS - with recasts and expansions shaping development in the data. Challenge: Chomsky's LAD and the poverty of stimulus (grammar acquired from imperfect input), virtuous errors absent from adult speech ('goed', Berko & Brown's 1960 'fis'), Brown & Hanlon's (1970) finding that caregivers correct truth value rather than grammatical form, and cross-cultural evidence that acquisition proceeds on schedule where CDS is minimal. Judgement: interaction clearly matters, but it cannot explain rule formation alone - a balanced conclusion weighing both sides.

Discursive craft: both sides engaged, theories evaluated against data patterns rather than bolted on, explicit conclusion. Question 5 (the writing-development option) works identically: analyse the children's writing samples against Kroll's phases and emergent-literacy features (AO1), then evaluate the purpose-driven-writing claim against genre, audience and instruction research (AO2).
practiceQuestions: Using the appropriate terminology to explain your findings, examine the language development stage of the child-participant as evidenced in the transcript. You should identify and analyse the phonology, grammar and meaning of his utterances. Use your knowledge of theories and concepts of child language acquisition to support your answer. [20 marks] (OCR H470/02, June 2024, Question 1)

'Writing with a sense of purpose is the most important skill to develop when learning to write.' Referring to Data Set 2 in detail, and to relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children's language development. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/1, June 2024, Question 5)
'Children learn to talk through imitation.' Referring to data and relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children's language development. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Section B style)

Examine the phonological development evidenced in the transcript, using appropriate terminology, and support your answer with theories and concepts of child language acquisition. [20 marks] (OCR H470/02 Section A style)

'Children's early language is used mainly to get things they want.' Referring to data in detail, and to relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children's language development. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/1 Section B style)

topics.title: Language Change
learningObjectives: Distinguish internal change (analogy and regularisation, phonological erosion) from external change (borrowing, contact, technology) and illustrate both with dated examples (AO1/AO2).
Apply the lexis processes of change - borrowing, coinage, compounding, blending, clipping, backformation, conversion - and recognise archaisms and their discourse uses (AO1).
Analyse semantic shift through broadening, narrowing, amelioration and pejoration, with ready-made example pairs (AO2).
Trace the standardisation chronology - Caxton 1476, Johnson 1755, Lowth 1762, Alford 1864, the 1870 Education Act, the BBC and OED - and evaluate Johnson's prescriptivism in aims and practice (AO2).
Evaluate the prescriptivism vs descriptivism debate - Aitchison's models, Cameron's verbal hygiene, the Beale/Partridge prescriptive tradition - and avoid nostalgia arguments (AO2).
Analyse change data: the OCR H470/02 Section C two-text comparison (36 marks) and the AQA 7702/2 evaluative essay (30 marks, AO1 10 + AO2 20).
keyPoints: AQA 7702/2 Section A = 30 marks: a choice of two evaluative essays - language diversity or language change - marked AO1 10 + AO2 20 (June 2023 mark scheme).

OCR H470/02 Section C = 36 marks: two texts from different periods (1600s to present), analysing variations and how contextual factors construct meaning; roughly 15 minutes preparation plus 50 minutes writing.
Johnson (1755) was prescriptive in ambition - to 'fix' and 'ascertain' the language - but descriptive in practice: his Dictionary records usage with literary citations and 'offers no law'.
Aitchison's three models (damp spoon, crumbling castle, infectious disease) are straw men to dismantle, not theories to accept - each fallacy has a named counter-argument.
Every change needs a cause (internal or external), a route (S-curve diffusion, lexical diffusion, waves) and an attitude (prescriptivist or descriptivist) - structure essays around that triad.
The semantic-shift quadrants - broadening/narrowing crossed with amelioration/pejoration - supply dateable examples: 'silly', 'pretty', 'meat', 'dog', 'villain'.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the idea that language change is caused by contact between different social groups. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 2 - Section A)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic (AQA 7702/2 Section A: 30 marks = AO1 10 + AO2 20, per the June 2023 mark scheme):

AO1 - language examples with accurate methods (10): the evaluation runs on precise, dated evidence: borrowing layers (Norse 'skirt'/'shirt' and 'they/them'; Norman French 'beef'/'cow' register split; colonial 'shampoo'; global 'sushi'); coinage and word formation from contact and technology ('selfie', 'brexit'); semantic shift where contact drives meaning (amelioration and pejoration following prestige contact); etymology and word-formation terminology applied accurately throughout.

AO2 - critical understanding of concepts and issues (20): the claim must be evaluated, not described. Support: contact is the best-documented route of external change - invasion, trade and migration demonstrably reshaped English lexis (the Norman Conquest is the textbook case); substratum and prestige explanations explain which loans survive; globalisation and digital contact accelerate 21st-century borrowing. Challenge: substantial change happens without contact - internal analogy and regularisation ('holp' to 'helped', kine to cows), phonological erosion of inflections, and the Great Vowel Shift whose causes are debated and internal; other explanations - functional theory (need), S-curve diffusion (internal mechanics of spread), random fluctuation (Hockett) - cover what contact cannot. Judgement: contact is a major cause, but a partial one: internal forces and standardisation also shape change, so the claim holds for lexis more than for grammar and phonology.

Essay craft: define 'contact' and 'change' first; evaluate both sides with named linguists (Aitchison, Crystal, Hockett, Chen) and dated examples; reach an explicit judgement. The same logic answers the diversity option (Question 1): evaluate the claim about varieties with code-switching research and standard-language ideology, then judge.
practiceQuestions: By detailed analysis of the writing in both passages, discuss and illustrate variations in language between the early years of the 20th and the 21st centuries. In your answer you should explore the ways language is used in each text as well as how contextual factors influence the way meaning is constructed. [36 marks] (OCR H470/02, June 2024, Question 3)
Evaluate the idea that the English language is in decline. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A style)
Evaluate the idea that new words entering the language weaken it. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2 Section A style)

By detailed analysis of the writing in both passages, discuss and illustrate variations in language between the 17th and 21st centuries. In your answer you should explore the ways language is used in each text as well as how contextual factors influence the way meaning is constructed. [36 marks] (OCR H470/02 Section C style)
Evaluate the idea that it is an advantage to be able to switch between different varieties of language. [30 marks] (AQA 7702/2, June 2023, Question 1 - Section A diversity option)

topics.title: Language Discourses
learningObjectives: Identify language discourses - texts debating language use, change, diversity, gender and power - and connect them to the wider debates they draw on (AO2).
Analyse attitudes and perspectives: how texts represent language, construct the producer's identity and position the reader (AQA spec 4.2.3; AO1/AO3).
Deploy the discursive-device catalogue - prescriptive claims, anecdotes, appeals to authority, modality, evaluative lexis, metaphor, hyperbole - as evidence of stance (AO1/AO3).
Compare how two texts present views on a language issue, evaluating how effectively each presents its case (AQA 7702/2 Question 3, 40 marks: AO1 10 + AO3 15 + AO4 15).
Write a directed or opinion piece for a non-specialist audience: assess ideas from the texts, refer to ideas from language study, argue a view (AQA 7702/2 Question 4, 30 marks: AO2 20 + AO5 10).
Adapt to OCR's discourse tasks: Language in the media (H470/02 Section B, 24 marks: AO2 12 + AO3 12) and the topical-issue directed writing (H470/01 Section B, 24 marks).
keyPoints: AQA 7702/2 Section B: Question 3 = 40 marks (AO1 10 + AO3 15 + AO4 15) analysing how two texts present views; Question 4 = 30 marks (AO2 20 + AO5 10) - an opinion article.
