keyPoints: SDLC stages: analysis (requirements), design (data structures, interfaces, modules), implementation, testing, evaluation (AQA 4.9, OCR 1.2.4)
Waterfall: linear, fixed requirements, cheap to manage — but change is expensive and feedback comes late
Agile: iterative sprints, working software early, embraces changing requirements — needs constant customer involvement
Spiral: risk-driven iterations (risk analysis each loop); incremental: deliver in stages, each adding functionality
OOP: class = attributes + methods; encapsulation hides state, inheritance reuses (is-a), polymorphism = one call, many behaviours (OCR 1.2.6)
Compiler: whole-program translation before run — fast execution; interpreter: line-by-line at run time — immediate error reporting; assembler: assembly to machine code (OCR 1.2.3)
Testing levels: unit (one subroutine), integration (modules together), alpha (in-house), beta (real users), acceptance (customer sign-off) (OCR 1.2.4)
Test data: normal (valid), boundary (edges of valid ranges), erroneous (invalid — must be rejected); white box tests internal paths, black box tests behaviour only
Legal: Data Protection Act 2018 (data principles), Computer Misuse Act 1990 (unauthorised access), Copyright Designs & Patents Act 1988, RIPA 2000 (OCR 1.5)
topics.exampleQuestion:
A charity is commissioning a database-driven membership system. Requirements are expected to change frequently as the charity grows, and the trustees want to see working software early.
(a) Explain why an agile SDLC is more suitable than a waterfall model for this project. [6 marks]
(b) State one weakness of the agile approach and explain how the charity could mitigate it. [2 marks]
topics.modelAnswer:
(a) Agile develops the system in short iterative sprints, each delivering working software reviewed by the customer (1). This matches the scenario: requirements are expected to change frequently, and agile re-prioritises requirements each sprint so change is embraced rather than treated as a costly deviation (1). The trustees want early visibility: each sprint ends with a working increment, so they see progress within weeks rather than at a single end-of-project delivery (1). By contrast, waterfall freezes requirements in analysis and completes each stage fully before the next (1), so frequent change would force expensive rework and the charity would not see working software until the end (1). Conclusion: agile's iteration aligns with both the changing requirements and the desire for early, reviewable deliveries (1).
(b) Agile's documentation can be thinner and final cost/timeline less predictable (1). Mitigation: agree a fixed sprint budget with review gates each sprint, and maintain minimal living documentation (e.g. up-to-date requirements backlog) so knowledge is not lost between iterations (1).

topics.title: Markets: Supply and Demand
learningObjectives: Draw and shift demand and supply curves correctly, distinguishing movements along from shifts of the curve
Calculate and interpret PED, YED, XED and PES, applying each to pricing, revenue, tax incidence and business strategy
Explain the three functions of the price mechanism and the interrelationship between markets (joint, competitive, composite and derived demand)
Analyse market equilibrium, shortage and surplus, and evaluate how elasticities determine the speed of adjustment

Analyse wage determination using MRP and the monopsony model, and evaluate the effect of a National Minimum Wage
topics.exampleQuestion: A monopolist faces the demand curve P = 100 − 2Q and has constant marginal cost MC = 20 with total cost TC = 20Q + 100. Calculate the profit-maximising output, price and profit, and explain two reasons why this outcome differs from a perfectly competitive market. (AQA 7136 Paper 1 style, 15 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark logic: [AO1] state the profit-maximising condition and competitive benchmark; [AO2] calculate accurately with working; [AO3/AO4] draw out the welfare implications. Working: MR = 100 − 4Q (twice the slope of a linear demand curve). Set MR = MC: 100 − 4Q = 20, so Q = 20. Price from the demand curve: P = 100 − 2(20) = £60. ATC = TC/Q = 20 + 100/20 = £25, so profit = (P − ATC) × Q = (60 − 25) × 20 = £700. Difference 1 — allocative inefficiency: P (60) > MC (20), so society values the last unit far above its marginal cost; the competitive output is where P = MC (Q = 40 at P = 20), so the monopolist restricts output and creates a deadweight welfare loss on units between Q = 20 and Q = 40. Difference 2 — supernormal profit persists: the £700 profit survives in the long run only because barriers to entry stop rival firms entering and bidding price down to minimum AC, where only normal profit would be earned. Evaluation: the static loss is not the final word — the £700 profit could fund R&D (dynamic efficiency), and economies of scale may give the monopolist a lower AC than small competitive firms would achieve, so the observed price could be below the textbook competitive price. The welfare verdict depends on the strength of entry barriers and the use made of the profit.

topics.title: Market Failure and Government Intervention
learningObjectives: Draw and interpret externality diagrams, identifying Q1, Q*, the welfare loss and which curve shifts
Distinguish merit from demerit goods and evaluate interventions for each
Explain the free-rider problem for public and quasi-public goods and evaluate state provision
Analyse adverse selection and moral hazard, and assess signalling, screening and regulatory remedies
Evaluate Pigouvian taxes, subsidies, tradable permits, regulation and price controls using elasticity, information and cost criteria
Identify the five causes of government failure and apply them to real interventions
Construct balanced judgements weighing the size of market failure against the risk of government failure
topics.exampleQuestion: A factory pollutes a river. Marginal private cost MPC = 20 + Q, marginal external cost MEC = 5, marginal private benefit MPB = 100 − Q. Find the market output, the social optimum, the corrective tax, and explain why the market fails. (AQA 7136 Paper 1 style, 15 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark logic: [AO1] define the externality and conditions; [AO2] calculate; [AO3/AO4] explain the failure and the correction. Market equilibrium: MPC = MPB → 20 + Q = 100 − Q → 2Q = 80 → Q = 40, price P = 100 − 40 = 60. Social optimum: MSC = MSB → (20 + Q + 5) = 100 − Q → 2Q = 75 → Q = 37.5. Why the market fails: the factory's private costs exclude the £5-per-unit cost imposed on river users (fisheries, water abstracters, recreation), so MSC > MPC; output Q = 40 exceeds the optimum Q = 37.5, and over that gap MSC exceeds MSB, so each extra unit destroys surplus — a deadweight welfare loss (roughly ½ × 5 × 2.5 = £6.25 per period on these figures). Correction: a Pigouvian tax of £5 per unit (equal to MEC) shifts MPC up to MSC, raising the price to £62.50 and cutting output to 37.5 — the externality is internalised; tax revenue = 5 × 37.5 = £187.50 per period, which could fund river clean-up. Evaluation: the tax works only if the government measures MEC accurately (information gap); if polluters can relocate or the demand for the firm's output is inelastic the output cut will be smaller; monitoring emissions has administrative costs; and the alternative of regulation (an emission standard at 37.5) is certain but gives no incentive to abate further.

topics.title: Macroeconomics: AD-AS and Objectives
learningObjectives: Calculate real GDP and the GDP deflator from nominal data, and evaluate GDP as a measure of living standards
Explain the circular flow of income, injections and withdrawals, and derive the multiplier
Analyse the determinants of C, I, G and (X − M) with accurate chains of reasoning
Draw SRAS, classical LRAS and Keynesian LRAS, and shift each correctly in response to cost and demand shocks
Determine macroeconomic equilibrium and interpret negative and positive output gaps

topics.exampleQuestion: Using an AD/AS diagram, analyse the effect of a rise in world oil prices on the price level and real output, and evaluate how the outcome differs according to the shape of the long-run aggregate supply curve. (AQA 7136 Paper 2 style, 15 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark logic: [AO1] define the shock and the AD/AS framework; [AO2] show the shift with an accurate diagram description; [AO3] chain of reasoning; [AO4] evaluate using LRAS shapes and evidence. Analysis: oil is a key input (transport, energy, petrochemicals). A sharp rise raises firms' costs of production, shifting SRAS left from SRAS1 to SRAS2. With AD unchanged, the new equilibrium is at a higher price level (cost-push inflation) and lower real output — stagflation: rising inflation with falling output and rising cyclical unemployment. The size of the shift depends on the oil intensity of production and on firms' ability to substitute. Evaluation: under the classical LRAS (vertical at Yf), output returns to Yf in the long run as wages and prices adjust — the shock is temporary and self-correcting; only the price level is permanently higher. Under the Keynesian LRAS, if the economy had spare capacity the SRAS shift may be partly absorbed; if second-round effects occur (wage demands chasing higher prices, expectations de-anchoring), the shift becomes persistent and the loss larger. Evidence: the 1970s oil shocks produced persistent stagflation (UK inflation 24% in 1975), while the 2022 shock raised UK CPI to 11.1% but with unemployment only ~3.6% — expectations were better anchored by an independent central bank, so the second-round effects were weaker. Judgement: the outcome depends on the persistence of the shock, wage-price flexibility and the credibility of monetary policy.
practiceQuestions: The government increases infrastructure spending by £50 billion. The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is 0.8. Calculate the size of the multiplier and the total rise in real GDP, and explain why the actual impact may be smaller.

Using a diagram, analyse a recessionary gap and explain two ways it could be closed.

topics.title: Inflation, Unemployment and Growth
learningObjectives: Explain how CPI is constructed and evaluate its limitations as a measure of the cost of living
Analyse the costs of inflation and deflation, including redistribution, fiscal drag and uncertainty
Draw and shift AD/AS diagrams for demand-pull and cost-push inflation with full chains of reasoning
Explain the short-run Phillips curve trade-off and why the long-run curve is vertical at the natural rate
Evaluate the Phillips curve using the 1970s stagflation and the 2022–25 UK evidence
Distinguish frictional, structural, seasonal and cyclical unemployment, and explain hysteresis
Distinguish actual from potential growth and evaluate the UK productivity puzzle with data
topics.exampleQuestion: Using the data and your economic knowledge, assess the causes of the rise in UK inflation to 11.1% in October 2022, and evaluate how the trade-off between inflation and unemployment changed as inflation fell in 2023–25. (AQA 7136 Paper 2 data-response style, 25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark logic: [AO1] define demand-pull and cost-push inflation; [AO2] apply to the data with a diagram; [AO3] analyse with chains and the Phillips curve; [AO4] evaluate the trade-off with evidence and a justified judgement. [AO1/AO2] Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. The 2022 peak of 11.1% (a 41-year high) had both causes. Cost-push: Russia's invasion of Ukraine (Feb 2022) drove energy and food prices up sharply; import costs shifted SRAS left — higher price level, lower output (stagflation risk). Regulated tariffs (the energy price guarantee capped bills at £2,500 but did not remove the shock) fed directly into CPI. Demand-pull: pandemic stimulus (furlough ~£70bn, QE taking the Bank's balance sheet to £895bn, Bank Rate 0.1%) left excess demand meeting constrained supply — a positive output gap component. [AO3] The Phillips curve frame: the tight post-pandemic labour market (unemployment ~3.6%) with 11% inflation is consistent with an upward movement along (or a shift of) the SRPC; wage demands chasing prices threatened a wage-price spiral (second-round effects). [AO4] Evaluation — the trade-off in 2023–25: monetary tightening (Bank Rate to 5.25% by August 2023) and falling energy prices brought inflation back to 2% in mid-2024, but unemployment rose only slightly (~4–4.5%) — a much flatter SRPC than the 1970s (inflation 24% in 1975 with unemployment then doubling). Explanations: inflation expectations better anchored by an independent, credible central bank; weaker trade-union power; lower pass-through of costs. But the trade-off was not abolished: disinflation coincided with sluggish growth and rising unemployment from 2023, and inflation re-accelerated above 3% in 2025 on administered price rises — showing supply shocks re-shift SRAS regardless of demand policy. Judgement: the 2022 episode was a mixed cost-push/demand-pull shock; the fall in the inflation–unemployment trade-off's steepness since the 1970s reflects anchored expectations and labour-market flexibility, but supply-side shocks still force a choice between accepting inflation or sacrificing output.
practiceQuestions: Explain two limitations of the CPI as a measure of the cost of living, using examples.
Using an AD/AS diagram, analyse how a depreciation of sterling could cause inflation, and evaluate the likely size of the effect.
Explain the difference between the short-run and long-run Phillips curve, and evaluate the monetarist claim that there is no permanent trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

Using the data and your knowledge, assess whether the UK's growth record since 2022 supports the view that demand-side policy alone can deliver sustained growth.

topics.title: Policy: Fiscal, Monetary and Supply-Side
learningObjectives: Distinguish discretionary fiscal policy from automatic stabilisers and explain the current budget position and national debt
Evaluate fiscal policy using the multiplier, crowding out, time lags and the Laffer curve
Explain the five channels of the monetary transmission mechanism with full chains of reasoning
Analyse QE and QT and evaluate monetary policy at the zero lower bound and against supply-side shocks
Classify supply-side policies as market-based or interventionist and evaluate each with time lags, cost and equity
Identify conflicts between macroeconomic objectives and explain how the policy mix manages them
Construct justified judgements on policy effectiveness using credibility, elasticities and the state of the cycle
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain the transmission mechanism of a central bank interest rate rise, and evaluate its effectiveness as a means of reducing demand-pull inflation. (AQA 7136 Paper 2 style, 25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark logic: [AO1] define monetary policy and the target; [AO2] apply the transmission chain; [AO3] analyse each channel; [AO4] evaluate effectiveness with evidence and a judgement. [AO1] Monetary policy: the MPC sets Bank Rate to meet the 2% CPI target. [AO2/AO3] Transmission of a rate rise: (1) higher Bank Rate raises commercial bank funding costs and market rates; (2) consumption falls — saving returns rise, mortgage and credit repayments rise, discretionary income falls; (3) investment falls — hurdle rates for capital projects rise and credit is rationed; (4) the currency appreciates (hot-money inflows seeking higher yields), making exports dearer and imports cheaper, so (X − M) falls; (5) asset prices (housing, equities) fall, adding wealth and collateral effects; (6) credible policy anchors inflation expectations. Net: AD shifts left, dampening demand-pull inflation — the correct tool for excess demand. [AO4] Evaluation: (1) effectiveness depends on the cause of inflation — rate rises do not fix supply-side shocks (the 2022 energy shock); tightening then deepens the output fall (the stagflation conflict — Bank Rate to 5.25% deepened the 2023–24 growth slowdown); (2) time lags — 12–18 months to affect inflation, so the MPC acts on forecasts and can overshoot as the shock fades (the 2024–25 cuts from 5.25% to 4% show the reversal); (3) the zero lower bound and low confidence blunt policy in slumps (liquidity trap, 2009–16) — hence QE as the substitute; (4) distributional effects — mortgage costs hit leveraged households while asset-price gains favour the wealthy; (5) independence and credibility strengthen the effect — anchored expectations meant the 2022–24 disinflation cost less unemployment than the 1970s equivalent. Judgement: rate rises are highly effective against demand-pull inflation (the correct diagnosis matters), but their effect is delayed, distributionally uneven, and counterproductive against supply shocks — which require targeted fiscal support and supply-side measures instead.
practiceQuestions: Evaluate the view that monetary policy is more effective than fiscal policy in controlling inflation.

topics.title: International Trade and Development
learningObjectives: Calculate opportunity-cost ratios, identify comparative advantage and explain the gains from trade and the terms-of-trade window
Evaluate comparative advantage theory using its assumptions: constant costs, transport costs, mobility and dynamic advantage
Draw the tariff diagram in words, marking consumer loss, producer gain, government revenue and the two deadweight losses
Evaluate the arguments for and against protectionism with real examples (US 2025 tariffs, EU EV duties, Smoot–Hawley)
Distinguish trade creation from trade diversion and evaluate trade blocs including Brexit and the UK's CPTPP accession
Explain floating, fixed and managed exchange rate systems, the Marshall–Lerner condition and the J-curve effect
Analyse the balance of payments structure and evaluate development strategies: export-led growth vs import substitution, aid, FDI and debt relief
topics.exampleQuestion: Country A can produce 1 unit of cloth with 10 labour hours or 1 unit of wine with 5 labour hours. Country B can produce 1 unit of cloth with 6 labour hours or 1 unit of wine with 4 labour hours. Identify each country's comparative advantage and explain how both can gain from trade. (AQA 7136 Paper 3 style, 15 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark logic: [AO1] define comparative vs absolute advantage; [AO2] compute opportunity costs accurately; [AO3] explain specialisation, terms of trade and mutual gains. [AO1] Absolute advantage: B produces both goods with fewer hours (6 < 10 for cloth; 4 < 5 for wine) — but absolute advantage does not determine trade patterns. Comparative advantage rests on opportunity cost. [AO2] Opportunity costs: Country A — 1 cloth costs 2 wine (10/5); 1 wine costs 0.5 cloth. Country B — 1 cloth costs 0.67 wine (6/4); 1 wine costs 1.5 cloth. [AO3] B has the comparative advantage in cloth (0.67 < 2 wine per cloth); A has it in wine (0.5 < 1.5 cloth per wine). A should specialise in wine and export it; B specialises in cloth and exports it. Gains: at any terms of trade between 0.5 and 1.5 wine per cloth (strictly between the two opportunity-cost ratios), both countries can consume combinations beyond their own PPFs — e.g. at 1 wine = 1 cloth, both gain relative to self-sufficiency: A gives up 0.5 cloth per wine domestically but receives 1 cloth per wine by trade; B gives up 1.5 cloth per wine domestically but receives 1. Total world output rises because resources move to their lowest-opportunity-cost uses. Evaluation: the theory assumes constant costs (real PPFs are concave, so full specialisation is never optimal), ignores transport costs and exchange rates, and assumes displaced workers redeploy instantly — specialisation creates structural adjustment costs; and the terms of trade determine how the gains are split, which is why primary exporters (Prebisch–Singer) may gain little.

topics.title: Social Influence
learningObjectives: Explain and evaluate the three types of conformity and the dual-process explanations NSI and ISI (AQA 4.1.1)
Describe Asch's research and situational variables affecting conformity, with AO3 evaluation (AQA 4.1.1)
Outline Milgram's baseline obedience study and situational variables; explain agency theory and legitimacy of authority (AQA 4.1.1; Edexcel Topic 1)
Explain resistance to social influence: social support and locus of control; authoritarian personality (AQA 4.1.1)
Describe and evaluate Moscovici's minority influence research and the role of influence processes in social change (AQA 4.1.1)
Evaluate social influence research: ethics, lab methods, cultural bias, demand characteristics (OCR Component 2)
keyPoints: Conformity: compliance (public only, NSI), identification (group membership), internalisation (true belief, ISI); Asch: 75% conformed at least once, 32% on critical trials
Asch variables: group size (plateaus at 3 confederates), unanimity (dissenter drops conformity to ~5%), task difficulty (harder = more ISI)
Obedience: Milgram (1963) 65% to 450V, 40 male volunteers, Yale, prods; agency theory (agentic vs autonomous state), legitimacy of authority, gradual commitment, buffers
Situational variables in obedience: proximity (same room 40%, touch 30%), location (run-down office 47.5%), uniform (65% lab coat vs 20% ordinary clothes)
Resistance: social support (ally breaks unanimity; Gamson 88% rebelled in groups), locus of control (internals resist); authoritarian personality (Adorno F-scale; Elms & Milgram)
Minority influence: consistency, commitment (augmentation), flexibility (Nemeth); Moscovici 8.4% of trials with consistent minority; snowball effect, social cryptomnesia
Social change: Suffragettes and civil rights show minority influence; Milgram's obedience research explains why resistance is hard; NSI via social norms (Nolan et al. 2008 energy conservation)
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA 4.1.1 (16 marks): Outline and evaluate research into obedience to authority. In your answer, you should refer to Milgram's baseline study and at least one situational variable.
topics.modelAnswer: 16-mark essay structure (AO1 = 6 marks description, AO3 = 10 marks evaluation). AO1 paragraph 1 (baseline): Milgram (1963) recruited 40 male volunteers, paid $4.50, for a study of learning at Yale; participants played teacher, delivering shocks from 15V to 450V each time the learner (confederate) erred, with standardised prods ('The experiment requires that you continue'); 65% went to the full 450V, 100% to 300V; participants showed distress (trembling, sweating, three seizures). AO1 paragraph 2 (situational variables): proximity - same room as learner 40%, forcing hand onto shock plate 30%, telephone orders 2.5%; location - run-down office in Bridgeport 47.5%; uniform - ordinary clothes confederate giving orders 20% versus 65% lab coat. AO3 point 1 (demand characteristics): Orne and Holland (1968) claimed participants guessed shocks were fake; but Sheridan and King (1972) - real shocks on a puppy, 77% maximum obedience - support genuineness. AO3 point 2 (ecological validity): artificial lab, but Hofling et al. (1966) - 21/22 nurses obeyed a doctor's telephone order for an excessive dose in a real hospital - supports validity. AO3 point 3 (ethics): deception and harm (Baumrind 1964); Milgram debriefed, 84% 'glad to have taken part'. AO3 point 4 (alternative explanation): Haslam and Reicher - engaged followership/social identity theory, obedience depends on identification with scientific goals, not blind agentic state. AO3 point 5 (replication/culture): Meeus and Raaijmakers (1986, Netherlands, 92% obedience) and Burger (2009, 67.5%) support cross-cultural robustness. Conclusion: the research robustly demonstrates situational obedience, though agentic theory's mental mechanism is contested and ethics would be unacceptable today.
practiceQuestions: Distinguish between compliance, identification and internalisation as forms of conformity. (6 marks)

topics.title: Memory
learningObjectives: Describe and evaluate the multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin 1968), citing coding, capacity and duration evidence (AQA 4.1.2)
Describe and evaluate the working memory model (Baddeley-Hitch 1974): central executive, phonological loop, visuo-spatial sketchpad, episodic buffer (AQA 4.1.2)
Distinguish episodic, semantic and procedural LTM with supporting case studies (HM, Clive Wearing) (AQA 4.1.2)
Evaluate interference (proactive/retroactive) and retrieval failure as explanations of forgetting (AQA 4.1.2)
Evaluate eyewitness testimony research: misleading information and anxiety (Loftus and Palmer, weapon focus) (AQA 4.1.2; OCR Loftus and Palmer 1974)
Describe and evaluate the cognitive interview and its effectiveness (AQA 4.1.2)
keyPoints: MSM: sensory (iconic/echoic, <1s) → attention → STM (acoustic, 7±2, 18-30s) → rehearsal → LTM (semantic, unlimited); supported by primacy/recency (Glanzer and Cunitz)
Evidence for stores: Peterson and Peterson (1959) STM duration; Bahrick et al. (1975) LTM duration; Baddeley (1966) acoustic vs semantic coding; KF case challenges unitary STM
WMM: CE (attention/allocation, limited), PL (articulatory process, word-length effect), VSSP (visual/spatial, Logie), EB (added 2000, integrates); supported by dual-task studies and KF
Types of LTM: episodic (time-stamped events), semantic (facts), procedural (skills); HM and Clive Wearing: episodic impaired, procedural intact; Tulving PET: episodic right prefrontal, semantic left
Forgetting: interference (proactive old→new, retroactive new→old; McGeoch and McDonald; Baddeley and Hitch rugby players), retrieval failure (Godden and Baddeley 1975 divers; Goodwin state cues)

EWT: misleading information (Loftus and Palmer 1974 'smashed' 41mph vs 'hit' 34mph; Gabbert et al. 2003 conformity effect 71%), anxiety (weapon focus, Deffenbacher 2004 inverted-U; Christianson and Hubinette better real recall)

Cognitive interview: context reinstatement, report everything, reverse order, change perspective; Fisher et al. 1990 more correct details; Kohnken et al. 1999 meta-analysis; enhanced CI used by UK police
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA 4.1.2 (16 marks): Discuss research into the effects of misleading information on the accuracy of eyewitness testimony.
topics.modelAnswer: 16-mark essay structure (AO1 = 6 marks description, AO3 = 10 marks evaluation). AO1 paragraph 1: Loftus and Palmer (1974) - 45 students watched car-crash clips; leading verb changed speed estimates ('smashed' 41 mph vs 'contacted' 32 mph) and produced false memory of broken glass a week later, showing post-event information distorts EWT. AO1 paragraph 2: Gabbert et al. (2003) - pairs watched different versions of an event, discussed it; 71% of witnesses recalled details they could not have seen (memory conformity); Loftus and Zanni (1975) - definite vs indefinite articles ('the broken headlight') changed false recall. AO3 point 1 (ecological validity): lab clips lack real stress; Yuille and Cutshall (1986) - real shooting witnesses accurate 4-5 months later and unaffected by misleading questions. AO3 point 2 (demand characteristics): participants may guess the aim (response bias rather than memory change); Foster et al. argue participants attend more when they believe a real court case is involved. AO3 point 3 (individual differences): older adults and high-anxiety witnesses are more susceptible; Anastasi and Rhodes found younger adults more accurate. AO3 point 4 (application): police avoid leading questions; post-event discussion is recognised in court - practical impact is strong. AO3 point 5 (methodological counterpoint): lab control isolates variables (verb type) - internally valid; Gabbert used video to control exposure, replicable. Conclusion: misleading information demonstrably distorts EWT, but lab effects may overstate real-world distortion, which depends on stress, awareness and witness characteristics.
practiceQuestions: Compare the multi-store model with the working memory model of memory. (8 marks)
Explain retrieval failure as an explanation for forgetting, using research evidence. (6 marks)

topics.title: Attachment
learningObjectives: Describe caregiver-infant interactions: reciprocity, interactional synchrony; Schaffer's stages of attachment (AQA 4.1.3)
Evaluate animal studies of attachment: Lorenz (imprinting) and Harlow (wire/cloth mothers) (AQA 4.1.3)
Compare learning theory and Bowlby's evolutionary explanation of attachment, with critical period, monotropy and IWM (AQA 4.1.3)
Describe and evaluate Ainsworth's Strange Situation and attachment types A/B/C (D) (AQA 4.1.3)
Evaluate cultural variations in attachment (van IJzendoorn, Takahashi) (AQA 4.1.3)
Evaluate maternal deprivation (44 thieves), institutionalisation and Romanian orphan research (Rutter, ERA); influence on later relationships (AQA 4.1.3)
keyPoints: Interactions: reciprocity (two-way turn-taking, Brazelton 'dance'), interactional synchrony (mirrored actions/emotions, Meltzoff and Moore 1977); support bonding, hard to observe accurately

Schaffer (1964, Glasgow, 60 infants): asocial (0-6 weeks), indiscriminate (6 weeks-6 months, accepts anyone), specific (7 months+, one special attachment, separation/stranger anxiety), multiple (10-11 months+)
Animal studies: Lorenz (1935) goslings imprinted on first moving object, critical period, irreversible; Harlow (1958) rhesus monkeys preferred cloth 'contact comfort' mother over wire milk mother

Learning theory: Dollard and Miller - classical (food = UCS) + operant (feeding as primary reinforcer); Bowlby evolutionary: monotropy, critical period 0-2.5yrs, IWM, social releasers, continuity hypothesis

Ainsworth (1971, Baltimore): secure B 66%, insecure-avoidant A 22%, insecure-resistant C 12%; disorganised (D, Main and Solomon 1990); measures proximity-seeking, separation anxiety, stranger anxiety, reunion behaviour

Cultural variations: van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg (1988) meta-analysis - secure most common everywhere but variations (China/Japan more resistant, Germany more avoidant); Takahashi (1990) Japanese infants harder to test

Maternal deprivation: Bowlby 44 thieves (1944) - 86% affectionless psychopaths had prolonged early separation; institutionalisation: Rutter ERA (Romanian orphans) - disinhibited attachment, but adoption before 6 months largely reversed effects
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA 4.1.3 (16 marks): Outline and evaluate Bowlby's explanation of attachment.
topics.modelAnswer: 16-mark essay structure (AO1 = 6 marks description, AO3 = 10 marks evaluation). AO1 paragraph 1: Bowlby (1969) proposed an evolutionary explanation - attachment is innate because it aids survival; monotropy (one special attachment to the mother-figure); the critical period (6 months to 2.5 years); social releasers (crying, smiling) elicit caregiving. AO1 paragraph 2: the internal working model is a template of the first attachment shaping all later relationships; the continuity hypothesis predicts secure early attachment leads to secure later relationships. AO3 point 1 (support from animal studies): Lorenz (imprinting, critical period) and Harlow (contact comfort) support innate attachment and critical periods. AO3 point 2 (support from human research): Hazan and Shaver (1987) love quiz - early attachment predicted adult romantic styles; Bailey et al. (2007) - mothers' attachment predicted their infants' attachment. AO3 point 3 (monotropy overstated): Schaffer and Emerson - multiple attachments common and healthy; Rutter - all attachment figures matter, not just the mother. AO3 point 4 (sensitive not critical): Romanian orphan research shows late adoption can largely reverse early damage - 'critical' period is better described as sensitive. AO3 point 5 (determinism/social implications): maternal determinism pressures women to stay home; temperament (Kagan) may explain attachment quality instead. Conclusion: the evolutionary account has strong converging support but monotropy and the critical period are overstated.
practiceQuestions: Outline the Strange Situation procedure and compare secure and insecure-resistant attachment types. (8 marks)

Evaluate Romanian orphan research into institutionalisation. (8 marks)

topics.title: Psychopathology
learningObjectives: Explain and evaluate four definitions of abnormality: statistical infrequency, deviation from social norms, failure to function adequately, deviation from ideal mental health (AQA 4.1.4)
Describe phobia characteristics (behavioural, emotional, cognitive) and the two-process model; evaluate systematic desensitisation and flooding (AQA 4.1.4)
Describe depression characteristics and cognitive explanations (Beck's negative triad, Ellis's ABC) with treatments (CBT, behavioural activation, SSRIs) (AQA 4.1.4)
Describe OCD characteristics and biological explanations (COMT, SLC1A1, basal ganglia, serotonin) with treatments (ERP, SSRIs) (AQA 4.1.4)
Evaluate diagnosis and classification: DSM-5/ICD-11 reliability, validity, comorbidity, culture-bound syndromes (AQA 4.1.4)
keyPoints: Definitions: statistical (rare, IQ<70), social norms (culture-specific), failure to function (Rosenhan and Seligman), ideal mental health (Jahoda's six criteria)
Phobias: two-process model (classical acquisition, operant maintenance via avoidance), preparedness (Seligman); treatments: systematic desensitisation (hierarchy + relaxation), flooding, CBT

Depression: Beck (negative triad, schemas, distortions), Ellis (ABC model), learned helplessness (Seligman); biological: 5-HTT gene, serotonin, cortisol/HPA axis; treatments: CBT, behavioural activation, SSRIs (6-8 weeks)

OCD: obsessions (intrusive thoughts), compulsions (repetitive rituals); biological: COMT and SLC1A1 genes, basal ganglia, serotonin-dopamine circuits; cognitive: thought-action fusion, inflated responsibility; treatments: ERP, SSRIs
Classification: DSM-5 (APA, 2013), ICD-11 (WHO); reliability (inter-rater), validity (construct/predictive), comorbidity (depression + anxiety), culture-bound syndromes
Treatments compared: SD (systematic, slow, effective for specific phobias), flooding (fast, high drop-out), CBT (gold standard, cognitive + behavioural), SSRIs (cheap, side effects, symptoms only)
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA 4.1.4 (16 marks): Discuss the cognitive approach to explaining depression. Refer to Beck's negative triad and Ellis's ABC model in your answer.
topics.modelAnswer: 16-mark essay structure (AO1 = 6 marks description, AO3 = 10 marks evaluation). AO1 paragraph 1 (Beck): Beck (1967) argued depression stems from negative schemas, formed in childhood, which are activated by adverse events; schemas produce the negative cognitive triad - negative view of the self ('I am worthless'), the world ('nothing goes right') and the future ('it will never improve'); cognitive distortions (overgeneralisation, catastrophising, minimising positives) maintain the triad in a vicious cycle. AO1 paragraph 2 (Ellis): Ellis (1962) proposed the ABC model - an Activating event (failing a test) triggers irrational Beliefs ('I must succeed at everything'), producing emotional Consequences (depression); 'musturbatory' irrational beliefs cause unhealthy emotions; learned helplessness (Seligman) adds that uncontrollable negative events teach passivity. AO3 point 1 (support): Clark and Beck (2010) - depressed people show biased processing; cognitive theories underpin CBT, whose effectiveness indirectly supports the explanation. AO3 point 2 (causal direction unclear): negative thoughts may be a consequence, not a cause - reactive depression follows real loss. AO3 point 3 (biological bases): the 5-HTT gene and cortisol/HPA dysfunction show some depression is biological - cognitive account incomplete. AO3 point 4 (application): CBT derived from these models is effective (March et al. 2007 - as effective as antidepressants), supporting the theory's practical validity. AO3 point 5 (reductionism/simplicity): ABC is simplistic - ignores biology, context and individual differences; Beck's triad overlaps with Ellis's model (both may describe one phenomenon). Conclusion: cognitive explanations are well-supported and practically useful but incomplete without biological and situational factors.
practiceQuestions: Compare statistical infrequency, deviation from social norms, failure to function adequately and deviation from ideal mental health as definitions of abnormality. (8 marks)
Explain the two-process model of phobias and evaluate it. (8 marks)
Explain systematic desensitisation as a treatment for phobias and evaluate its effectiveness. (8 marks)

topics.title: Research Methods and Statistics
learningObjectives: Design experiments: lab, field, natural, quasi; operationalise IV/DV; control extraneous variables, demand characteristics and investigator effects (AQA 4.2.3)
Choose and justify experimental designs (independent measures, repeated measures, matched pairs) with counterbalancing and random allocation (AQA 4.2.3)
Describe non-experimental methods (observations, self-report, correlations, case studies) and sampling techniques (random, stratified, systematic, opportunity, volunteer) (AQA 4.2.3)
Apply BPS ethical guidelines and evaluate reliability (test-retest, inter-rater) and validity (internal, external, ecological, construct) (AQA 4.2.3)
Compute and interpret descriptive statistics, distributions and levels of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval) (AQA 4.2.3)
Conduct hypothesis testing: probability, significance, critical values, type I/II errors; choose the correct inferential test from the seven (AQA 4.2.3)
Explain features of science (falsifiability, replicability, objectivity) and the peer review process (AQA 4.2.3)
keyPoints: Experiments: lab (control, low EV), field (natural setting, less control), natural (IV occurs naturally), quasi (IV pre-existing); operationalise IV/DV; control extraneous/confounding variables

Designs: independent measures (different people per condition, no order effects but participant variables), repeated measures (same people, no participant variables but order effects - counterbalance), matched pairs (matched on key variables)

Sampling: random (unbiased, needs target population list), stratified (proportional subgroups, most representative), systematic (every nth), opportunity (convenient, biased), volunteer (self-selecting, biased but willing)
Ethics (BPS): informed consent, deception (cost-benefit + debrief), protection from harm, right to withdraw, confidentiality, privacy; presumpptive consent, retrospective consent
Descriptive stats: mean (sensitive, uses all data), median (skewed data), mode (nominal); SD (precise spread), range (crude); distributions: normal (symmetrical, bell curve), positive/negative skew
Hypothesis testing: null/alternative hypotheses, p ≤ 0.05 significance, calculated vs critical value, one-/two-tailed; type I error (false positive, lenient) vs type II (false negative, stringent)

Choosing the test: difference vs correlation/association × related/unrelated design × nominal/ordinal/interval data → chi-square, sign test, Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon, related/unrelated t, Spearman's rho, Pearson's r
Features of science: theory construction, falsifiability (Popper), replicability, objectivity, empirical methods, paradigm shifts (Kuhn); peer review checks validity before publication
topics.exampleQuestion: AQA 4.2.3 (12-mark design question): A researcher wants to investigate whether background music affects memory recall. Design an experiment to investigate this and justify your design decisions.
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic: design (8 marks) + justification (4 marks). Hypothesis (operationalised, non-directional): 'Participants will recall a different number of words from a 15-word list in a music condition compared with a silence condition.' Method: a lab experiment with a repeated measures design - the same 20 participants complete both conditions (15 words with music, 15 different words in silence), with counterbalancing (half do music first, half silence first - ABBA) to spread order effects (practice, fatigue) evenly. Random allocation to the two orders. Controls: same time of day, same room, same word lists (matched for word frequency and length), 60-second learning and 2-minute recall for both. IV: presence of background music (instrumental track vs silence); DV: number of words correctly recalled. Sampling: opportunity sample of sixth-form students (practical) - acknowledge the limitation (unrepresentative) or use random/stratified sampling for marks. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, debrief, no deception needed, protection from harm. Analysis: descriptive statistics (mean and SD for each condition); inferential test - related t-test (test of difference, related design, interval data - number of words recalled) if the data are normally distributed; otherwise Wilcoxon (ordinal). Significance at p ≤ 0.05: if the calculated value exceeds the critical value, reject the null hypothesis. Justification: repeated measures controls participant variables and needs fewer participants; counterbalancing controls order effects; the related t-test is the most powerful test for interval data, minimising type II error risk.
practiceQuestions: A researcher compares two independent groups using ordinal data. State which inferential test should be used and explain why. (4 marks)
Explain counterbalancing as a way of controlling order effects in a repeated measures design. (4 marks)

A researcher has collected ordinal data on hours of sleep and exam scores and wants to test for a relationship. Explain which test of correlation should be used and outline one limitation of correlational analysis. (6 marks)

Outline the BPS ethical guidelines a researcher must follow, and one way each issue can be dealt with. (8 marks)
