topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that the Prime Minister and Cabinet have the power to dictate events and determine policy making (AQA 7152, 25 marks) | Evaluate the extent to which the prime minister is able to dominate the cabinet (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 2, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1 (knowledge, ~40%): accurate account of PM powers — patronage, prerogative, media leadership, chairing Cabinet — and the core executive concept; two case studies matching the AQA period requirement (poll tax 1990 pre-1997; Iraq 2003 post-1997). AO2 (analysis, ~30%): factor analysis — majority size (Thatcher 1983/Blair 1997 vs May 2017), party unity (Howe 1990; the 2022 resignations), cabinet management (sofa government vs Truss's exclusion of the Treasury), events (Falklands, COVID, the 2022 markets). AO3 (evaluation, ~30%): a sustained judgement — power is contingent, not presidential: dictation succeeds with landslide majorities and unity (Thatcher, Blair, Johnson 2019) and fails against party (Truss), Parliament (May's 432–202 defeat) and courts (Miller II). Strong answers end by weighing Foley's presidentialism against Hennessy's core executive and concluding on operational variables rather than a flat 'it depends'.
practiceQuestions: Analyse the difference between individual and collective responsibility (AQA, 9 marks)
Explain and analyse three factors that affect the power of the prime minister (Edexcel, 12 marks)
Evaluate the view that the UK prime minister is now effectively a president (Edexcel, 30 marks)
Evaluate the view that prime ministerial power is determined more by circumstances than by personality (AQA, 25 marks)
Explain and analyse three ways in which Parliament can hold the prime minister to account (Edexcel, 12 marks)

topics.title: The Judiciary and Civil Liberties
learningObjectives: Describe the composition of the judiciary and the appointments process — the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, the Supreme Court (2009) and the Judicial Appointments Commission (AQA 3.1.1.4; Edexcel P2 Topic 4)
Distinguish judicial independence from judicial impartiality (neutrality) and evaluate how each is protected or threatened (AO1/AO2)
Explain the role and powers of the Supreme Court: judicial review, ultra vires, statutory interpretation under HRA ss.3 and 4 (AO1/AO2)
Evaluate the impact of Miller I (2017) and Miller II (2019) on the executive, legislature and the policy process (AO2/AO3)
Assess how far the Human Rights Act 1998 protects civil liberties, using cases such as A v SSHD (2004) and PJS v News UK (2016) (AO2/AO3)
Construct balanced judgements on the politicisation of the judiciary and on further reform, linking to the location of sovereignty (AO3)
keyPoints: Miller I (2017, 8–3): triggering Article 50 required an Act of Parliament — the prerogative cannot override statute.
Miller II (2019, 11–0): the five-week prorogation was unlawful, 'void and of no effect' — a direct check on the executive.
A v SSHD (2004, Belmarsh): detention of foreign terror suspects was incompatible with ECHR Arts 5 and 14 — a s.4 declaration that forced the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005.
Declarations of incompatibility do not strike down Acts — parliamentary sovereignty survives Miller I/II.
The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 limited quashing orders and abolished Cart judicial reviews — executive push-back against judicial power.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that the UK Supreme Court is now the most powerful branch of government (AQA 7152, 25 marks) | Evaluate the extent to which the UK judiciary is independent and impartial (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 2, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1: accurate account of composition and appointments (CRA 2005, JAC 2006, Supreme Court 2009), powers (judicial review, ultra vires, HRA s.3/s.4) and key cases — Miller I (2017), Miller II (2019), A v SSHD (2004), UNISON (2017), PJS (2016). AO2: analysis of the Court's impact on the executive and legislature (forcing the EU (Notification of Withdrawal) Act 2017; voiding prorogation; Belmarsh forcing new terror legislation) balanced against its limits (cannot strike down Acts; Sewel non-justiciable; Parliament ignored Hirst). AO3: sustained judgement — the Court is a genuine but deliberately limited check: 'most powerful branch' overstates because parliamentary sovereignty survives (s.4, Miller I) and the executive pushed back legislatively (DCPA 2022, JRCA 2022); on independence/impartiality versions, conclude that independence is institutionally robust (tenure, JAC, rulings against both parties) while impartiality concerns from elite composition are real but weakening.
practiceQuestions: Analyse the importance of ultra vires and judicial review (AQA, 9 marks)
Explain and analyse three ways in which judicial independence is protected (Edexcel, 12 marks)
Evaluate the impact of the Supreme Court on government, legislature and the policy process (AQA, 25 marks)
Evaluate the extent to which the UK judiciary is both independent and impartial (Edexcel, 30 marks)
Evaluate the view that the Human Rights Act 1998 has done more to protect civil liberties in the UK than any other constitutional reform since 1997 (Edexcel, 30 marks)

topics.title: Democracy and Participation
learningObjectives: Distinguish direct from representative democracy and assess the advantages of each with UK examples (AQA 3.1.2.1; Edexcel P1 Topic 1)
Evaluate claims that the UK suffers a participation crisis, using turnout, party membership and partisan dealignment data (AO2/AO3)
Trace the development of the franchise from the Great Reform Act (1832) to the present, with the roles of the Chartists, Suffragists and Suffragettes (AO1)
Analyse the influence of pressure groups, think tanks, lobbyists and corporations on government and Parliament (AQA 3.1.2.4; Edexcel P1 Topic 1.4)
Evaluate democratic reforms since 1997 — devolution, the HRA, referendums, Lords reform, recall — and remaining deficits (AO2/AO3)
Construct top-band judgements on franchise extension, compulsory voting and the health of UK democracy (AO3)
keyPoints: Turnout collapsed to 59.4% in 2001 but recovered to 67.3% (2019) — the participation crisis is contested, not settled.
2016 EU referendum: 72% turnout, 52–48 — the biggest act of direct democracy in UK history.
Franchise milestones: 1832 → 1867 → 1884 → 1918 → 1928 → 1969 (age 18); Chartists, Suffragists, Suffragettes drove change.
Recall of MPs Act 2015 triggered two by-elections (Onasanya and Davies, both 2019) — first successful recalls in UK history.
Other influences named in both specs: think tanks (Policy Exchange, IPPR), lobbyists (Transparency of Lobbying Act 2014), corporations (CBI) and the media.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that the UK is now suffering from a participation crisis (AQA 7152, 25 marks) | Evaluate the extent to which democracy in the UK would be improved by further reform (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1: accurate data and examples — turnout (84% in 1950, 59.4% in 2001, 72% in 2016), party membership (millions in the 1950s to under 500,000), partisan dealignment, referendums (1975, 2011, 2016, Scottish 2014), e-petitions (2019 revoke petition, 6.1m), franchise acts (1832–1969), reforms since 1997 (devolution, HRA, FOIA, Lords Act 1999, Recall Act 2015). AO2: analysis in both directions — for crisis: turnout, membership, trust post-expenses, safe seats; against: referendum turnout surges, online activism, pressure-group membership. AO3: sustained judgement — participation has migrated from parties and elections to causes and referendums rather than collapsed; 'crisis' requires a threshold the data does not uniformly meet; for reform versions, conclude reform widened participation but left institutional power (Lords, FPTP, executive dominance) largely intact.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three features of direct democracy in the UK (AQA, 9 marks)
Analyse how suffrage has changed since the Great Reform Act of 1832 (AQA, 9 marks)
Evaluate the extent to which the UK suffers from a participation crisis (Edexcel, 30 marks)
Evaluate the view that pressure groups enhance democracy in the UK (AQA, 25 marks)
Evaluate the extent to which the franchise should be extended to 16-year-olds (Edexcel, 30 marks)

topics.title: Political Parties
learningObjectives: Outline the functions performed by political parties — representation, participation, policy formulation, leadership recruitment, mobilisation and government formation — and classify the UK party system (AQA 3.1.2.3; Edexcel P1 Topic 2)
Explain how the main parties are organised and funded, and evaluate the case for and against state funding of political parties (AQA 3.1.2.3; Edexcel P1 Topic 2)
Trace the ideological and policy development of the Conservative Party from one-nation conservatism through the New Right to modernisation and beyond (Edexcel P1 Topic 2)
Trace the ideological and policy development of the Labour Party from democratic socialism through New Labour's Third Way to Corbynism and Starmerism (Edexcel P1 Topic 2)
Explain the origins, policies and influence of the Liberal Democrats and of minor parties, including the SNP, Greens, UKIP/Brexit Party and Reform UK (AO1/AO2)
Evaluate the view that the main parties have converged on the centre ground, and assess the effects of convergence and divergence on choice, mandates and the party system (AO2/AO3)
Construct balanced judgements on the emerging UK party system and on the factors that affect party success (AO3)
keyPoints: Functions of parties: representation, participation, policy formulation, leadership recruitment, electoral mobilisation, government formation and opposition.
UK party systems: two-party (1945–70s), Conservative dominance (1979–97), two-and-a-half party (1997–2010), multiparty era since 2010 (coalition, SNP surge, DUP confidence-and-supply, Reform 2024).
Funding: membership, donations, union affiliation fees (Labour), Short money and Cranborne money; PPERA 2000 governs disclosure and spending; scandals fuel the state-funding debate.
Conservative development: Tamworth Manifesto (1834) → one-nation → Thatcherism/New Right → Cameron modernisation → Johnson's levelling up → Truss → 2024 defeat.
Labour development: Clause IV (1918) → Attlee's welfare state → SDP split (1981) → New Labour Third Way → Corbynism → Starmer's fiscal rules.
Convergence narrows voter choice and weakens exclusive mandates; divergence returned over Brexit and in 2024 (tax, immigration, net zero).
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the view that the UK is moving towards a multiparty system (AQA 7152, 25 marks) | Evaluate the extent to which the policies of the Conservative and Labour parties have converged since 1997 (Edexcel 9PL0, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1: accurate account of party functions and system classification (two-party 1945–70s, Conservative dominance 1979–97, multiparty since 2010), funding rules (PPERA 2000, Short money) and party development with named leaders and policies (Thatcher's privatisation, Blair's Clause IV revision, Starmer's fiscal rules). AO2: analysis of convergence — Butskellism, New Labour's acceptance of spending plans and PFI, Cameron's NHS pledge and Big Society, Starmer's fiscal rules — against divergence — Brexit, the 2019 and 2024 manifestos, Labour's employer NI rise versus Reform's tax cuts; analysis of multiparty evidence (2010 coalition, SNP 56 seats, DUP confidence-and-supply, Reform and Green gains) against FPTP's two-party pull (Duverger's law; Labour and Conservative still forming governments). AO3: justified judgement with criteria — voter choice, mandates, representation and accountability — e.g. voting has fragmented but government formation remains two-party, so the UK is best seen as a two-party system with an emerging multiparty electorate; convergence has narrowed economic policy but cultural and constitutional issues now carry the differentiation, sustaining minor-party growth.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three functions performed by political parties in UK politics. [AQA 7152, 9 marks]
Explain and analyse three ways in which party funding creates problems for UK democracy. [Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, 12 marks]
Evaluate the extent to which the Labour Party remains a socialist party. [Edexcel 9PL0, 30 marks]
Evaluate the view that minor parties have little influence on UK politics. [Edexcel 9PL0, 30 marks]
Evaluate the extent to which the Conservative Party remains committed to one-nation conservatism. [AQA 7152, 25 marks]

topics.title: Liberalism: Classical and Modern
learningObjectives: State the six core themes of liberalism (individualism, freedom, rationalism, equality and social justice, the state, liberal democracy) and attach a named thinker to each (AQA 3.3.1; Edexcel 9PL0 core political ideas) (AO1).
Distinguish classical from modern liberalism on the meaning of freedom, the role of the state and the nature of equality, citing Locke, Mill, Rawls and Friedan (AO1/AO2).
Explain why Hobbes is quoted in liberal debates for his state-of-nature and social-contract method despite illiberal conclusions (AO2).
Analyse tensions within liberalism - negative vs positive freedom, atomistic vs developmental individualism, minimal vs enabling state - and judge how fundamental they are (AO2/AO3).
Apply liberal ideas to liberal democracy: consent, constitutionalism, toleration, rule of law (AO2).
Construct balanced essay arguments with substantiated judgements that meet AQA 25-mark extract criteria and Edexcel 30-mark essay criteria (AO3).
keyPoints: Shared ground of all liberals: humans are rational; individuals have equal moral worth; the state must rest on consent, be limited by law and protect rights.
Classical strand (Locke, Mill, Nozick): negative freedom, minimal night-watchman state, laissez-faire economics, formal equality and meritocracy.
Modern strand (Green, Rawls, Friedan): positive freedom, enabling welfare state, managed capitalism, social justice as fairness.
The central tension is the meaning of freedom and the size of the state - crystallised in Nozick vs Rawls over redistribution ('forced labour' vs the difference principle).
Friedan applies liberal individualism to gender: legal equality is empty without tackling cultural conditioning ('the problem that has no name').
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain and analyse three ways in which liberal thinkers have supported the concept of the state. [9 marks] (AQA 7152 Paper 3 style) --- AND --- To what extent do liberals agree about the role of the state? [30 marks] (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, core political ideas)
topics.modelAnswer: 9-marker: three points, each claim + thinker + analysis. (1) Locke - the state is created by consent through the social contract to protect natural rights (life, liberty, property); without it, rights are insecure in the state of nature. (2) Mill - the state is justified by the harm principle: it may restrain only other-regarding actions, leaving self-regarding liberty untouched. (3) Rawls - the enabling state is what rational individuals behind the veil of ignorance would consent to: equal basic liberties plus the difference principle. The 30-marker additionally needs: agreements (the state as a necessary evil, limited by law, resting on consent, protecting property); disagreements (minimal vs enabling state; negative vs positive freedom; Nozick's 'forced labour' claim vs Rawls' difference principle); a substantiated judgement (e.g. the strands agree the state must be consent-based and limited but diverge radically on how large it should be - or that moderns extend Locke rather than contradict him); balanced paragraphs with counter-arguments and dated key works.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three ways in which liberal thinkers have supported the idea of freedom. [9 marks]
Explain and analyse three ways in which liberal ideas have influenced liberal democracy. [9 marks]
To what extent do modern liberals differ from classical liberals? [25 marks] (AQA-style essay practice - in the real paper this is extract-based)
To what extent do liberals agree about human nature? [30 marks]
To what extent do liberals support democracy? [30 marks]

topics.title: Conservatism: Traditional and New Right
learningObjectives: State the core themes of conservatism - pragmatism, tradition, human imperfection, organic society, paternalism, property (AQA 3.3.2; Edexcel 9PL0 core political ideas) - with thinker anchors (AO1).
Distinguish traditional/One-Nation conservatism from the New Right, citing Hobbes, Burke, Oakeshott, Rand and Nozick (AO1/AO2).
Explain the two halves of the New Right (neo-liberalism and neo-conservatism) and the internal tension between them (AO2).
Analyse tensions over change, the state, society and the economy, and judge how far conservatism is a coherent ideology (AO2/AO3).
Apply conservatism in practice: Thatcherism's rolling back of the state and the One-Nation post-war consensus (AO2).
Construct balanced essay arguments with substantiated judgements that meet AQA 25-mark and Edexcel 30-mark criteria (AO3).
keyPoints: Shared ground of all conservatives: property, order, tradition broadly defined, human imperfection, and incremental reform ('change to conserve').
Traditional/One-Nation strand (Hobbes, Burke, Oakeshott): paternalism, organic society, pragmatism, acceptance of the post-war welfare settlement.
New Right combines neo-liberal economics (Rand, Nozick) with neo-conservative social policy; its society is atomistic, not organic.
Sharpest tension: organic paternalism vs atomistic self-ownership - welfare as duty vs welfare as 'forced labour'.
The New Right looks ideological, breaching Oakeshott's pragmatism - but its defenders call it pragmatism responding to the 1970s crisis.
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain and analyse three ways in which conservative thinkers have viewed human nature. [9 marks] (AQA 7152 Paper 3 style) --- AND --- To what extent do conservatives agree about the role of the state? [30 marks] (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, core political ideas)
topics.modelAnswer: 9-marker: three points, each claim + thinker + analysis. (1) Hobbes - humans are driven by fear and appetite, morally and intellectually imperfect; they need an overwhelming sovereign to escape the war of all against all. (2) Oakeshott - humans are intellectually imperfect and cannot design society from first principles; politics must be pragmatic improvisation guided by tradition. (3) Rand - humans are rational and self-interested; imperfection claims are rejected because state welfare saps self-reliance, so self-ownership demands the minimal state. The 30-marker additionally needs: agreements (order, property, tradition, incremental change, human imperfection broadly); disagreements (paternalistic vs minimal state; organic vs atomistic society; welfare as duty vs welfare as 'forced labour'; Keynesian vs monetarist economics); a substantiated judgement (e.g. the New Right is ideological and breaks with Burkean/Oakeshottian pragmatism - or is pragmatism responding to the 1970s crisis); balanced paragraphs with counter-arguments and dated key works.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three ways in which conservative thinkers have supported the idea of tradition. [9 marks]
Explain and analyse three ways in which the ideas of the New Right have influenced conservatism. [9 marks]
To what extent do conservatives agree about human nature? [30 marks]
To what extent is conservatism an ideology rather than a pragmatic disposition? [30 marks]
To what extent have conservatives supported paternalism? [30 marks]

topics.title: Socialism: Revolutionary and Democratic
learningObjectives: State the core themes of socialism - equality, social justice, common ownership, class, workers' control (AQA 3.3.3; Edexcel 9PL0 core political ideas) - with thinker anchors (AO1).
Distinguish revolutionary from democratic socialism, citing Marx, Engels, Luxemburg, Webb and Crosland (AO1/AO2).
Explain the Third Way (Giddens) and assess how far it breaks from earlier socialism (AO2).
Analyse tensions over means, ownership, equality and the role of the state, and judge how far socialism is a coherent ideology (AO2/AO3).
Apply socialism to Labour Party history: Clause IV (1918) and its revision (1995) (AO2).
Construct balanced essay arguments with substantiated judgements that meet AQA 25-mark and Edexcel 30-mark criteria (AO3).
keyPoints: Shared ground of all socialists: equality, community, cooperation, social justice, and a critique of unrestrained capitalism.
Revolutionary strand (Marx, Engels, Luxemburg): class struggle, common ownership, revolution - though Luxemburg insists revolution must be spontaneous and democratic.
Democratic strand (Webb, Crosland): gradualism via the ballot box, nationalisation then welfare, mixed economy.
Third Way (Giddens): equality of opportunity, social investment, communitarianism - it accepts the market and globalisation.
Sharpest tensions: means (revolution vs reform) and ends (common ownership vs regulated market); Clause IV 1918 vs 1995 dramatises both.
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain and analyse three ways in which socialist thinkers have viewed equality. [9 marks] (AQA 7152 Paper 3 style) --- AND --- To what extent do socialists agree about the economy? [30 marks] (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 1, core political ideas)
topics.modelAnswer: 9-marker: three points, each claim + thinker + analysis. (1) Marx - equality of outcome in communism: 'to each according to his needs'; class and exploitation abolished through common ownership. (2) Crosland - equality of opportunity and fair distribution through the welfare state and comprehensive education, not common ownership; social justice is the goal. (3) Giddens - equality of opportunity via social investment (education, skills); relative poverty matters but incentives are preserved. The 30-marker additionally needs: agreements (equality as the core value, social justice, community and cooperation, criticism of unrestrained capitalism); disagreements (common ownership vs mixed economy vs regulated market; revolution vs ballot box; outcome vs opportunity); a substantiated judgement (e.g. socialists agree on ends but divide on route and destination - or that the Third Way's acceptance of the market abandons the core); balanced paragraphs with counter-arguments and dated key works.
practiceQuestions: Explain and analyse three ways in which socialist thinkers have supported common ownership. [9 marks]
Explain and analyse three ways in which socialist thinkers have viewed class. [9 marks]
To what extent do socialists agree about the means of achieving socialism? [30 marks]
To what extent have socialists supported equality of outcome over equality of opportunity? [30 marks]
To what extent did the Third Way abandon socialism? [30 marks]

topics.title: US Politics: Comparative Politics
learningObjectives: Outline the three comparative theories - rational choice, cultural and structural - and apply each to a US/UK difference or similarity (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 3, comparative theories) (AO1/AO2).
Compare the US codified constitution and federalism with the UK's uncodified, unitary-devolved arrangement (AO1/AO2).
Compare Congress with Parliament and the presidency with the premiership, including divided government, checks and gridlock (AO2).
Compare the US Supreme Court's powers and appointment process with the UK Supreme Court, and civil rights protection in both (AO2).
Compare US and UK elections, parties and participation, including the Electoral College, primaries and campaign finance (AO2).
Write comparative essays that synthesise US and UK content and use comparative theories to reach substantiated judgements (AO3).
keyPoints: Comparative essays demand synthesis: two-way comparison plus explicit use of rational choice, cultural or structural theory - not parallel description of each system.
Constitutions: US codified and entrenched (27 amendments since 1787) vs UK uncodified and flexible; separation of powers vs parliamentary fusion.
Executive: president checks Congress (veto, appointments) but faces gridlock under divided government; PM fuses executive and legislature and usually dominates it.
Courts: US Supreme Court strikes down legislation (Marbury 1803) with politicised appointments; UK Supreme Court (2009) only declares incompatibility under HRA s.4.
Elections: fixed terms, Electoral College swing-state focus and popular-vote splits (2000, 2016) vs UK flexible dates, FPTP and referendums.
topics.exampleQuestion: To what extent is the US presidency more powerful than the UK premiership? [30 marks] (Edexcel 9PL0 Paper 3, Section B) --- AND --- Using the comparative theories, to what extent are the US and UK constitutions similar? [30 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Presidency question: AO1 - accurate comparative knowledge (formal powers: veto, appointments, Commander-in-Chief vs royal assent, patronage, collective responsibility; fixed terms; divided government). AO2 - analysis of strengths and limits: the president checks Congress but faces gridlock under divided government and reversals of executive orders; the PM fuses executive and legislature and usually dominates, but is checked by party rebellion and lost majorities. AO3 - judgement with criteria: domestically the PM is usually more powerful (fusion, majority, control of the legislative timetable); in foreign affairs the president is stronger (Commander-in-Chief, executive agreements); structural theory explains the contrast (separation vs fusion). Constitutional question: AO1 - codified vs uncodified, entrenchment, separation of powers vs fusion, federal vs unitary-devolved, entrenched Bill of Rights vs HRA. AO2 - similarities (both limit government, protect rights, establish representative democracy) and differences (rigidity vs flexibility; judicial supremacy vs parliamentary sovereignty). AO3 - judgement: more different than similar, or vice versa, with criteria and a named theory applied throughout.
practiceQuestions: To what extent are the US and UK constitutions similar? [30 marks]
To what extent is Congress more powerful than Parliament? [30 marks]
To what extent are the US Supreme Court and UK Supreme Court similar? [30 marks]
To what extent does the Electoral College undermine US democracy? [30 marks]
To what extent are rational choice theory and cultural theory useful for comparing US and UK politics? [30 marks]

topics.title: The English Legal System
learningObjectives: Describe the hierarchy of the civil courts (County Court, High Court, Court of Appeal, Supreme Court) and apply the track system (small claims, fast, intermediate, multi) to a claim scenario (AQA 3.1.1; OCR H418 Component 1; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1)
Set out the criminal court structure, including the summary/either-way/indictable classification and the magistrates' plea-before-venue and mode-of-trial procedures
Trace appeal routes in both systems, including case stated, second appeals (Access to Justice Act 1999 s.55), leapfrog appeals (Administration of Justice Act 1969) and appeals to the Supreme Court
Distinguish civil from criminal law using purpose, parties, terminology, remedies and the standards of proof (Woolmington v DPP; Miller v Minister of Pensions)
Explain the role, appointment and independence of the judiciary, citing the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, Pinochet (No 2) and Miller (No 2)
Apply the rules on jury qualification, selection, disqualification and majority verdicts (Juries Act 1974 s.17; Bushel's Case; R v Ponting), and evaluate jury equity
Compare court and non-court dispute resolution (negotiation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, tribunals, ombudsmen) and assess access to justice after LASPO 2012
keyPoints: Civil hierarchy: County Court → High Court (KBD, Chancery, Family) → Court of Appeal (Civil Division) → Supreme Court.
Criminal hierarchy: Magistrates' Court → Crown Court → Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) → Supreme Court.
Criminal standard: beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington v DPP). Civil standard: balance of probabilities (Miller v Minister of Pensions).
Magistrates deal with roughly 95% of criminal cases; juries of 12 try indictable offences in the Crown Court.
Majority verdicts: 10:1, or 9:1 if the panel has been reduced, after at least 2 hours (Juries Act 1974 s.17).
CCRC (Criminal Appeal Act 1995) refers suspected miscarriages of justice back to the Court of Appeal.
LASPO 2012 cut civil legal aid; funding now relies heavily on CFAs, ombudsmen and free advice services.
topics.exampleQuestion: Priya is suing her former landlord in the County Court for £35,000 in damages for disrepair and personal injury. Separately, her neighbour Theo is charged with unlawful wounding (either-way) after an argument in the street. (a) Explain which track Priya's claim is likely to be allocated and how it could be appealed. (b) Explain how Theo's case will proceed through the criminal courts, including appeal routes, and how the standard of proof differs between his case and Priya's. [OCR H418 Component 1 style scenario; AQA Paper 1 style — 25 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 — state the law: (a) civil hierarchy — County Court, High Court divisions, Court of Appeal (Civil Division), Supreme Court; track system under CPR 1998: small claims (under £10,000; £1,000 for PI), fast track (£10,000–£25,000), intermediate track (£25,000–£100,000, fixed recoverable costs from 2023), multi-track (complex/high value); appeal routes: next level of judge/High Court, second appeal test (Access to Justice Act 1999 s.55 — important point of principle/practice or compelling reason), leapfrog (Administration of Justice Act 1969). (b) criminal classification — summary, either-way, indictable only; plea before venue and mode of trial; magistrates' powers (6 months per offence; 12 months total); Crown Court for trial before judge and jury; appeals — defendant: s.108 MCA 1980 to Crown Court, case stated s.111 to High Court, Crown Court to CoA Crim Div if unsafe (Criminal Appeal Act 1968); prosecution: no appeal against acquittal, A-G's reference on point of law (CJA 1972 s.36), unduly lenient sentences (CJA 1988 s.36); CCRC (Criminal Appeal Act 1995); standards of proof — beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington v DPP) for the prosecution, balance of probabilities (Miller v Minister of Pensions) for Priya as claimant. AO2 — apply: Priya's claim is £35,000 including personal injury above £1,000, so small claims is excluded; £35,000 falls in the intermediate track (fixed recoverable costs), appealed to a High Court judge then CoA (Civil Division) only with permission under the s.55 second-appeal test; leapfrog only if a certified point of law arises with consent. Theo's wounding is either-way: he pleads before venue; if he pleads not guilty, magistrates decide mode of trial — likely acceptable and suitable, but given injury severity may send to Crown Court; appeal by defendant via s.108 to Crown Court or case stated to High Court (s.111), or from Crown Court to CoA Crim Div if conviction unsafe. The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington); Priya must prove her claim only on the balance of probabilities (Miller) — Theo's burden is heavier because liberty is at stake. AO3 — evaluate: tracks prioritise proportionality (Woolf aims — cost, speed, fairness); fixed recoverable costs control expense but may squeeze representation; the criminal/civil proof gap prevents inconsistent punishment but can produce apparently conflicting verdicts (O J Simpson); CCRC and relaxed double jeopardy (CJA 2003; R v Dunlop; R v Dobson) balance finality with correcting miscarriages of justice.
practiceQuestions: Distinguish civil law from criminal law. Refer to purpose, parties, standard of proof and outcomes. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]
Describe the appeal routes from a magistrates' court and from the Crown Court. [OCR H418 Component 1, 10 marks]
Explain how juries are qualified, selected and controlled, and evaluate the idea of jury equity. [WJEC/Eduqas Component 1, 15 marks]

Theo is dismissed and claims unfair dismissal. His employer wants arbitration; Theo wants to go to an employment tribunal. Explain arbitration and tribunals, then evaluate which suits Theo better. [OCR H418 Component 1, 20 marks]
Evaluate the extent to which LASPO 2012 and cuts to civil legal aid have undermined access to justice. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]

topics.title: Parliamentary Law Making and Delegated Legislation
learningObjectives: Trace the full legislative process — Green and White Papers, bill types (public, private, hybrid, private members'), all stages in both Houses, ping-pong and Royal Assent — citing the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 (AQA 3.1.2; OCR H418 Component 3, Section A; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1)
Explain the influences on parliamentary law making, including pressure groups (Snowdrop campaign), the media, public opinion and the Law Commission under the Law Commissions Act 1965
Distinguish the three types of delegated legislation — statutory instruments, byelaws and Orders in Council — with examples, and explain why Parliament delegates (AQA 3.1.3)
Apply parliamentary controls: enabling act limits, affirmative and negative resolutions (Statutory Instruments Act 1946), the Joint Select Committee on Statutory Instruments and Henry VIII clauses

Apply judicial control by ultra vires, substantive (A-G v Fulham Corporation; Strickland v Hayes BC; Cure and Deeley) and procedural (Aylesbury Mushrooms), plus the brake on prerogative power (Laker Airways; Fire Brigades Union; Ahmed v HM Treasury)
Evaluate delegated legislation against democratic deficit, sub-delegation, publicity and flexibility, using accurate case law in problem questions and 25-mark essays
keyPoints: Bill stages: First Reading (formal) → Second Reading (debate, vote) → Committee (Public Bill Committee, line by line) → Report → Third Reading → Lords → ping-pong → Royal Assent.
Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 allow a bill to pass without Lords consent after delay — used for the War Crimes Act 1991 and Hunting Act 2004.
Over 3,000 statutory instruments a year against roughly 50–60 public Acts — delegation saves parliamentary time.
Affirmative resolution: SI needs active approval; negative resolution: annulled within 40 days unless objected to (Statutory Instruments Act 1946).
JCSI scrutinises SIs on technical grounds (e.g. charging money, retrospective effect, doubtful legality).
Ultra vires has two limbs: substantive (beyond the enabling act — Fulham Corporation) and procedural (required consultation skipped — Aylesbury Mushrooms).
Courts also brake prerogative power used to defeat statute: Laker Airways; Fire Brigades Union; Ahmed v HM Treasury.
topics.exampleQuestion: The Motor Scooters Act 2023 s.3 enables the Secretary of State to make regulations 'for the safe operation of motor scooters on roads'. The Secretary of State makes the Motor Scooters Regulations 2024 banning riding on pavements and requiring crash helmets, without consulting manufacturers. Separately, Brightsea Council makes a byelaw banning all two-wheeled vehicles from the seafront. Advise the manufacturers and Brightsea riders on the validity of the regulations and the byelaw. [OCR H418 Component 3 style scenario; AQA Paper 1 style — 25 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 — state the law: delegated legislation must stay within the enabling act (ultra vires): substantive limb — beyond the words or purpose of the power (A-G v Fulham Corporation; Strickland v Hayes BC; Cure and Deeley); procedural limb — required procedures skipped (Agricultural Training Board v Aylesbury Mushrooms — consultation with representative organisations mandatory); byelaws made under LGA 1972 must be confirmed centrally and can be challenged in criminal proceedings (Boddington v British Transport Police); parliamentary control via JCSI, affirmative/negative resolutions; courts police the boundary between delegated and prerogative power (Laker Airways; Fire Brigades Union). AO2 — apply: (1) Regulations: the enabling power covers 'safe operation on roads'; the pavement ban arguably exceeds 'on roads' — substantive ultra vires in the Fulham/Strickland tradition (wider purpose than conferred); the helmet requirement is defensible as safety regulation. No consultation with manufacturers: if the Act requires consultation with representative industry bodies, Aylesbury Mushrooms makes the Regulations void for procedural ultra vires — the parallel is exact (growers excluded from Agricultural Training Board consultation). (2) Byelaw: Brightsea Council has power under LGA 1972 to make byelaws for good rule and government of its district; a blanket ban on all two-wheeled vehicles from the seafront may go beyond maintaining public order — Strickland v Hayes BC (obscene singing byelaw beyond powers) suggests over-broad byelaws are void; if not confirmed centrally it never takes effect; riders can challenge validity even if prosecuted in criminal proceedings (Boddington). AO3 — evaluate: ultra vires review gives teeth to parliamentary limits but operates only after challenges are brought; Aylesbury-type consultation protects affected interests; the democracy v flexibility tension means ministers may overreach (pavement ban) while genuine safety regulation (helmets) shows delegation working well; conclusion — both instruments are vulnerable, the regulations for substantive overreach and skipped consultation (Aylesbury; Fulham), the byelaw for disproportionate breadth (Strickland; Boddington).
practiceQuestions: Describe the stages a public bill passes through before becoming an Act of Parliament. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]
Explain the differences between statutory instruments, byelaws and Orders in Council, giving an example of each. [OCR H418 Component 3, 10 marks]
Explain how Parliament controls delegated legislation, and evaluate whether the controls are effective. [WJEC/Eduqas Component 1, 15 marks]
Explain how the courts control delegated legislation. Refer to substantive and procedural ultra vires. [OCR H418 Component 3, 10 marks]
Evaluate the argument that delegated legislation is a necessary but dangerous form of law-making. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]

topics.title: Statutory Interpretation
learningObjectives: Explain why statutes need interpretation — broad terms, drafting errors, ambiguity, new technology and changing social meanings — and name the four rules (AQA 3.1.4; OCR H418 Component 3, Section A; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1)

Apply the literal rule with authority (R v Judge of the City of London Court; Whitely v Chappell; London and North Eastern Railway v Berriman; Fisher v Bell; Partridge v Crittenden; DPP v Cheeseman) and evaluate its certainty against absurd outcomes
Apply the golden rule in its narrow and wide forms (R v Allen; Re Sigsworth; Adler v George) and contrast with the literal outcome in Inland Revenue Commissioners v Hinchy

Work through Heydon's four mischief questions (Heydon's Case) and apply them (Corkery v Carpenter; Smith v Hughes; Royal College of Nursing v DHSS), explaining how the mischief rule shades into the purposive approach

Apply the purposive approach and Pepper v Hart conditions for using Hansard, with limits (R (Spath Holm) v Secretary of State), plus the Human Rights Act 1998 s.3 interpretive duty (R v Lambert) and R v R as a creativity example

Use intrinsic aids (titles, preamble, schedules, other sections, Interpretation Act 1978), extrinsic aids (Hansard, historical setting, Law Commission reports, international conventions) and the presumptions (against retroactivity; mens rea required — Sweet v Parsley; penal provisions construed narrowly)
Evaluate the rules for certainty versus flexibility and the judicial creativity debate (Duport Steels v Sirs; Magor and St Mellons v Newport Corporation) in 25-mark essays and scenario questions
keyPoints: Literal rule: plain ordinary meaning, even if absurd (Whitely v Chappell; LNER v Berriman; Fisher v Bell; DPP v Cheeseman).
Golden rule: modify the literal meaning to avoid absurdity — narrow (R v Allen), wide (Re Sigsworth; Adler v George).
Mischief rule: Heydon's Case (1584) four questions — suppress the mischief, advance the remedy (Corkery v Carpenter; Smith v Hughes; RCN v DHSS).
Purposive approach: give effect to the Act's overall purpose (R (Quintavalle); Litster); required by EU law and HRA 1998 s.3.
Pepper v Hart (1993): Hansard admissible where ambiguous/obscure/absurd + one clear ministerial statement + it removes the ambiguity.
Presumptions: against retroactivity; mens rea required (Sweet v Parsley); penal provisions construed narrowly.
topics.exampleQuestion: The Street Offences (Amendment) Act 2024 s.2 makes it an offence for a person to 'solicit in a street or public place for the purpose of prostitution'. The Act was passed to combat kerb-crawling and street soliciting that was troubling residents. Dora solicits men from her first-floor window overlooking a street. Meanwhile, the same Act s.5 creates an offence of supplying 'a controlled drug', and Ewan holds cocaine for his friend Farid, intending to return it. Advise Dora and Ewan on their liability, referring to the rules of statutory interpretation and the cases that support them. [OCR H418 Component 3 style scenario; AQA Paper 1 style — 25 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 — state the law: literal rule — plain ordinary grammatical meaning even if absurd (R v Judge of the City of London Court; Whitely v Chappell; LNER v Berriman; Partridge v Crittenden); golden rule — modify the meaning to avoid absurdity/repugnance (narrow: R v Allen; wide: Re Sigsworth; Adler v George); mischief rule — Heydon's Case (1584) four questions: common law before, unremedied mischief, remedy appointed, true reason — then suppress the mischief and advance the remedy (Corkery v Carpenter; Smith v Hughes; RCN v DHSS); purposive approach — give effect to the Act's overall purpose (R (Quintavalle); Litster v Forth Dry Dock); aids — intrinsic (titles, other sections, Interpretation Act 1978), extrinsic (Hansard under Pepper v Hart conditions: ambiguity/obscure/absurdity + one clear ministerial statement + removes ambiguity; R (Spath Holm) limits), presumptions — mens rea required for criminal offences (Sweet v Parsley) and penal provisions construed narrowly. AO2 — apply: Dora: literal reading — she is not physically 'in a street', so no offence (the loophole Smith v Hughes closed); mischief — the Act's unremedied mischief was kerb-crawling and street solicitation troubling residents, its remedy the soliciting offence, its true reason protecting residents — so soliciting from a window is within the mischief, exactly as in Smith v Hughes (balconies and windows convicted); purposive — same result, giving effect to the Act's purpose. Advise Dora: liable under mischief/purposive interpretation. Ewan: 'supplying' — narrow literal reading in R v Maginnis meant holding drugs to return to a friend was not supplying; applying Maginnis, Ewan may not be guilty of supplying; but penal provisions are construed narrowly and mens rea is required (Sweet v Parsley), and if the court takes a purposive view of drug supply (closing the friendship loophole), liability could follow; the safer advice is that Maginnis points away from liability for mere return. AO3 — evaluate: literal certainty creates the Dora loophole Parliament must patch (Fisher v Bell pattern); mischief/purposive close it but trade certainty for judicial discretion (RCN v DHSS majority v Diplock dissent); the choice of rule decides the outcome — conclusion: Dora is liable because courts suppress the mischief (Smith v Hughes), Ewan likely not liable on the Maginnis literal line, and the contrast shows interpretation, not the words alone, determines liability.
practiceQuestions: Explain the literal rule of statutory interpretation and evaluate its use. Refer to Whitely v Chappell and London and North Eastern Railway v Berriman. [OCR H418 Component 3, 10 marks]
Explain the golden rule in its narrow and wide forms. Refer to R v Allen, Re Sigsworth and Adler v George. [OCR H418 Component 3, 10 marks]
Explain the mischief rule using Heydon's Case, and apply it to Royal College of Nursing v DHSS. [WJEC/Eduqas Component 1, 15 marks]
Explain when Hansard may be used in statutory interpretation, and outline the other intrinsic and extrinsic aids available to judges. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]
Evaluate the view that judges should not make law when interpreting statutes. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]

topics.title: Judicial Precedent
learningObjectives: Explain stare decisis and the hierarchy of the courts, and identify ratio decidendi and obiter dicta in judgments, with the reasons for law reporting (AQA 3.1.5; OCR H418 Component 3, Section A)
Explain the operation of the Practice Statement 1966 with authority — Conway v Rimmer (1968), Herrington v British Railways Board (1972), Miliangos (1976), R v Shivpuri (1986) (AO1/AO2)

State and apply the three exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane (1944), including per incuriam (Williams v Fawcett; Rickard v Rickard), and explain the Criminal Division's greater flexibility (R v Taylor; R v R) (AO1/AO2)
Distinguish overruling, reversing and distinguishing, using Balfour v Balfour and Merritt v Merritt (AO1/AO2)
Explain the sources of persuasive precedent, including Privy Council decisions — Holley (2005) and its treatment in R v James; R v Karimi (2006) (AO1/AO2)
Evaluate the doctrine: certainty against flexibility and justice, and the role of law reporting (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Hierarchy: Supreme Court binds all; Court of Appeal binds lower courts and generally itself (Young v Bristol Aeroplane 1944); High Court binds the courts below; Crown, county and magistrates' courts create no precedent.
Ratio decidendi binds; obiter dicta persuade — the neighbour principle in Donoghue v Stevenson was applied as ratio by later decisions.

Practice Statement 1966: the Supreme Court may depart from its own decisions 'when it appears right' — Conway v Rimmer (1968), Herrington (1972), Miliangos (1976), R v Shivpuri (1986, first criminal use).
Young v Bristol Aeroplane exceptions: conflicting Court of Appeal decisions; decision overruled by the Supreme Court; per incuriam (Williams v Fawcett).
Criminal Division flexibility: R v Taylor (1950), R v Gould (1968), R v Magro (2000); R v R (1991) declared the marital rape exemption obsolete.
Avoiding precedent: distinguishing (Balfour v Balfour / Merritt v Merritt); persuasive precedent includes the Privy Council — Holley (2005) treated as binding in R v James; R v Karimi (2006).
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain, using the Practice Statement 1966 and one case, how the House of Lords/Supreme Court can depart from its own previous decisions. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks] | 'The doctrine of judicial precedent strikes the right balance between certainty and flexibility.' Evaluate this statement. [OCR H418 Component 3, 20 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a top-band answer. AO1: accurate statement of the doctrine (stare decisis, ratio decidendi, obiter dicta, the hierarchy including the Supreme Court) and of the avoidance mechanisms — the Practice Statement 1966 ('departed from when it appears right to do so'), the Young v Bristol Aeroplane (1944) exceptions (conflicting decisions; overruled by a superior court; per incuriam), reversing and distinguishing. AO2: application with named authority — Conway v Rimmer (1968) overruling Duncan v Cammell Laird (1942); Herrington (1972) overruling Addie v Dumbreck (1929); Miliangos (1976); R v Shivpuri (1986) overruling Anderton v Ryan as the first criminal use; Williams v Fawcett (1986) on per incuriam; Merritt v Merritt (1976) distinguishing Balfour v Balfour (1919); Holley (2005) followed in R v James; R v Karimi (2006); R v R (1991). AO3 for the evaluation: weigh certainty (like cases alike; planning; rule of law) against flexibility (justice; outdated rules — R v R; cost of appeals); reach a justified conclusion, e.g. the balance is broadly right because the Practice Statement is used sparingly and the Young exceptions are narrow, but the system depends on judicial willingness to depart — Shivpuri and Herrington show the courts will act when a decision is plainly wrong.
practiceQuestions: Explain the exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co Ltd (1944) and evaluate their effect. Refer to Williams v Fawcett. [OCR H418 Component 3, 10 marks]
Explain, using the Practice Statement 1966, how the Supreme Court has avoided its own previous decisions. Refer to R v Shivpuri. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]
Explain the difference between overruling, reversing and distinguishing. Refer to Balfour v Balfour and Merritt v Merritt. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]
Evaluate the extent to which the Court of Appeal can avoid its own previous decisions. [OCR H418 Component 3, 20 marks]
'Persuasive precedent should be treated as binding.' Evaluate this statement. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]

topics.title: Criminal Law: Actus Reus and Mens Rea
learningObjectives: Identify and apply the actus reus of an offence, distinguishing conduct, state of affairs and consequence crimes, and the six duty situations where an omission satisfies the actus reus (R v Pittwood; R v Stone & Dobinson; R v Miller) (AQA 3.2.1; OCR H418 Component 3)

Apply the two-stage causation test — factual (but-for; R v White) and legal (operating and substantial; R v Pagett; R v Kimsey; R v Cheshire) — including the thin skull rule (R v Blaue) and the victim's own act (R v Kennedy)
State the rules of intention — direct (R v Mohan) and oblique (R v Woollin virtual-certainty direction) — and apply them to problem scenarios with the R v Matthews & Alleyne evidential gloss
Distinguish subjective recklessness (R v Cunningham; R v G and another) from negligence, and explain the limited role of negligence as mens rea (R v Adomako)
Explain the doctrine of transferred malice (R v Latimer; R v Gnango) and its limits (R v Pembliton)
Define strict liability, apply the Gammon presumptions, contrast absolute liability (R v Larsonneur) and evaluate the arguments for and against offences of strict liability
Deploy the elements, two-stage causation and mens rea ladder accurately in 25-mark AQA problem questions and 20-mark OCR/WJEC scenario questions
topics.exampleQuestion: Devon, a qualified marksman, aims a rifle at a scarecrow in his garden. He knows that the bullet will pass through the scarecrow and land in a field where his neighbour, Kai, often walks, but decides to fire anyway, betting that the field is empty. The bullet hits Kai, who dies in hospital despite negligent treatment from a junior doctor. Discuss Devon's criminal liability for the death of Kai. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 (law) + AO2 (application) + AO3 (evaluation) the answer must hit: Actus reus — murder requires the unlawful killing of a human being in being under the Queen's peace; Devon's firing is a conduct element and Kai's death the consequence element. Factual causation — the but-for test (R v White): Kai would not have died but for Devon's act. Legal causation — Devon must be a substantial and operating cause (R v Pagett) and more than a slight or trifling link (R v Kimsey); the negligent hospital treatment does not break the chain unless it is so independent of Devon's acts and in itself so potent a cause of death (R v Cheshire; R v Malcherek & Steel; contrast R v Jordan for palpably wrong treatment). Mens rea — direct intention (R v Mohan) is absent because Devon did not aim at Kai; oblique intention turns on R v Woollin: was Kai's death a virtual certainty of firing into a field and did Devon appreciate that? If yes, the jury may find intention (R v Matthews & Alleyne — foresight as evidence); if the risk was merely probable, intention is not made out and recklessness (R v Cunningham; R v G) is insufficient for murder, so liability falls to unlawful act manslaughter or a s.20 OAPA 1861 analysis. Conclusion — a definite verdict on murder (likely made out on the Woollin route if virtual certainty is found) with reasons, not 'it depends'. A* answers apply each authority to the facts in one or two sentences and evaluate the Woollin virtual-certainty standard (certainty vs probability) before concluding.
practiceQuestions: Explain the circumstances in which an omission can satisfy the actus reus of a criminal offence. Refer to at least three duty situations. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]

Nina stabs Rex in the thigh with a kitchen knife. At hospital a junior doctor fails to diagnose internal bleeding for three days; by the time surgery is performed Rex has developed pneumonia and dies. Rex had also refused an early transfusion on religious grounds. Discuss Nina's criminal liability for the death of Rex. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]

Tessa is due to give evidence against Zane, who blocks the only exit of her home knowing that firefighters have said anyone inside will 'almost certainly' die within minutes. Discuss whether Zane has the mens rea for Tessa's death. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]

'Offences of strict liability are unjust because they punish the blameless.' Evaluate this statement. Refer to Gammon, Sweet v Parsley, Harrow LBC v Shah and R v G and another. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]
Explain the significance of R v G and another (2003) for the law of recklessness. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]

topics.title: Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person
learningObjectives: Define and apply the actus reus and mens rea of assault and battery, citing the Criminal Justice Act 1988, s.39 (AQA 3.2.4; OCR 1.2.3; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1)
Set out the elements of s.47 OAPA 1861 (ABH) and apply the R v Roberts and R v Savage; R v Parmenter rules on occasioning and mens rea
Distinguish a wound from other injury (R v Eisenhower) and define grievous bodily harm for s.20 (DPP v Smith; R v Saunders; R v Bollom)
Apply the s.20 mens rea (R v Mowatt; R v Savage) and contrast it with the specific intent required for s.18 (R v Mohan; R v Woollin)
Assess the availability and limits of consent as a defence to non-fatal offences (R v Brown; R v Wilson; R v Barnes; A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980))
Evaluate the OAPA 1861 and the Law Commission (2015) reform recommendations, including the s.47/s.20 sentencing anomaly
Deploy offence ladder and case law accurately in 25-mark problem questions (AQA) and scenario questions (OCR/WJEC/Eduqas)
keyPoints: Offence ladder by maximum sentence: assault/battery (6 months, CJA 1988 s.39) < s.47 ABH (5 years) = s.20 wounding/GBH (5 years) < s.18 GBH with intent (life imprisonment)
Mens rea never rises above the base offence of assault/battery except for s.18, which requires specific intent
R v Ireland; R v Burstow: words (even silence) can be an assault, and psychiatric injury can be ABH and GBH
Wound = both layers of skin broken (R v Eisenhower); GBH = really serious harm (DPP v Smith; R v Saunders)
R v Savage; R v Parmenter fixed the mens rea of s.47 and s.20: recklessness as to some harm suffices; foreseeing GBH is never required
R v Woollin: oblique intention requires virtual certainty plus defendant's appreciation — jury may find intention
Law Commission report 361 (2015) recommended replacing the OAPA 1861 with a modern statute graded by culpability — use for AO3
topics.exampleQuestion: Sally repeatedly telephones Mike at night in silence until he suffers a recognised psychiatric illness and needs three months off work. At a party later that year, Karl shoves Joe, who stumbles into a glass table that shatters, deeply cutting his arm and severing a nerve. Discuss the criminal liability of Sally and Karl for offences against the person. (AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 — state the law: assault/battery under CJA 1988 s.39 (Ireland; Collins v Wilcock); s.47 ABH (Miller; Chan-Fook; Roberts; Savage; Parmenter); s.20 wounding/GBH (Eisenhower; DPP v Smith; Saunders; Mowatt; Burstow); s.18 GBH with intent (Mohan; Woollin). AO2 — apply: SALLY: silent calls = assault (R v Ireland; R v Burstow); repeated campaign gives well-founded fear of immediate violence (Constanza). Her depressive illness is a recognised condition = ABH (Chan-Fook; Ireland) and could be GBH if really serious; mens rea: intention or recklessness to cause apprehension (Parmenter); occasioning satisfied — no foreseeability of the harm needed (Roberts). Likely s.47 ABH; s.20 possible if illness is really serious (Burstow). KARL: shove = battery (Faulkner v Talbot); the battery factually occasioned Joe's injuries (but for the shove he would not have fallen). Shattered-table cut is a wound (both skin layers broken — Eisenhower) and deep cut with nerve damage is really serious harm (DPP v Smith; Saunders). Mens rea: recklessness as to some force/contact (Parmenter; DPP v Spratt) makes out s.20 (Mowatt — no need to foresee GBH); whether s.18 applies depends on oblique intent — severing a nerve would have to be a virtual certainty Karl appreciated (Woollin); on these facts s.20 is the better conclusion, with s.18 as an alternative considered and rejected. Consent: none arises (no consensual activity). AO3 — evaluation: s.47 and s.20 share a 5-year maximum though Karl's s.20 mens rea is arguably no worse than Sally's s.47 recklessness; the wound/GBH split (Eisenhower) is arbitrary; Law Commission 361 (2015) would grade by culpability and end the anomaly. Conclude: Sally — s.47 ABH (s.20 alternative); Karl — s.20 (s.18 not made out).
practiceQuestions: Nadia, a police officer, seizes Nadine by the wrist to escort her from a shop; when Nadine resists, Nadia twists the arm. Separately, Owen blocks a doorway and tells a frightened customer: Move, or I will move you — but only if you refuse to leave lawfully. Discuss the liability of Nadia and Owen for assault and battery. (10 marks)
The mens rea of s.47 OAPA 1861 is too low for an offence carrying five years' imprisonment. Discuss. (15 marks)
Dana throws a beer glass at Perry after a quarrel. It slips from her hand, shatters and a splinter cuts Perry's wrist deeply, requiring eight stitches. Discuss Dana's liability. (10 marks)

Tom and Ravi, both adult footballers, consent to a hard but legal challenge in a five-a-side match; Tom's tackle is outside the rules and breaks Ravi's leg. Would Tom's liability differ if the injury occurred in consensual, private fist-fighting? (15 marks)
The Offences Against the Person Act 1861 is a serious defect in the criminal law. Discuss with reference to law reform. (25 marks, AQA Paper 1 evaluation style)

topics.title: Tort: Negligence and Occupiers' Liability
learningObjectives: Apply the Caparo three-part test for a duty of care and explain the neighbour principle (Donoghue v Stevenson) (AQA 3.3.2; OCR 2.2.2; WJEC/Eduqas Component 2)
Assess duty of care for omissions and public bodies, including Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire, Hill, Michael and Poole Borough Council
Evaluate breach against the standard of care, including Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee, Bolitho, Nettleship v Weston and Mullin v Richards
Apply factual causation (but-for test; material contribution), legal causation, remoteness (The Wagon Mound (No 1); Hughes v Lord Advocate) and intervening acts
Distinguish primary and secondary victims for psychiatric injury (Page v Smith; Alcock; White) and the recoverability of pure economic loss (Murphy v Brentwood; Spring v Guardian Assurance)
State and apply the common duty of care under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 and the s.1(3) conditions of the 1984 Act for trespassers
Apply civil defences — volenti non fit injuria, contributory negligence and illegality — with Froom v Butcher, Pitts v Hunt and Revill v Newbery
Deploy the structure of a negligence problem answer in 25-mark AQA and 20-mark OCR/WJEC scenario questions
keyPoints: Duty of care: Caparo three-part test (foreseeability, proximity, fair/just/reasonable) — but Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] reasserted ordinary principles for positive acts, overruling Hill
Omissions are generally not actionable (Smith v Littlewoods; Stovin v Wise), even for public bodies (Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales; Poole Borough Council)

Breach is fact-sensitive: probability (Bolton v Stone), gravity (Paris v Stepney), precautions vs utility (Latimer v AEC); professions use Bolam with the Bolitho logical caveat; learners and children: Nettleship v Weston; Mullin v Richards

Causation: but-for (Barnett); material contribution (Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw); multiple sufficient causes (Fairchild; Barker v Corus); remoteness = foreseeable kind of harm (Wagon Mound; Hughes v Lord Advocate; Jolley v Sutton)
Psychiatric injury: primary victims (Page v Smith) vs secondary victims restricted by Alcock; rescuers must satisfy the primary victim rules (White v Chief Constable; contrast Chadwick)

Pure economic loss is irrecoverable except where the defendant assumed responsibility, e.g. negligent misstatement (Hedley Byrne; Spring v Guardian Assurance) and some solicitor cases (Ross v Caunters)
OLA 1957: visitors, common duty of care, special rules for children (s.2(3)(a)), workers (s.2(3)(b)), warnings (s.2(4)(a)) and independent contractors (s.2(4)(b))
OLA 1984: trespassers protected only where the s.1(3) conditions are met; Tomlinson and Keown show courts refusing duties where the risk arises from the claimant's own activity
Defences: volenti is complete but rarely succeeds; contributory negligence reduces damages by a percentage (Froom v Butcher); illegality may bar or reduce (Pitts v Hunt; Revill v Newbery)
topics.exampleQuestion: Ola, the occupier of a block of flats, has failed to repair a lift maintained by an independent contractor; the lift drops two floors and Priya, a lawful visitor, breaks her wrist and later suffers a recognised depressive illness. Separately, Ravi, a surveyor, carelessly values a house for a prospective buyer, Priya, who relies on the valuation and overpays by £40,000. Discuss the liability of Ola and Ravi. (AQA 7162 Paper 2 style problem question, 25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 — state the law: negligence requires duty (Donoghue v Stevenson; Caparo Industries plc v Dickman), breach (Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks) and causation (but-for; Wagon Mound (No 1)); occupiers owe the common duty of care to visitors under Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 s.2(2) and are liable for independent contractors under s.2(4)(b) (Haseldine v Daw; Ogwo v Taylor); pure economic loss is irrecoverable except on assumption of responsibility (Hedley Byrne v Heller; Spring v Guardian Assurance; Ross v Caunters). AO2 — apply: OLA: Priya is a lawful visitor; Ola is the occupier (Wheat v Lacon). The common duty of care extends to the lift: failure to repair is a breach; under s.2(4)(b) Ola is liable for the contractor's negligence (Haseldine v Daw) and for failing to check; factual causation is straightforward (but for the unrepaired lift, no fall); the wrist fracture is foreseeable; psychiatric injury: Priya is a primary victim — foreseeable physical injury suffices for the depression (Page v Smith). RAVI: pure economic loss of £40,000 is not generally recoverable (Murphy v Brentwood); but a surveyor valuing for a prospective buyer assumes responsibility — duty owed under the Hedley Byrne principle (Spring v Guardian Assurance; Ross v Caunters); breach on the facts; the buyer relied and the loss flowed directly; duty not excluded. Damages: expectation-based economic loss recoverable here; no volenti (no knowledge of the lift defect); contributory negligence not indicated. AO3 — evaluation: the special-status rules (children s.2(3)(a), workers s.2(3)(b)) show the 1957 Act calibrating duty to visitor type; the Hedley Byrne exception to Murphy v Brentwood is principled (voluntary assumption) but leaves the general bar on economic loss arbitrary; Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] shows the courts refusing blanket immunities. Conclude: Ola liable for the wrist injury and depression (1957 Act, s.2(2) and s.2(4)(b)); Ravi liable for the £40,000 under the negligent-misstatement exception.
practiceQuestions: Tom, a police officer, knocked Priya to the ground while making an arrest; separately, the force failed to send officers after Priya's 999 call reporting an intruder, and she was injured. Discuss whether a duty of care was owed in each situation. (15 marks)
Wayne, a learner driver, swerved to avoid a cat and crashed; would his liability differ if he were a qualified doctor driving home after a 24-hour shift? Discuss breach. (15 marks)
Fairchild Ltd exposed three workers to asbestos; each developed mesothelioma. Priya inhaled dust from a single source. Explain how causation operates for each worker. (10 marks)

Ravi watches television as a live news report shows his brother crushed at a football ground; he suffers a recognised psychiatric illness. Would his position differ had he stood two rows away? Discuss. (15 marks)
A council left a boating lake open with no lifeguard; Priya, 19, dived in after drinking and was paralysed. Discuss the council's liability under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984. (15 marks)
Pure economic loss should be recoverable in negligence like any other loss. Discuss. (25 marks, AQA Paper 2 evaluation style)

topics.title: Defences
learningObjectives: State and apply the M'Naghten rules (defect of reason, disease of the mind, not knowing the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong) and the special verdict disposal options (AQA 3.2.5; OCR H418 Component 3)
Distinguish sane from insane automatism using the internal/external cause test (R v Quick; R v Hennessy; R v Burgess) and apply the rules on self-induced automatism (R v Bailey; R v Hardie)

Apply the Majewski distinction — why voluntary intoxication is no defence to crimes of basic intent but may negative intention for specific intent crimes (R v Sheehan & Moore; R v O'Grady; R v Heard) — and the rules on involuntary intoxication (R v Kingston)
State and apply the mistake rules — honest belief negating mens rea (DPP v Morgan; R v Williams) and the honest AND reasonable requirement under the Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.5(2)(a)

Apply the two-stage duress test (R v Graham), the relevant-characteristics limits (R v Bowen) and R v Hasan's foreseeability restrictions, and explain why duress is never available for murder (R v Howe; R v Gotts)

Apply self-defence and prevention of crime under the common law and Criminal Law Act 1967, s.3 as codified by the CJI Act 2008, s.76 — necessity, reasonableness (R v Owino) and householder force (Crime and Courts Act 2013)

Apply the loss of control qualifying triggers (CJA 2009, s.55; R v Clinton; R v Dawes; R v Asmelash) and diminished responsibility elements (Homicide Act 1957, s.2 as amended; R v Golds; R v Dowds; R v Dietschmann) as partial defences to murder (AQA 3.2.2)
topics.exampleQuestion: Dev, 34, suffers a recognised depressive disorder. His wife tells him she has been sleeping with his brother and is leaving with the children. Dev, who has been drinking heavily all evening, strangles her to death. Advise Dev on any defences to a charge of murder. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: The answer must hit: Murder made out — AR (unlawful killing) and MR (intention to kill or cause GBH) are present, so move to full and partial defences. Loss of control (CJA 2009, s.54): loss of self-control is arguable (strangling after the revelation); qualifying trigger — the wife's words: were they of an extremely grave character and did they give Dev a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged (s.55(4))? Note sexual infidelity is expressly excluded (s.55(6)(c)) but per R v Clinton infidelity can be background context to other grave words; the revelation that she is leaving with the children may supply the grave element. Voluntary intoxication is disregarded when deciding trigger and loss of control (R v Asmelash). Objective test (s.54(1)(c)): a person of Dev's sex and age with normal tolerance in the same circumstances — argue both ways (R v Jewell). Diminished responsibility (Homicide Act 1957, s.2 as amended by CJA 2009, s.52): depressive disorder is a recognised medical condition; it must substantially impair his ability to form a rational judgment (most apt here) — 'substantially' means more than trivially (R v Golds); the drink alone cannot found the plea (R v Dowds) but does not defeat it where the condition remains a substantial cause (R v Dietschmann). Conclusion: if the trigger is made out and the objective test satisfied, or the depressive disorder substantially impaired him, murder reduces to voluntary manslaughter; otherwise murder stands. A* answers sequence the defences (full defences first — insanity/automatism are implausible on the facts), apply s.54/s.52 element by element, and weigh the Clinton/Asmelash/Golds authorities before concluding.
practiceQuestions: Explain the distinction between insanity and automatism, referring to the internal/external cause approach. Refer to R v Quick, R v Hennessy and R v Burgess. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]

Terri becomes paranoid after smoking cannabis, believing her flatmate Ivan is stealing from her, and hits him with a lamp, breaking his arm. She later takes a Valium tablet prescribed for a friend before driving and crashes into a wall, damaging it. Advise Terri on her liability for s.20 and on any defences. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]
'Duress should be a full defence to murder.' Evaluate this statement. Refer to R v Howe, R v Gotts and R v Hasan. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]

Perry, an elderly householder, hears a window break at night and, believing an intruder is entering, hits him with a cricket bat, breaking his arm. The intruder was a drunk neighbour who had mistaken the house. Advise Perry on self-defence. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]

Callum's girlfriend taunts him about his sexual dysfunction in front of his friends, saying he is 'less than a man'; Callum, devastated, punches her, causing grievous bodily harm. Advise Callum on loss of control. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]
Explain the exceptions to the rule that consent is no defence to a charge of actual bodily harm, and evaluate the decision in R v Brown. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]

topics.title: Remedies and Sentencing
learningObjectives: Distinguish the types of damages — general, special, aggravated, exemplary and nominal — and apply them to claim scenarios (AQA 3.1.1; OCR H418 Component 1; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1)
Explain injunctions (prohibitory and mandatory; interim and final) and the contempt sanction, including the American Cyanamid test for interim injunctions
Explain when specific performance and rescission are available, including the bars to rescission (affirmation, lapse of time, restitutio in integrum, third-party rights)
State the five purposes of sentencing under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, s.142 and explain how judges weigh competing aims, including the welfare principle for under-18s (CYPA 1933, s.44)
Explain how the minimum term (tariff) is set for murder — the mandatory life sentence, Schedule 21 CJA 2003 starting points and whole life orders — and the role of the Sentencing Council
Apply statutory and guideline aggravating and mitigating factors, including the reduction for a guilty plea (Sentencing Act 2020, s.73) and aggravation for hostility (CJA 2003, ss.145-146)
Distinguish custodial, community, fine and discharge sentences — their thresholds, limits and relative effectiveness — and evaluate the aims of sentencing in problem and essay answers
topics.exampleQuestion: Holli was seriously injured when Kane drove carelessly through a red light. Kane has been convicted. (a) Advise Holli on the types of damages she may claim. (b) Kane has two previous convictions for driving while disqualified, committed this offence while on bail, and pleaded guilty only on the day of trial; he also suffers severe depression and cares for his elderly mother. Explain the sentence the judge may impose, including the aggravating and mitigating factors. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: The answer must hit: (a) Damages (AO1/AO2) — compensatory principle (Livingstone v Rawyards Coal Co); special damages — pecuniary losses provable to trial (lost earnings, medical expenses); general damages — pain, suffering and loss of amenity assessed by the judge; aggravated damages only if Kane's conduct was injurious or humiliating (unlikely for careless driving — note this); exemplary damages are unavailable — Rookes v Barnard categories not engaged. (b) Sentencing (AO1/AO2) — purposes under CJA 2003, s.142: punishment, reduction of crime (deterrence), reform and rehabilitation, protection of the public, reparation. Aggravating — two previous convictions for similar offences (s.143(2)); offence committed while on bail (s.143(2)); culpability (careless driving through a red light) and harm (serious injury) under s.143. Mitigating — guilty plea only at trial (reduction minimal under Sentencing Act 2020, s.73 — up to one-third at first opportunity, less here); severe depression (mental illness); caring responsibilities. Sentence — apply the custodial threshold (Sentencing Act 2020, s.230): the offending is serious but the strong mitigation may justify a suspended sentence or a community order with requirements (unpaid work, supervision, mental health treatment); custody with extended licence if the risk of harm justifies it. AO3 — weigh the aims: previous convictions and bail point to protection and retribution; depression and care responsibilities point to rehabilitation; conclude with a reasoned, definite sentence recommendation. A* answers apply each statutory section to the facts in one sentence and state the likely outcome, not 'it depends'.
practiceQuestions: Explain the different types of damages available in the civil courts. Refer to Rookes v Barnard. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]
Explain when the courts will grant specific performance and rescission, and state the bars to rescission. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]

A factory's fumes drift into Priya's garden and damage her plants; the factory refuses to change its filters. Advise Priya on the remedies available, including an injunction. [OCR H418 Component 1 style scenario, 20 marks]
'Prison does not work.' Evaluate this statement with reference to the aims of sentencing and to community orders. [AQA Paper 1, 25 marks]

Dev, 19, of previous good character, pleads guilty at the first opportunity to a single assault occasioning actual bodily harm on an emergency worker, committed while drunk and distressed after a family bereavement. Advise the court on the likely sentence, applying the aggravating and mitigating factors. [AQA 7162 Paper 1 style problem question, 25 marks]
Explain how judges set the minimum term for murder and when a whole life order may be imposed. [AQA Paper 1, 10 marks]

topics.title: Contract and Human Rights
learningObjectives: Distinguish offers from invitations to treat and apply the termination rules - revocation, rejection, counter-offer, lapse - to a scenario, citing Partridge v Crittenden, Fisher v Bell, Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball and Hyde v Wrench (AQA 3.4.1; OCR H418 Component 3, contract option)

Apply the postal rule in Adams v Lindsell and its exceptions - wrongly addressed letters (Household Fire v Grant), post not reasonable or excluded by the offeror (Holwell Securities v Hughes), instantaneous communications (Entores; Brinkibon)

Apply the rules of consideration - sufficiency not adequacy (Chappell v Nestle), past consideration (Re McArdle), existing duty (Stilk v Myrick; Williams v Roffey), part payment of debt (Foakes v Beer; Pinnel's Case) and promissory estoppel (High Trees; Combe v Combe)

Apply the presumptions on intention to create legal relations and their rebuttal (Balfour v Balfour; Merritt v Merritt), and the privity rule with the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, s.1 (Dunlop v Selfridge; Prudential Assurance v Ayers)

Explain how ECHR Articles 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10 and 11 are protected through the HRA 1998 - s.3 interpretation (R v Lambert; Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza), s.4 declarations of incompatibility (A v SSHD, Belmarsh), s.6 public authorities

Apply PACE 1984 police powers - s.1 stop and search, s.24 arrest, detention limits under ss.41-44 and the safeguards (Fox, Campbell and Hartley) - and evaluate the balance between individual rights and effective law enforcement
topics.exampleQuestion: Jai posts a letter to Kim on 1 March offering to sell her his motorbike for £3,000, adding that the offer will remain open until 10 March. On 3 March Kim posts a letter accepting the offer. On 4 March Jai posts a letter revoking the offer, which arrives on 5 March, one hour after Kim's acceptance. The written contract of sale includes a clause stating that Lila, Kim's sister, may borrow the motorbike at weekends. Jai now refuses to sell, arguing first that the motorbike is really worth £4,500, and secondly that Lila has no rights under the contract because she was never a party to it. Discuss. [AQA Paper 3, 25 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: The answer must hit: (1) Formation by post (AO1/AO2) - state the postal rule (Adams v Lindsell (1818)): Kim's acceptance took effect on posting on 3 March, so the contract was formed before Jai's revocation was even posted; revocation arriving on 5 March is ineffective (Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880) - revocation must be communicated before acceptance). (2) The promise to keep the offer open (AO1/AO2) - although Jai promised to keep the offer open until 10 March, Kim gave no consideration for that promise, so it is not an enforceable option and the offer was in principle revocable (Routledge v Grant (1828)) - but here revocation came too late. (3) Adequacy of consideration (AO1/AO2) - Jai's argument that the bike is worth £4,500 fails: consideration need not be adequate, only sufficient (Chappell v Nestle (1960); Currie v Misa (1875)) - £3,000 is plainly sufficient. (4) Intention (AO1/AO2) - this is a commercial transaction for the sale of goods, so legal intention is presumed (Balfour v Balfour presumption does not apply). (5) Lila's position (AO1/AO2/AO3) - at common law Lila has no rights: only parties may sue (Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co v Selfridge (1915); Tweddle v Atkinson (1861)). But under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, s.1(1)(b) the clause purports to confer a benefit on Lila, who is expressly identified by name (s.1(3)); she may enforce it with the same remedies as a party (s.1(4)), and Jai and Kim cannot vary or rescind so as to remove her entitlement once she has relied or assented (s.2). Contrast Prudential Assurance v Ayers (2007) - third parties can rely on benefit clauses even when unnamed. (6) Conclusion (AO3) - Kim can enforce the sale (contract formed 3 March); Jai's arguments fail; Lila may enforce the weekend borrowing clause under s.1(1)(b), though she could not sue on the price terms of the contract. Stronger answers evaluate whether reform of privity has gone too far or strikes the right balance.
practiceQuestions: Explain, with reference to Partridge v Crittenden, Fisher v Bell and Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co, when an advertisement is an offer rather than an invitation to treat. [AQA Paper 3, 12 marks]
