Ravi posts a letter of acceptance of Ben's offer to sell his car for £4,000, correctly addressed and stamped. The letter is lost in the post and never arrives. Ben, hearing nothing, sells the car to Chandra for £4,500. Advise Ravi. [OCR H418 Component 3, 20 marks]

Theo promises his builders a £1,000 bonus to finish an extension on time, although the contract already required on-time completion, which they then do; Theo refuses to pay. Separately, Theo owes Uma £10,000; Uma agrees in writing to accept £6,000 in full settlement, which Theo pays; Uma now sues for the £4,000 balance. Advise the builders and Uma. [AQA Paper 3, 25 marks]

Explain and evaluate how the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 has reformed the common law rule in Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co v Selfridge. Refer to Prudential Assurance Co Ltd v Ayers. [AQA Paper 3, 15 marks]

Police officers stop and search Sadiq in a public street under PACE 1984, s.1 on reasonable suspicion that he is carrying a bladed article; nothing is found. He is then arrested under s.24 on suspicion of theft and detained for 40 hours before release without charge. He never asked for a solicitor and the custody officer did not tell him of the right. Discuss whether the police acted lawfully and whether Sadiq has any remedy. [OCR H418 Component 3, 20 marks]

topics.title: The Tudors: 1485-1603
learningObjectives: Explain Henry VII's consolidation: legitimacy, the Yorkist marriage, pretenders, financial control (AO1)
Analyse the break with Rome and the roles of Wolsey, Cromwell and parliament (AO1/AO2)
Assess the mid-Tudor crisis: Edwardian radicalism, Marian restoration, rebellion (AO2)
Evaluate the Elizabethan settlement and the Puritan, Catholic and Spanish threats (AO1/AO2)
Deploy historiography (Elton, Duffy, Neale, Ives, Loades) as sustained argument (AO2)
Construct 30-mark causation essays and source analyses via nature, origin, purpose (AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'The dissolution of the monasteries was the main reason for the Pilgrimage of Grace of 1536.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: 30-mark causation logic: sustained argument with supported judgement, not narrative. FOR the dissolution: the direct trigger - Lincolnshire rising within weeks of commissioners arriving (1536); the 1536 Act closing smaller houses; pilgrims' fear that parish property would follow (Pontefract Articles opened with monasteries). OTHER causes to weigh: economic - bad harvests 1535-36, the 1534 subsidy, the Amicable Grant's memory, the Statute of Uses hitting gentry conveyancing; political-religious - the Treasons Act (1534) and the Pontefract demand to punish Cromwell and Cranmer as 'heretics'; coordination - gentry leadership (Aske, Darcy, Hussey) turning local riots into a 'pilgrimage'. Judgement: dissolution was the necessary trigger uniting commons and gentry, but the rising was multi-causal - A* needs a hierarchy showing the Act politicised economic and religious resentment. Source questions (Edexcel/AQA): judge utility by NATURE (royal letter, pilgrim oath, proclamation), ORIGIN (author's position - Norfolk minimises grievances, Aske justifies the pilgrimage) and PURPOSE (persuade, justify, inform), then test against context and corroboration; a partial source can still be highly useful for attitudes.
practiceQuestions: 'Henry VII's marriage to Elizabeth of York was the most important reason for the security of his rule by 1509.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
'Cromwell, not Henry VIII, was the driving force behind the English Reformation.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
How useful are a royal letter from Norfolk and a pilgrim's oath to a historian studying the causes of the Pilgrimage of Grace? [20 marks]
'The Marian burnings strengthened rather than weakened Catholicism in England.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
'Religion was the main cause of the Spanish Armada.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]

topics.title: Russia: Tsardom to Communism, 1917-1991
learningObjectives: Explain the collapse of Tsardom: autocracy's rigidity, the 1905 Revolution and the role of the First World War
Analyse the causes and character of the February and October 1917 revolutions, including dual power and the Bolshevik seizure
Evaluate Lenin's and Stalin's state-building: War Communism, NEP, the Cheka, the Five-Year Plans, collectivisation and the Terror
Assess how far destalinisation under Khrushchev and the stagnation under Brezhnev changed the Stalinist system
Weigh the causes of the USSR's collapse in 1991: Gorbachev's reforms, economic failure and nationalism
Deploy the interpretations of Figes, Service, Pipes, Conquest, Getty, Brown and Kotkin as frames for 30-mark argument
topics.exampleQuestion: To what extent were Gorbachev's reforms the main cause of the collapse of the USSR in 1991? Explain your answer. (30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Level 5 (25-30): a sustained, analytically structured argument with a substantiated judgement, a wide range of accurate AO1 detail and factors weighed against each other throughout. Required AO1 knowledge: uskoreniye and its failure; glasnost (press freedom, Chernobyl 1986, historical reappraisal) destroying ideological legitimacy; perestroika (1987 State Enterprise Law, 1988 Cooperatives Law) worsening shortages; political liberalisation (1988 constitutional reforms, semi-contested 1989 elections) ending the party monopoly in practice; the 'Sinatra Doctrine' and loss of Eastern Europe; nationalist surge (Baltic sovereignty, Nagorno-Karabakh 1988, Yeltsin's Russia); the failed August 1991 GKChP coup; the Belovezha Accords and dissolution (25-26 December 1991); background structural decline under Brezhnev (stagnation, oil dependence, Afghanistan). Argument FOR Gorbachev as main cause: no systemic crisis was irreversible in 1985; glasnost converted private doubt into open opposition; political liberalisation dismantled the coercive and ideological instruments that had preserved the Union in 1956 and 1968; the coup his reforms provoked finished the party. Argument AGAINST: terminal economic stagnation and imperial overstretch predated him; nationalism was organic and long-suppressed; the coup itself came from reform's opponents, showing the system was already divided. Historians to deploy: Service (reforms necessary yet destabilising), Archie Brown (the 'Gorbachev factor' — without his choices collapse was not inevitable), Pipes and the structural school (economic failure decisive), Kotkin (elite defection). Judgement: Gorbachev's reforms were the proximate cause — structural decay created the possibility, but his sequencing (openness before markets, politicisation before economics) made collapse happen in 1991. Answers that list events without weighing causes, or that omit a clear judgement, cap at Levels 3-4.
practiceQuestions: Assess the reasons for the February Revolution of 1917. (30 marks)
To what extent was the October Revolution a coup d'etat rather than a popular revolution? (30 marks)
To what extent did Lenin's economic policies compromise Bolshevik ideology? (30 marks)
Collectivisation was economically disastrous but politically successful. How far do you agree? (30 marks)
To what extent did Khrushchev's and Brezhnev's rule solve the problems created by Stalinism? (30 marks)

topics.title: USA: Civil Rights and the Making of Modern America
learningObjectives: Explain how Reconstruction's constitutional promises were reversed by Jim Crow laws, disenfranchisement and segregation
Evaluate the NAACP's legal strategy and the real impact of Brown v Board of Education (1954)
Assess the relative importance of grassroots protest, national leaders (King, Parks, SNCC) and the federal government from Montgomery (1955-56) to Selma (1965)
Compare nonviolent direct action and Black Power: aims, methods and results after 1965
Weigh the King-centred orthodoxy against 'long civil rights movement' revisionism in essay arguments
Reach substantiated judgements on the significance of the Civil Rights Acts (1964/1965) and King's assassination (1968)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'The Civil Rights Act of 1964 owed more to the protests of 1963 than to any other factor.' Assess the validity of this view. (30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Level 5 (25-30): a sustained, analytically structured argument reaching a weighted judgement, with a wide range of accurate AO1 detail and factors weighed against each other throughout. Required AO1 knowledge: Birmingham (Project C, April-May 1963; Connor's dogs and fire hoses; televised children's marches; the 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'); the Kennedy administration's embarrassment and the June 1963 civil rights bill; the March on Washington (28 August 1963; c.250,000; 'I Have a Dream'); the Civil Rights Act's provisions (2 July 1964: public accommodations, Title VII employment, federal enforcement power). Other factors to weigh: the NAACP's legal campaign (Brown 1954; Browder v Gayle 1956) establishing the legal climate; Montgomery (1955-56) and the sit-ins and Freedom Rides (1960-61) building the protest repertoire; grassroots voter-registration work (SNCC, Mississippi Freedom Summer 1964) underpinning Selma and the 1965 Act; electoral timing — Johnson's 1964 landslide and Democratic majorities; Cold War image pressures shaping executive action since Truman (1948). FOR the 1963 protests: Birmingham's televised brutality converted northern opinion and forced the bill onto the agenda; the March demonstrated discipline and national scale. AGAINST: the Act was the product of a decade-long chain (Brown -> Montgomery -> sit-ins -> Freedom Rides -> Birmingham) — no single year was sufficient; the 1964 election mattered for passage; administrations acted only when protest made inaction costlier, as Kennedy's 'cooling-off' preference proves. Historians to deploy: Lawson (federal politics decisive), Fairclough and Payne (local movements built the pressure), Hall (the long civil rights movement). Judgement: the protests of 1963 — Birmingham above all — were the necessary catalyst, not the sufficient cause: the Act owed most to the accumulated pressure of the whole movement, with Birmingham the decisive escalation. Answers that narrate events without weighing factors, or lack a clear judgement, cap at Levels 3-4.
practiceQuestions: To what extent did Brown v Board of Education (1954) transform the lives of black Americans by 1965? (30 marks)
Assess the importance of Martin Luther King to the success of the Montgomery Bus Boycott. (30 marks)
To what extent did the rise of Black Power undermine the civil rights movement after 1965? (30 marks)
Assess the view that the federal government was the main driver of civil rights progress, 1954-1965. (30 marks)
How far did Reconstruction fail black Americans? (30 marks)

topics.title: Germany: Kaiser to Hitler, 1871-1945
learningObjectives: Explain Bismarck's fall (1890) and the domestic and international dynamics of Weltpolitik to 1914 (AO1)
Analyse the Weimar constitution's structural weaknesses and the political impact of Versailles (AO1/AO2)
Assess the crises of 1919-23 and the extent of genuine stability under Stresemann, 1924-29 (AO2)
Evaluate the roles of the Depression, conservative elites and Hitler in the Nazi rise and consolidation, 1929-34 (AO1/AO2)
Assess the nature of the Third Reich: totalitarian control, the economy, Volksgemeinschaft and racial policy (AO1/AO2)
Deploy historiography (Bullock, Kershaw, Evans, Fischer, Wehler) as sustained argument in 30-mark essays (AO2)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'The Enabling Act was the most important reason for the establishment of Hitler's dictatorship by 1934.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: 30-mark argument logic: sustained line with supported judgement, not narrative. FOR the Enabling Act: 23 March 1933 (444-94) legalised rule without the Reichstag for four years - the platform for Gleichschaltung (unions 2 May, all parties banned 14 July) and the whole one-party state; without it, Hitler governed as head of a coalition. OTHER factors to weigh: the Reichstag Fire Decree (28 February 1933) suspended civil liberties first - arguably the operative instrument of terror (Dachau opened March 1933; KPD/SPD deputies arrested); elite sanction - Papen's 'we have hired him' appointment (30 January 1933) was the precondition without which no Act could be passed; mass support - 43.9% in March 1933, propaganda and SA intimidation (still short of a majority, so the Act needed the Centre's votes); completion in 1934 - the Night of the Long Knives (30 June) won the army, and Hindenburg's death (2 August) with the personal oath created the Führer state. Judgement: the Act was the legal keystone but not self-sufficient - it worked only with the February Decree's terror and elite permission, and the dictatorship was complete only by August 1934. A* requires a hierarchy of causes and historians deployed as argument (Kershaw: elite miscalculation and the Führer myth; Evans: legal counter-revolution; Bracher: constitutional weakness predating Hitler). Source questions (AQA/Edexcel): judge utility by NATURE, ORIGIN and PURPOSE, then test against context.
practiceQuestions: 'Weltpolitik was the main cause of Germany's international isolation by 1914.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
'Hyperinflation (1923) posed the greatest threat to the Weimar Republic in its early years.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
How useful are Stresemann's private letters and a Nazi Party election poster from 1932 for a historian studying German attitudes to the Weimar Republic? [20 marks]
'The Great Depression was the main reason for the Nazi rise to power, 1929-33.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
'The Nazi economy was, by 1939, already prepared for war.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]

topics.title: The Cold War
learningObjectives: Explain the ideological and geopolitical origins of the Cold War: Yalta, Potsdam, the Iron Curtain (AO1)
Analyse containment's evolution: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Berlin Blockade, NATO and Warsaw Pact (AO1/AO2)
Assess the globalisation of the conflict: Korea 1950-53 and the Cuban Missile Crisis 1962 (AO2)
Evaluate Vietnam's impact and the achievements and limits of détente (SALT I/II, Helsinki) (AO1/AO2)
Explain the end of the Cold War: Afghanistan 1979, Reagan and SDI, Gorbachev's reforms, the revolutions of 1989-91 (AO1/AO2)
Deploy historiography (Gaddis, revisionists - Williams, Kolko, Alperovitz - and Zubok, Kotkin) as sustained argument (AO2)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Soviet expansionism, rather than American economic imperialism, was responsible for the outbreak of the Cold War.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
topics.modelAnswer: 30-mark historiographical argument logic: deploy schools as frameworks, not name-drops. FOR Soviet expansionism (orthodox - Feis, Schlesinger; post-1991 Gaddis): the broken Yalta promise of free elections, the buffer zone 1945-48 (Romania 1945, Poland 1947, Czech coup February 1948), Cominform (1947)/Comecon (1949), the Berlin Blockade (1948-49) - expansion beyond the agreed spheres. FOR American responsibility (revisionists - Williams's 'Open Door', Kolko, Alperovitz): the Marshall Plan as economic penetration of Europe ($13bn, conditions favouring US trade), 'atomic diplomacy' (bomb unbriefed at Yalta, deployed at Potsdam), the Truman Doctrine's polarising universalism, NATO (1949) entrenching division. Weigh: post-revisionism (Gaddis) - neither side solely guilty; a security dilemma in which each defensive move (Marshall Plan, Cominform; NATO, Warsaw) read as offensive; Stalin's paranoia and US confidence in an open world economy were structurally incompatible. Judgement: Soviet expansionism was primary within Europe (physical seizure of ground), US economic statecraft primary in globalising the conflict (dollar diplomacy, Greek-Turkish commitment); A* requires the orthodox-revisionist-post-revisionist triad explicitly, a hierarchy, and a supported final judgement.
practiceQuestions: 'The Berlin Blockade (1948-49) was the most dangerous moment of the Cold War before 1962.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
'The Cuban Missile Crisis was a triumph for Kennedy's policy of containment.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
'US failure in Vietnam was primarily a military failure.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
'Gorbachev's reforms were the main reason for the collapse of Soviet control in Eastern Europe by 1989.' How far do you agree? [30 marks]
How useful are Khrushchev's memoirs and a US State Department telegram from October 1962 for a historian studying the Cuban Missile Crisis? [20 marks]

topics.title: Water and Carbon Cycles
learningObjectives: Explain the systems concept (inputs, outputs, stores, fluxes) applied to the water and carbon cycles, distinguishing open, closed and dynamic equilibrium systems (AQA 3.1.1.1; Edexcel 2.1; OCR 1.2.a)
Describe and explain the global water budget, the water balance equation and the relationship between drainage basin stores, flows and hydrographs (AQA 3.1.1.2-3.1.1.3; Edexcel 2.2; OCR 1.1)
Compare the magnitude and location of global carbon stores and evaluate the role of the carbon budget in planetary temperature regulation (AQA 3.1.1.4; Edexcel 2.4; OCR 1.2.b)
Analyse positive and negative feedback loops linking the water and carbon cycles, including at least one Amazon-specific feedback (AQA 3.1.1.5; Edexcel 2.1, 2.7; OCR 1.3)
Evaluate the impact of deforestation on the Amazon's water and carbon cycles using specific data (AQA 3.1.1.6; Edexcel 2.5-2.6; OCR 1.3)
Assess the role of the two cycles in regulating planetary climate and the consequences of anthropogenic change for stores and fluxes (AQA 3.1.1.7-3.1.1.8; Edexcel 2.7; OCR 1.3)
Evaluate local and global management strategies for maintaining water and carbon security (AQA 3.1.1.9; Edexcel 2.8; OCR 1.4)
keyPoints: Hydrosphere: 96.5% ocean; freshwater dominated by ice sheets (~68.7%) and groundwater (~30.1%), not rivers
Geological carbon store dwarfs all others; ocean is the largest active (near-surface) store
Fast carbon cycle (photosynthesis ~120 GtC/yr) vs slow carbon cycle (weathering, burial, volcanism ~0.1-0.3 GtC/yr)
Fossil fuel flux ~10 GtC/yr; sinks absorb only ~50%, so CO2 rose from 280 to >420 ppm
Amazon: ~2,000 mm/yr rainfall, 50-75% recycled by transpiration, ~120-150 GtC in biomass
Positive feedbacks: water vapour, ice-albedo, permafrost methane, forest dieback; negative: CO2 fertilisation, water-use efficiency
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Cycles and feedbacks within the water and carbon cycles maintain dynamic equilibrium at a global scale.' To what extent do you agree with this view? (20 marks) - AQA-style synoptic question (AQA 3.1.1.1, 3.1.1.5, 3.1.1.7; Edexcel 2.1, 2.7; OCR 1.3)
topics.modelAnswer: Task: 'To what extent' demands a supported judgement. Plan: (1) evidence FOR equilibrium - closed global water cycle, balanced pre-industrial carbon cycle, negative feedbacks; (2) evidence AGAINST - anthropogenic perturbation, positive feedbacks, tipping points; (3) judgement. AO1 (knowledge, ~6 marks): define dynamic equilibrium; water cycle as closed system with evaporation approximating precipitation globally; pre-industrial carbon balance (atmosphere ~280 ppm stable for millennia per ice cores); negative feedbacks - CO2 fertilisation, silicate weathering thermostat, water-use efficiency. AO2 (application/analysis, ~8 marks): apply feedback chains to stores/fluxes with data: fossil fuel flux ~10 GtC/yr vs volcanic ~0.1-0.3 GtC/yr; sinks absorb ~50% of emissions, so equilibrium is broken - CO2 rose from 280 to >420 ppm; positive feedbacks (water vapour roughly doubling CO2 forcing, ice-albedo, permafrost 1,400-1,700 GtC, Amazon dieback beyond ~20-25% clearing) push the system toward a new equilibrium, not the old one. Worked example: Amazon deforestation → less transpiration → less recycled rainfall → further dieback → carbon release. AO3 (evaluation, ~6 marks): equilibrium is a useful model at geological timescales (slow carbon cycle thermostat) but not on human timescales; the system has been out of dynamic equilibrium since industrialisation and may be approaching tipping points; caveat - negative feedbacks still absorb ~half of emissions, so the system is disturbed but not yet runaway; cloud-feedback uncertainty adds error bars. Conclude: agree at long timescales, disagree at the scale that matters for 21st-century climate policy.
practiceQuestions: Outline the stores and fluxes of the global water cycle. (4 marks) - AQA-style short question
Explain one way in which changes in the water cycle can affect the carbon cycle. (6 marks) - AQA-style
'Deforestation of the tropical rainforest has a greater impact on the water cycle than on the carbon cycle.' Discuss. (9 marks) - Edexcel-style
Evaluate the effectiveness of management strategies in protecting the Amazon's water and carbon cycles. (20 marks)
Assess the relative importance of stores of carbon in regulating planetary temperature. (9 marks) - AQA/OCR style
Using Figure X (storm hydrograph), explain how urbanisation changes a drainage basin's water balance and flows. (6 marks) - OCR/AQA skills question

topics.title: Coastal Systems and Landscapes
learningObjectives: Explain coasts as open systems with inputs, stores and outputs, and describe sediment cells as closed sub-systems (AQA 3.1.3.1, 3.1.3.3; Edexcel 2B.1; OCR 1.1.a)
Distinguish marine erosion and transport processes (hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, longshore drift) from sub-aerial weathering and mass movement (AQA 3.1.3.2; Edexcel 2B.3; OCR 1.1.a)
Explain the formation of erosional and depositional landforms - cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves-arches-stacks, spits, bars - as interacting systems (AQA 3.1.3.4; Edexcel 2B.4-2B.5; OCR 1.1.b)
Distinguish eustatic from isostatic sea-level change and explain landforms of emergence and submergence plus coastal flooding risk (AQA 3.1.3.5-3.1.3.7; Edexcel 2B.7-2B.8; OCR 1.1.c)
Evaluate hard and soft engineering (including gabions, managed retreat) using the Holderness case study with specific data (AQA 3.1.3.8; Edexcel 2B.9-2B.10; OCR 1.1.c)
Assess the strengths and weaknesses of Shoreline Management Plans and ICZM as holistic, sustainable management frameworks (AQA 3.1.3.8; Edexcel 2B.10; OCR 1.1.c)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Coastal management schemes do more harm than good.' To what extent do you agree with this view? (20 marks) - AQA-style synoptic question (AQA 3.1.3.8; Edexcel 2B.9-2B.10; OCR 1.1.c)
topics.modelAnswer: Task: 'To what extent' requires a supported judgement weighing harms against benefits. AO1 (~6 marks): define hard vs soft engineering (sea walls, groynes, gabions, rock armour vs nourishment, realignment, do-nothing) and the sediment-cell/system context (11 cells, drift, terminal scour). AO2 (~8 marks): apply evidence - Holderness: Mappleton groynes (~£2 m, 1991) protected the village but accelerated downdrift erosion at Great Cowden (~10 m/yr); sea walls reflect wave energy, causing scour and high maintenance; gabions corrode within decades; conversely benefits are real - Withernsea/Hornsea town defences protect hundreds of homes and infrastructure (Easington gas terminal supplies ~20%+ of UK gas); managed realignment (Medmerry ~£28 m) delivers flood protection plus salt-marsh habitat and carbon storage at lower lifetime cost than holding the line. AO3 (~6 marks): judgement - harms are mostly artefacts of mis-sited hard engineering within an open system; schemes that respect cell dynamics (realignment, nourishment) cause fewer externalities; benefit-cost analysis shows do-nothing is rational where protected assets are low-value farmland; rising seas make blanket Hold-the-Line fiscally unsustainable. Conclude: schemes do harm when they ignore sediment-cell connectivity, but properly integrated schemes (ICZM/SMP-framed realignment) do more good than harm - so agree only partially.
practiceQuestions: Outline the process of longshore drift and its role in forming a spit. (4 marks) - AQA-style short question
Explain the formation of a wave-cut platform. (6 marks) - AQA/OCR style
'Sea level change is caused by both eustatic and isostatic factors.' Explain the difference between the two. (6 marks) - Edexcel-style
Evaluate the role of hard engineering in managing coastal erosion at Holderness. (9 marks) - Edexcel-style with resource support
Assess the advantages and disadvantages of managed retreat (managed realignment) as a coastal management strategy. (20 marks)
With reference to a named sediment cell, explain why coastal management should be integrated across the whole cell. (9 marks) - OCR style

topics.title: Hazards
learningObjectives: Explain plate movement mechanisms (slab pull, ridge push, convection) and describe the hazards and landforms of constructive, destructive, conservative and collision boundaries (AQA 3.1.5.1; Edexcel 2A.1; OCR 1.1.a)
Explain volcanic hazards - pyroclastic flows, lahars, ashfall, gases, lava - and evaluate monitoring and prediction using the VEI and Mount Pinatubo 1991 (AQA 3.1.5.2; Edexcel 2A.2; OCR 1.2.a)
Describe earthquake waves and compare the Richter, moment magnitude and Mercalli scales; explain liquefaction and secondary hazards (AQA 3.1.5.3; Edexcel 2A.2; OCR 1.2.a)
Explain tsunami formation, characteristics and warning systems, using the 2004 Indian Ocean and 2011 Tohoku tsunamis (AQA 3.1.5.4; Edexcel 2A.3; OCR 1.2.b)
Explain tropical storm formation and structure, apply the Saffir-Simpson scale, and assess wildfire causes, conditions and impacts (AQA 3.1.5.5-3.1.5.6; Edexcel 2A.2; OCR 1.2.c)

Apply hazard perception and the Park model, and evaluate a multi-hazard environment (Philippines) plus local, national and international responses using Nepal 2015 (AQA 3.1.5.1, 3.1.5.7; Edexcel 2A.4-2A.6; OCR 1.3.a)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'The impact of tectonic hazards on people and property is determined more by the level of development than by the magnitude of the event.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks) - AQA-style synoptic question (AQA 3.1.5.7; Edexcel 2A.4; OCR 1.3.a)
topics.modelAnswer: Task: 'To what extent' demands a supported judgement weighing development against physical factors (magnitude, depth, location). AO1 (~6 marks): define magnitude measures (Mw vs Mercalli), hazard vs disaster, and the development-preparedness link (hazard perception, Park model stages). AO2 (~8 marks): evidence that development dominates - Nepal 2015 (Mw 7.8): ~9,000 deaths, ~600,000 homes destroyed, weak building codes and unreinforced masonry, liquefaction-amplified shaking, slow reconstruction (Park-model recovery stretched over years); contrast Japan 2011 (Mw 9.0, far larger) with ~18,000 deaths but warning systems, engineered buildings and sea walls limiting losses and enabling recovery within years; Pinatubo 1991 shows monitoring and evacuation (~200,000 people) cutting primary deaths where agencies function. Evidence for magnitude's role: the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami (Mw 9.1, ~230,000 deaths) would have killed far fewer with warning systems regardless of development; shallow focus and proximity to cities magnify any quake's toll; only Mw 7+ seabed displacement triggers tsunami at all. AO3 (~6 marks): judgement - development determines the vulnerability side of risk (risk = hazard x exposure x vulnerability / capacity), so at equal magnitude richer countries suffer fewer deaths; but magnitude sets the ceiling of physical energy, and secondary hazards (tsunami) can overwhelm even well-developed protection. Conclude: largely agree - development is the more decisive factor for deaths and recovery in most tectonic events, though at the highest magnitudes (Mw 9+) physical force limits what any development level can achieve.
practiceQuestions: Distinguish between the characteristics of P-waves and S-waves. (4 marks)
Explain the formation of a tropical storm. (6 marks)
Assess the effectiveness of monitoring and prediction in reducing the impacts of volcanic hazards. (9 marks)
Using a case study, assess the impacts of a tectonic hazard in a developing country. (9 marks)
'Warning systems have removed the main threat from tsunami.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks)

topics.title: Global Systems and Governance
learningObjectives: Explain globalisation as the widening, deepening and speeding-up of worldwide interconnectedness, describe its economic, political, social and environmental dimensions, and account for the factors accelerating it - transport, communications, finance, management/information systems, security, trade agreements and global marketing (AQA 3.2.1.1)

Describe and explain unequal flows of people, money, ideas and technology, and analyse the asymmetries (capital concentration, brain drain, terms of trade) that make globalisation winners and losers (AQA 3.2.1.1)

Describe global trade flows and patterns, explain commodity chains and market access, and assess how unequal power relations are reproduced through the IMF, World Bank, WTO, structural adjustment and trade blocs (AQA 3.2.1.2-3.2.1.3)
Explain the spatial organisation of TNCs - global production networks, outsourcing, FDI, transfer pricing - using Apple/Foxconn, and evaluate TNC power relative to states (AQA 3.2.1.2)

Explain the concept of the global commons and describe the Antarctic Treaty system (1959 Treaty, Madrid Protocol 1991, CCAMLR, MPAs), threats to Antarctica, and the role of NGOs and international law (AQA 3.2.1.4)
Evaluate the effectiveness of global governance of Antarctica and discuss sovereignty versus interdependence in a globalised world (AQA 3.2.1.4)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Global governance of Antarctica is effective because the Antarctic Treaty has frozen territorial claims and banned mining.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks) - AQA-style synoptic question (AQA 3.2.1.4)
topics.modelAnswer: Task: 'To what extent' demands a supported judgement weighing governance successes (claims frozen, mining ban) against weaknesses and external pressures. AO1 (~6 marks): define the global commons (shared, non-excludable, no sovereignty) and the Antarctic Treaty system: the 1959 Treaty (Article IV freezing claims, peaceful purposes, military and nuclear activity banned, freedom of science, consensus decisions), the Madrid Protocol 1991 (Article 7 mining ban, natural-reserve designation, 2048 review), CCAMLR and marine protected areas, plus supporting international law (Montreal Protocol 1987, UNCLOS, Polar Code). AO2 (~8 marks): evidence of effectiveness - claims frozen for 65+ years among seven claimants with overlapping sectors (Argentina, Chile, UK) and no conflict; all mining banned indefinitely under the Madrid Protocol despite known mineral potential; science open across 57 parties with mutual inspections; the Ross Sea MPA (2017, 2 million km2) as the world's largest; the ozone hole recovering under the Montreal Protocol (~2066). Evidence of limits: consensus allows veto - Russia and China have blocked successive MPA proposals; compliance is voluntary with no enforcement police (Japan left the IWC in 2019 and resumed whaling in its own EEZ); IUU fishing of Patagonian toothfish persists; tourism has quadrupled since the 1990s (~74,000 visitors 2019-20) and bioprospecting is unregulated; climate change - Peninsula warming ~3 degrees C since 1950, Thwaites thinning - is governed by a separate, weaker regime; the 2048 mining-ban review is a real pressure point. AO3 (~6 marks): judgement - the Treaty system is effective at what it was designed for (conflict prevention, demilitarisation, science, and now mining prohibition), but effective governance of a global common requires controlling all threats, and climate change plus unregulated activities fall largely outside the system. Conclude: agree to a large extent - the Antarctic Treaty is the most successful global-commons regime and the claims/mining provisions are its strongest elements - but effectiveness is conditional on consensus holding, and climate impacts and the 2048 review mean governance must extend beyond the Treaty itself to remain effective.
practiceQuestions: Explain the concept of the global commons. (4 marks)
Assess the role of TNCs in accelerating globalisation. (9 marks)
Explain how the IMF and World Bank can create unequal power relations. (6 marks)
Assess the effectiveness of global governance of Antarctica. (9 marks)
'Globalisation increases interdependence but reduces national sovereignty.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks)

topics.title: Changing Places
learningObjectives: Define place through location, locale and sense of place, explain placelessness (Relph 1976) and non-places (Auge 1992), and distinguish insider and outsider perspectives on place (AQA 3.2.2.1)

Categorise endogenous factors (location, topography, physical geography, land use, built environment, infrastructure, demographic and economic characteristics) and exogenous factors (flows of people, capital, resources and ideas) and analyse how they interact to shape place character (AQA 3.2.2.1)

Explain how shifting flows of people, resources, money and investment reshape the demographic, cultural and economic character of places, using deindustrialisation and the Detroit case study (AQA 3.2.2.2)

Describe and evaluate rebranding and regeneration strategies - flagship, market-led and heritage/legacy approaches - and assess their effectiveness in Detroit (AQA 3.2.2.2; Edexcel Regenerating Places)

Plan and evaluate a local place study using quantitative sources (census, Index of Multiple Deprivation), qualitative sources (interviews, media, photographs) and GIS, and discuss how places are represented (AQA 3.2.2.3; OCR Changing Spaces; Making Places)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Rebranding is the most effective response to the problems created by deindustrialisation.' To what extent do you agree with this view? (20 marks) - AQA-style 3.2.2 synoptic question
topics.modelAnswer: Task: 'To what extent' demands a judgement comparing rebranding's effectiveness against other responses to deindustrialisation - diversification, housing and infrastructure renewal, retraining, and population strategies. AO1 (~6 marks): define rebranding (re-presenting a place to change perceptions: logotypes, media campaigns, flagship projects) and regeneration (physical-economic renewal), set against deindustrialisation's problems: mass manufacturing job loss (Detroit: about 296,000 manufacturing jobs in 1950 to under 20,000 today), depopulation (1.85 million in 1950 to 639,111 in 2020), dereliction (about 40 square miles of vacant land; the Packard Plant), poverty and fiscal collapse (largest-ever US municipal bankruptcy, 2013, about 18 billion dollars). AO2 (~8 marks): evidence for rebranding's effectiveness - the RiverWalk (three-plus miles, three million-plus visits a year) recast the riverfront image; Rocket Mortgage's 2010 downtown relocation and Dan Gilbert's roughly 5.6 billion dollars of property investment restarted the commercial core; Michigan Central Station's 950-million-dollar reopening (2024) rebranded the city around mobility technology; Shinola and Motown heritage sell a credible story; population loss slowed to near-stability (about 633,000 by 2023) and downtown employment grew. Against: benefits are spatially concentrated downtown and in Midtown, outer neighbourhoods continue to lose services and housing; rebranding attracts tourism, graduates and tech jobs but not mass manufacturing employment; gentrification and 'comeback island' inequality follow; and the strategy depends on exogenous investment that can leave as fast as it arrived, as the auto industry proved. Weigh alternatives: diversification (health, education, tech campuses) addresses employment directly; blight-removal and housing programmes address dereliction where flagships do not; but without a new image neither attracts the people and capital required - image and substance are mutually dependent. AO3 (~6 marks): judgement - rebranding is effective as a necessary gateway (it reverses the perception problem that deters investment) but insufficient alone; agree with the statement in the short term, since Detroit's image recovery preceded measurable economic recovery, but disagree in the long term, because only diversified employment, housing and neighbourhood-level regeneration - not just flagship re-presentation - can reverse the underlying deindustrialisation. Best answers conclude: rebranding is the most visible response and the most effective first move, not the most complete one.
practiceQuestions: Explain the difference between endogenous and exogenous factors in shaping the character of a place. (4 marks)
Explain what Relph (1976) meant by placelessness. (6 marks)
Assess the usefulness of census data and GIS in investigating the character of your local place. (9 marks)
Assess the effectiveness of the strategies used to regenerate Detroit. (9 marks)
'The character of places is determined more by relationships and connections than by physical endowment.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks)

topics.title: Arguments for the Existence of God
learningObjectives: Set out Anselm's Proslogion 2-3 argument and Descartes' version, then evaluate Gaunilo's perfect-island parody and Kant's 'existence is not a predicate' reply (AO1/AO2)
Reproduce Paley's watchmaker analogy and Aquinas' Fifth Way, distinguishing regularity from purpose (AO1)
Explain modern design arguments: Tennant's anthropic principle, aesthetic argument and Swinburne's probability reasoning (AO1)
Recite Hume's five Dialogues critiques and Mill's objection from nature's cruelty, and weigh them against the anthropic counter (AO2)
Outline Aquinas' First, Second and Third Ways for WJEC/CCEA coverage, including infinite regress and contingency (AO1)
Distinguish a priori, a posteriori and abductive reasoning and classify each argument correctly (AO1)
Plan an evaluative essay with a structured argument, scholarly support and a justified verdict rather than a summary (AO2/AO3)
keyPoints: Ontological: a priori, from definition; Anselm (Proslogion 2-3) vs Gaunilo and Kant.
Design: a posteriori, from order; Paley's watchmaker vs Hume's five critiques and Dawkins.
Modern design: Tennant's anthropic principle; Swinburne's probabilistic cumulative case.
Cosmological (WJEC/CCEA): Aquinas' First, Second and Third Ways; contingency and regress.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'The ontological argument fails to demonstrate the existence of God.' Critically discuss this claim. [AQA 7062 15-mark AO2 essay / OCR H573 extended essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: Anselm's Proslogion 2-3 (definition of God, intellectu vs in re, necessary existence, reductio); Descartes' version (existence as a perfection); Gaunilo's parody and Anselm's reply; Kant's 'existence is not a real predicate'; optionally Malcolm's defence and Barth's revelation-only objection. AO2 required: a sustained evaluation - (1) Gaunilo shows definition-to-existence moves fail for contingent things, but Anselm's reply is that a uniquely necessary being is different in kind; (2) Kant shows that even coherent concepts need not be instantiated, so 'necessary existence' is suspect - this is the decisive critique and should be weighed most heavily; (3) Malcolm's defence only restores coherence, not instantiation; (4) Barth: even if the argument worked it would be theology, not neutral proof, since it begins from faith; (5) weigh and conclude - e.g. the argument fails as demonstration but retains apologetic or theological value, and justify which verdict the weight of critique supports.
practiceQuestions: Explain Anselm's ontological argument as set out in the Proslogion. [10 marks AO1]
'The design argument shows that the universe was created by God.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Hume's objections to the design argument. [10 marks AO1]
'Existence is not a predicate.' Critically assess Kant's objection to the ontological argument. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Tennant's anthropic principle and Swinburne's version of the design argument. [10 marks AO1]
'Hume's critiques of the design argument are decisive.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: The Problem of Evil
learningObjectives: State the logical problem of evil (Mackie's inconsistent triad) and the free will defence response, and evaluate both (AO1/AO2)
Explain the evidential problem, including Rowe's fawn and pointless suffering (AO1)
Set out Augustine's theodicy: privatio boni, the Fall, original sin - and its standard critiques (AO1/AO2)
Set out Irenaeus' theodicy as developed by Hick: epistemic distance, soul-making, eschatological justification - and its critiques (AO1/AO2)
Distinguish moral from natural evil and explain why the distinction matters for each theodicy (AO1)
Apply D.Z. Phillips' protest that theodicies can be morally obscene and weigh it in a verdict (AO2)
Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified conclusion (AO2/AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Hick's soul-making theodicy successfully answers the problem of evil.' Critically discuss this claim. [AQA 7062 15-mark AO2 essay / OCR H573 extended essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: Irenaeus' image/likeness distinction and vale of soul-making; Hick's epistemic distance, soul-making environment, eschatological justification and universalism; contrast with Augustine (privation, Fall) and Schleiermacher's objection to it. AO2 required: (1) strength - epistemic distance is philosophically robust and the account fits evolutionary immaturity, avoiding Augustine's incoherent perfect creation; (2) critique - disproportionate evil (child suffering, Holocaust, animal pain) exceeds any plausible soul-making need (Mackie); (3) D.Z. Phillips' protest - treating suffering as a means to an end is morally obscene; (4) universalism undermines responsibility and judgement; (5) weigh - the theodicy explains some evil but not the worst; conclude with a justified verdict, e.g. it answers the logical problem's spirit but fails the evidential and moral challenges.
practiceQuestions: Explain the logical problem of evil. [10 marks AO1]
'Evil and suffering disprove the existence of God.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Augustine's theodicy. [10 marks AO1]
'Hick's soul-making theodicy is more convincing than Augustine's.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain the free will defence and its main criticism. [10 marks AO1]
'Theodicies are morally obscene.' Critically assess D.Z. Phillips' protest. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: Religious Experience and Miracles
learningObjectives: Classify types of religious experience (visions, voices, numinous, mystical, corporate) with James' four qualities and Stace's distinction (AO1)
Explain Swinburne's principles of credulity and testimony as the main argument from experience to God (AO1)
Set out the challenges from Freud (wish-fulfilment), Jung (collective unconscious) and Feuerbach (projection) (AO1/AO2)
Reproduce Hume's definition of miracles and his four a posteriori arguments, and Wiles' objection (AO1)
Evaluate whether religious experience and miracles justify belief in God, using conversion evidence (Lourdes, Alister Hardy) (AO2)
Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Religious experience is more convincing evidence for God than miracles.' Critically discuss this claim. [AQA 7062 15-mark AO2 essay / OCR H573 extended essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: types of experience (James' four qualities; Stace; Otto's numinous); Swinburne's principles of credulity and testimony; challenges (Freud's wish-fulfilment, Jung's collective unconscious, ambiguity of object); Hume's definition of a miracle and four testimony arguments; Wiles' moral objection and Aquinas' definition. AO2 required: (1) experience - credulity makes millions of reports prima facie evidence, but the ambiguity of object across traditions limits the inference to any one God; (2) miracles - Hume attacks testimony, not God's power; educated-witness replies (Lourdes) weaken Hume; (3) Wiles: selective intervention is morally arbitrary, but believers accept inscrutable providence; (4) James' fruits-not-roots supports the value of experience without proving veridicality; (5) weigh - experience survives Hume's challenges better than miracles do (no law-transgression issue, larger body of testimony), but both remain evidential rather than demonstrative; conclude with a justified verdict.
practiceQuestions: Explain William James' four qualities of mystical experience. [10 marks AO1]
'Religious experience provides no evidence for the existence of God.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Swinburne's principles of credulity and testimony. [10 marks AO1]
'Hume's critique of miracles is decisive.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Freud's and Jung's challenges to religious experience. [10 marks AO1]
'Corporate religious experiences are more reliable than individual experiences.' Critically assess. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: Religious Language
learningObjectives: Distinguish cognitive and non-cognitive uses of religious language (AO1)
Reproduce the verification principle (Ayer) and Flew's falsification challenge, with Hare's bliks, Mitchell's partisan and Hick's eschatological verification as responses (AO1/AO2)
Explain Aquinas' doctrine of analogy (attribution and proportion) and Ramsey's models and qualifiers (AO1)
Set out Tillich's view of religious symbols (participation in the divine) and its critiques (AO1/AO2)
Explain the via negativa (Pseudo-Dionysius, Maimonides) and its strengths and weaknesses (AO1/AO2)
Explain Wittgenstein's language games and D.Z. Phillips' non-realism, and evaluate all approaches comparatively (AO2)
Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Religious language is meaningful.' Critically assess this claim with reference to verification and falsification. [OCR H573 extended essay / WJEC/Eduqas essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: cognitive vs non-cognitive distinction; Ayer's verification principle; Flew's falsification principle with the gardener parable; replies - Hare's bliks, Mitchell's partisan, Hick's eschatological verification; optionally analogy (Aquinas), Tillich's symbols, via negativa and Wittgenstein's language games. AO2 required: (1) the verification principle is self-defeating - it fails its own test, so it cannot rule out religious language; (2) Flew's challenge is sharper: believers qualify claims until nothing is asserted; (3) Hare and Mitchell show unfalsifiable bliks and trust against evidence are not meaningless, but they dodge the realist question; (4) Hick gives a checkable condition, though it verifies survival not God; (5) analogy and via negativa preserve meaning but may say too little; (6) weigh - e.g. religious language is meaningful analogically or as language games, but verificationism fails on its own terms; conclude with a justified verdict.
practiceQuestions: Explain the verification principle and its application to religious language. [10 marks AO1]
'Religious language is meaningless.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Flew's falsification challenge and the responses of Hare, Mitchell and Hick. [10 marks AO1]
'Analogy is the best account of religious language.' Critically assess. [15 marks AO2]
Explain the via negativa and its main weakness. [10 marks AO1]
'Wittgenstein's language games make religious language immune from criticism.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: Utilitarianism
learningObjectives: State Bentham's principle of utility and apply the seven criteria of the hedonic calculus to a case (AO1)
Explain Mill's distinction between higher and lower pleasures, the harm principle and rule utilitarianism (AO1)
Explain later developments: preference utilitarianism (Singer, Hare) and negative utilitarianism (Popper) (AO1)
Evaluate the main strengths (impartiality, common sense, empirical) and weaknesses (tyranny of the majority, measurement, integrity) (AO2)
Compare utilitarianism with religious ethics (natural law, situation ethics) and apply to euthanasia and business cases (AO2)
Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Act utilitarianism is the most convincing form of utilitarianism.' Critically discuss this claim. [AQA 7062 15-mark AO2 essay / OCR H573 extended essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: Bentham's principle of utility and hedonic calculus (seven criteria); act utilitarianism per-act assessment; Mill's higher/lower pleasures, harm principle and rule utilitarianism; Singer's preference utilitarianism and Hare's two-level variant. AO2 required: (1) strength of act utilitarianism - purity and flexibility: no act is intrinsically wrong, the calculus fits dilemmas; (2) critique - measurement is impractical and rights may be sacrificed to the majority (transplant case); (3) rule utilitarianism protects rights and integrity but faces rule worship and collapse into act utilitarianism; (4) Mill's quality distinction answers 'swine philosophy' but breaks measurability; (5) Singer avoids hedonic measurement but must exclude offensive preferences somehow; (6) weigh and conclude - e.g. two-level or preference variants are more convincing than pure act utilitarianism because they protect integrity while keeping the utility principle, and justify the verdict.
practiceQuestions: Explain Bentham's hedonic calculus. [10 marks AO1]
'Rule utilitarianism is more convincing than act utilitarianism.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Mill's distinction between higher and lower pleasures and the harm principle. [10 marks AO1]
'Utilitarianism is a good theory but not a good guide to action.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Singer's preference utilitarianism. [10 marks AO1]
'The tyranny of the majority objection defeats utilitarianism.' Critically assess. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: Kantian Ethics
learningObjectives: Explain Kant's good will, duty and the distinction between hypothetical and categorical imperatives (AO1)
State the first formulation of the categorical imperative (universalisability) and apply it to a case (AO1)
State the second formulation (humanity as an end in itself) and apply it to euthanasia and business cases (AO1)
Explain the third formulation (kingdom of ends), the summum bonum and Kant's postulates of freedom, God and immortality (AO1)
Evaluate strengths (dignity, universalisability) and weaknesses (conflicts of duty, cold formalism, lying to the murderer) (AO2)
Explain W.D. Ross' prima facie duties as a response to Kant's rigidity and weigh it in a verdict (AO2)
Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Kantian ethics provides a convincing approach to moral decision-making.' Critically discuss this claim. [AQA 7062 15-mark AO2 essay / OCR H573 extended essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: good will (only thing good without qualification); duty vs inclination (shopkeeper example); hypothetical vs categorical imperatives; first formulation (universalisability, four-step test); second formulation (humanity as an end, dignity vs price); third formulation (kingdom of ends); summum bonum and postulates (freedom, God, immortality); optionally Ross' prima facie duties. AO2 required: (1) strengths - universalisability matches fairness convictions, dignity grounds human rights, motive matters; (2) weaknesses - conflicts of duty (lying to the murderer at the door) and Kant's indefensible reply; Hegel's 'empty formalism'; absurd universalisable maxims show the test is too permissive; (3) consequentialist reply - ignoring outcomes is irrational (Bentham/Mill); (4) Ross: prima facie duties resolve conflicts but 'judgement' is unexplained; (5) weigh - e.g. Kantian ethics secures dignity but rigidity over conflicts is decisive, so Ross' moderated deontology is more convincing; conclude with a justified verdict.
practiceQuestions: Explain Kant's first formulation of the categorical imperative. [10 marks AO1]
'Kantian ethics provides a convincing approach to moral decision-making.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Kant's second formulation (humanity as an end in itself) and one application. [10 marks AO1]
'Kant's reply to the murderer at the door is indefensible.' Critically assess. [15 marks AO2]
Explain the summum bonum and Kant's postulates of practical reason. [10 marks AO1]
'Ross' prima facie duties improve on Kant.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: Natural Law and Situation Ethics
learningObjectives: Explain Aquinas' Natural Law: telos, primary and secondary precepts, real vs apparent goods, interior vs exterior acts (AO1)
Explain the doctrine of double effect and apply it to a case (ectopic pregnancy) (AO1)
Explain Fletcher's situation ethics: four working principles, six propositions and agape (AO1)
Compare Natural Law and situation ethics as legalistic vs antinomian extremes with situation ethics between (AO2)
Evaluate strengths and weaknesses of both, including Hume's is-ought gap and the objection that 'natural' does not entail 'good' (AO2)
Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Situation ethics is more convincing than Natural Law for moral decision-making.' Critically discuss this claim. [AQA 7062 15-mark AO2 essay / OCR H573 extended essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: Aquinas' Natural Law (telos, five primary precepts, secondary precepts, real vs apparent goods, double effect); Fletcher's situation ethics (four working principles, six propositions, agape); contrast legalism/antinomianism. AO2 required: (1) NL strengths - objective, universal precepts protect the innocent; double effect resolves conflicts (ectopic pregnancy); (2) NL weaknesses - 'natural' does not entail 'good' (Hume's is-ought gap); rigid precepts produce harmful outcomes; telos is contested in a secular age; (3) situation ethics strengths - flexible, person-centred, fits Jesus' love over law; (4) weaknesses - agape is undefined and may license anything; collapses into act utilitarianism with a religious label; (5) weigh - Fletcher better fits dilemmas, NL better secures objectivity; conclude with a justified verdict grounded in whether morality is grounded in nature or love.
practiceQuestions: Explain Aquinas' primary precepts and how secondary precepts are derived. [10 marks AO1]
'Natural Law provides a convincing approach to moral decision-making.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain the doctrine of double effect and one application. [10 marks AO1]
'Fletcher's situation ethics is just utilitarianism with a religious label.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Fletcher's four working principles and six propositions. [10 marks AO1]
''Natural' does not entail 'good'.' Critically assess this objection to Natural Law. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: Applied Ethics: Business, Sexual Ethics and Euthanasia
learningObjectives: Distinguish types of euthanasia (active/passive, voluntary/non-voluntary/involuntary) and apply ethical theories to each (AO1)
Evaluate sanctity of life vs quality of life arguments, with Case studies (Tony Bland, Charlie Gard) (AO2)
Explain business ethics concepts: CSR, stakeholders, whistle-blowing, good/bad practice - and apply Kant, utilitarianism and NL (AO1/AO2)
Explain sexual ethics issues: pre/extra-marital sex, homosexuality, contraception, consent - religious and secular approaches (AO1/AO2)
Apply Kantian dignity, utilitarian outcomes, NL precepts and agape across all three issues comparatively (AO2)
Structure an applied-ethics essay with case anchors, scholars and a justified verdict (AO2/AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Ethical theories provide convincing approaches to euthanasia.' Critically discuss this claim with reference to Natural Law and utilitarianism. [AQA 7062 15-mark AO2 essay / OCR H573 extended essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: types of euthanasia (active/passive, voluntary/non-voluntary/involuntary); NL application (intrinsically wrong, double effect, palliative sedation); utilitarian application (hedonic calculus per case, Mill's harm principle, Singer's preference); case anchors (Tony Bland, Charlie Gard). AO2 required: (1) NL strengths - sanctity of life (imago Dei) protects the vulnerable; double effect permits palliative care without intended killing; (2) NL weaknesses - intended/foreseen distinction is arbitrary; rigid precepts ignore suffering; (3) utilitarian strengths - flexible, respects autonomy and preference, fits pain-centred cases; (4) weaknesses - slippery slope, resource pressure on the vulnerable, non-voluntary euthanasia violates equal-weight; (5) weigh - NL protects but fails in dilemmas, utilitarianism flexes but endangers the vulnerable; conclude with a justified verdict on which approach better serves the dying.
practiceQuestions: Explain the different types of euthanasia. [10 marks AO1]
'Active euthanasia should be legalised in the UK.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain corporate social responsibility and one ethical theory's application to it. [10 marks AO1]
'Whistle-blowing is always a duty.' Critically assess. [15 marks AO2]
Explain religious and secular approaches to sexual ethics. [10 marks AO1]
'Ethical theories provide convincing approaches to euthanasia.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: Christianity: Death and the Afterlife, Developments and Dialogues
learningObjectives: Explain Christian teaching on death, judgement, heaven, hell, purgatory, resurrection and the intermediate state (AO1)
Evaluate resurrection of the body vs immortality of the soul, using 1 Corinthians 15, Aquinas and Hick (AO2)
Explain Bonhoeffer's theology: costly grace, solidarity, religionless Christianity - and its critiques (AO1/AO2)
Explain liberation theology: Gutierrez, orthopraxis, base ecclesial communities - and its critiques (AO1/AO2)
Explain exclusivism, inclusivism and pluralism (Hick's copernican revolution, Rahner's anonymous Christians) and interfaith dialogue (AO1/AO2)
Explain Christianity's dialogue with science (Darwin, Polkinghorne, process thought) and secularisation (Wilson, Bonhoeffer) (AO1/AO2)
Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3)
topics.exampleQuestion: 'The resurrection of the body is the most convincing Christian teaching on life after death.' Critically discuss this claim. [AQA 7062 15-mark AO2 essay / OCR H573 extended essay]
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: resurrection of the body (1 Corinthians 15 - 'sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body'); immortality of the soul (Platonic; Augustine); Aquinas' hylomorphism (soul as form of the body, resurrection completes the person); Hick's replica theory and eschatological verification; judgement (particular and final, Matthew 25), purgatory and election where relevant. AO2 required: (1) resurrection strengths - bodily doctrine fits 1 Corinthians 15 and the creed; the person is restored whole; (2) resurrection weaknesses - identity problem for the replica (Geach); 'spiritual body' is unclear; (3) immortality of the soul strengths - natural survival fits near-death intuitions; but it is Platonic rather than biblical; (4) Hick - replica theory secures identity by God's act, but the replica may not be the same person; (5) weigh - e.g. resurrection better preserves Christian doctrine, but the identity problem is decisive against Hick's version; conclude with a justified verdict.
practiceQuestions: Explain Christian teaching on death and the afterlife. [10 marks AO1]
'The resurrection of the body is the most convincing Christian teaching on life after death.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Bonhoeffer's theology of costly grace and religionless Christianity. [10 marks AO1]
'Liberation theology is Christianity's response to poverty.' Critically assess. [15 marks AO2]
Explain Hick's religious pluralism and Rahner's inclusivism. [10 marks AO1]
'Secularisation shows Christianity has no future in the West.' Critically discuss. [15 marks AO2]

topics.title: Epistemology: Perception, Knowledge and Gettier
learningObjectives: Define knowledge using the tripartite (justified true belief) view and construct Gettier-style counter-examples against it (Spec 3.1.1).
Explain and evaluate direct realism, indirect realism and Berkeleian idealism, including illusion, hallucination and veil-of-perception issues (Spec 3.1.2).
Explain Plato's innate knowledge thesis and Descartes' intuition and deduction thesis, with Locke's and Hume's critiques (Spec 3.1.3).
Distinguish a priori from a posteriori knowledge and apply Hume's fork to a priori claims about the world.
Analyse and evaluate philosophical arguments to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2, 'arguing with intent').
Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; balanced evaluation only on 25-mark essays.
keyPoints: Gettier cases show JTB is not sufficient for knowledge: true belief + justification + epistemic luck is not knowledge.
Direct realism: perception is immediate awareness of physical objects; attacked by perceptual variation, illusion, hallucination and time-lag.
Indirect realism (Locke): we perceive the world via sense-data; attacked by the veil of perception, answered by Russell's inference to the best explanation.
Idealism (Berkeley): only minds and ideas exist; the master argument plus God's perception; attacked on the act/object conflation and pre-mind worlds.
Rationalism (Plato, Descartes) grounds knowledge in reason; empiricism (Locke, Hume) in experience; Hume's fork restricts a priori knowledge to relations of ideas.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Indirect realism means we can never know anything about the external world.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: define indirect realism (we perceive mind-independent objects indirectly via sense-data; Locke; primary/secondary qualities); explain the veil-of-perception and sceptical issues — if only sense-data are perceived, their causal link to external objects is unverifiable and the world's existence does not follow. AO2 required: argue with intent, e.g. AGAINST the claim — (1) inference to the best explanation (Russell): mind-independent objects are the best explanation of the involuntary, coherent and unpredictable pattern of sense-data, so indirect realism licenses a posteriori knowledge of the world; (2) cross-sensory coherence: what I see I can touch, which dream/demon hypotheses explain less well. Consider the strongest objection FOR the claim: best explanation is only inductive — a demon or brain-in-a-vat hypothesis explains the same data, so the inference underdetermines and yields at most probability, not knowledge; respond: demanding deductive certainty sets the bar higher than empirical science meets anywhere, and reliability, not certainty, is the right standard for knowledge. Weigh up and conclude consistently (e.g. the claim fails: indirect realism, via best explanation, secures fallible but genuine knowledge of the external world).
practiceQuestions: Explain the tripartite view of knowledge. (5 marks)
Explain Gettier-style problems for the tripartite view of knowledge and one response. (12 marks)
Explain Berkeley's 'master argument' for idealism. (5 marks)
Explain Locke's distinction between primary and secondary qualities. (5 marks)
'Berkeley's idealism is more convincing than indirect realism.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Scepticism and Descartes' Meditations
learningObjectives: Distinguish normal incredulity from philosophical scepticism and set out Descartes' method of doubt (Spec 3.1.4).
Explain the dreaming and evil demon arguments with their premises and conclusions.
Explain the cogito and Descartes' clear and distinct ideas thesis, including the charge of the Cartesian circle.
Explain the problem of other minds with the argument from analogy and the 'best hypothesis' response (Spec 3.1.4).
Evaluate sceptical arguments and their responses to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2).
Answer 3/5/12-mark questions with pure AO1 explanation, using correct command-word technique.
keyPoints: Descartes' method of doubt is a search for certainty, not an endorsement of scepticism — sceptical arguments are his tools.
The evil demon is the strongest sceptical scenario because it attacks reason (mathematics) as well as the senses.
The cogito survives all doubt: 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true whenever it is thought.
The Cartesian circle: clear and distinct ideas prove God; God guarantees clear and distinct ideas — Descartes' reply turns on present attention vs memory.
The problem of other minds is answered by the argument from analogy and the 'best hypothesis' response — both inductive, never deductive.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Descartes' sceptical arguments show we cannot know anything beyond our own minds.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: set out the method of doubt, the dreaming argument (no infallible marks; dreams present non-existent things; so the senses cannot give knowledge of the external world), the evil demon (supreme deceiver attacks mathematics as well as the senses), the cogito ('I am, I exist' — necessarily true whenever thought), the clear and distinct ideas truth rule, and the Cartesian circle charge. AO2 — argue with intent, e.g. AGAINST the claim: (1) the cogito defeats the demon: doubting presupposes thinking, so 'I am, I exist' is indubitable — knowledge beyond doubt survives, though only about my own mind at the moment of thought; (2) the dreaming argument localises: it removes knowledge of particular external objects at particular times, not all knowledge. Consider the strongest objection FOR the claim: the evil demon attacks even a priori beliefs, and the Cartesian circle means God never certifies clear and distinct ideas — so nothing beyond the cogito is secure. Respond: Descartes' remembered-vs-present distinction blocks the circle (self-evidence needs no guarantee while attending; God secures memory), and if that fails, the reliabilist route still leaves fallible knowledge of the world. Weigh up and conclude consistently (e.g. the claim overstates: global scepticism is not established, but knowledge beyond one's own mind does require rejecting Descartes' standard of certainty).
practiceQuestions: Explain the difference between ordinary incredulity and philosophical scepticism. (5 marks)
Explain Descartes' dreaming argument and one response. (12 marks)
Explain the problem of other minds and the argument from analogy. (12 marks)
Explain Descartes' cogito. (5 marks)
'The argument from analogy successfully answers the problem of other minds.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Moral Philosophy: Utilitarianism, Kant and Aristotelian Virtue Ethics
learningObjectives: Explain and evaluate Bentham's act utilitarianism (hedonism, felicific calculus) and Mill's qualitative, rule-based refinement (Spec 3.2.1).
Explain and evaluate Kantian deontology: the good will, duty, the categorical imperative's formulations and clashing-duty issues (Spec 3.2.1).
Explain and evaluate Aristotelian virtue ethics: eudaimonia, the function argument, the doctrine of the mean and phronesis (Spec 3.2.1).
Apply utilitarianism, Kantian deontology and virtue ethics to stealing, eating animals, simulated killing and telling lies (Spec 3.2.2).
Compare the three theories' decision procedures, strengths and weaknesses to form reasoned judgements (AO2).
Write 25-mark essays 'arguing with intent' with balanced argument sandwiches and consistent conclusions.
keyPoints: Bentham: quantitative hedonism + felicific calculus; Mill: qualitative pleasures + rule utilitarianism + competent-judges 'proof'.
Kant: act from duty via the categorical imperative — universal law, humanity as an end, kingdom of ends; consequences are irrelevant to rightness.
Aristotle: eudaimonia via the function argument; virtues are means between vices, hit by practical wisdom and habituation.
Classic critiques: tyranny of the majority and integrity (utilitarianism); clashing duties and rigidity (Kant); circularity and guidance (Aristotle).
Applied ethics on spec: stealing, eating animals, simulated killing, telling lies — each theory delivers a different verdict.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Utilitarianism is a better account of morality than Kantian ethics.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: set out Bentham's act utilitarianism (hedonism, felicific calculus) and Mill's refinement (higher/lower pleasures, rule utilitarianism); set out Kantian ethics (good will, duty vs inclination, universal law and humanity formulations, with the false-promise example). AO2 — argue with intent, e.g. FOR utilitarianism: (1) moral reach: sentience, not rational nature, grounds moral status (Bentham), so utilitarianism captures duties to animals and future people that Kant cannot; (2) flexibility: consequences matter — refusing to lie to the murderer at the door (Kant/Constant) is intuitively unacceptable. Consider the strongest objection AGAINST: aggregation permits injustice — punishing the innocent to stop a riot (tyranny of the majority) and Jim and the Indians (Williams' integrity) show utilitarianism alienates agents from morality; respond: rule utilitarianism forbids such acts by general-utility rules. Counter-response: extreme scenarios (overruling a rule would save everyone) reveal rule utilitarianism collapsing back into act utilitarianism. Weigh up: utilitarianism's reach and flexibility vs Kant's absolute protection of persons; conclude consistently (either direction is defensible if argued with intent — e.g. Kantian ethics better respects dignity, but utilitarianism better handles real cases).
practiceQuestions: Explain Bentham's felicific calculus. (5 marks)
Explain Kant's universal law formulation of the categorical imperative and how it applies to false promising. (12 marks)
Explain Aristotle's function argument. (5 marks)
Explain Mill's distinction between higher and lower pleasures. (5 marks)
'Kantian ethics cannot be applied in practice.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Metaethics: Cognitivism, Realism and Moral Language
learningObjectives: Distinguish the two metaethical axes — cognitivism vs non-cognitivism and realism vs anti-realism — and locate each theory on both axes (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain the possible origins of moral principles in reason, in emotion/attitudes or in society (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain moral naturalism, including naturalist forms of utilitarianism (Bentham) and of virtue ethics, and evaluate it using Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain moral non-naturalism — Moore's intuitionism and Ross's prima facie duties — and evaluate the challenges from Hume's fork, the is-ought gap and the motivation argument (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain Mackie's error theory — the arguments from relativity and from queerness — and assess the nihilism charge (Spec 3.2.3).
Explain and evaluate emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson) and prescriptivism (Hare), including whether anti-realism can account for moral reasoning, disagreement and moral progress (Spec 3.2.3).
Analyse and evaluate metaethical arguments to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2, 'arguing with intent').
keyPoints: Two independent axes: cognitivism (moral judgements truth-apt) vs non-cognitivism (not truth-apt); realism (mind-independent moral facts) vs anti-realism (none). Every theory sits on both.
Moral principles may originate in reason (Moore, Ross), emotion/attitudes (Ayer) or society (Mackie: 'inventing' right and wrong).
Naturalism: good = natural property — Bentham: pleasure; naturalist virtue ethics: flourishing. Attacked by Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy.

Non-naturalism (Moore, Ross): good is simple, non-natural, known by intuition; Ross adds plural, self-evident prima facie duties. Attacked by Hume's fork, the is-ought gap, the motivation argument and Mackie's queerness.

Error theory (Mackie): judgements aim at objective truth but all fail — arguments from relativity and queerness; nihilism charge. Emotivism (boo/hurrah, persuasion) and prescriptivism (universalisable prescriptions) deny truth-aptness; attacked via embedded contexts, disagreement, the fanatic and moral progress.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Moral judgements do not state facts but express emotions.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: define the axes — cognitivism (moral judgements state propositions and are truth-apt; naturalism: Bentham's good = pleasure; non-naturalism: Moore's simple non-natural property known by intuition) vs non-cognitivism (moral judgements express non-cognitive states, not truth-apt); explain emotivism — Ayer's verification principle (moral judgements neither analytic nor empirically verifiable, so they state nothing) and the boo/hurrah analysis, plus Stevenson's emotive meaning and persuasive function. AO2 required — argue with intent, e.g. FOR the claim: (1) Hume's motivation argument — beliefs alone are inert but moral judgements reliably motivate, so they are not pure beliefs but expressions of attitude; (2) Mackie's argument from relativity — persistent cross-cultural disagreement is best explained by different ways of life, not by misperception of mind-independent facts; (3) the verificationist point that no observation confirms 'stealing is wrong'. Consider the strongest objection AGAINST: the embedded-context (Frege–Geach) problem — 'if stealing is wrong, getting your little brother to steal is wrong' is valid, yet the unasserted antecedent expresses no emotion, so moral claims must retain truth-apt meaning; and moral disagreement is genuine contradiction supported by reasons on both sides, not a clash of cheers — Stevenson's 'persuasion' analysis re-describes rather than explains it. Respond: sophisticated non-cognitivism (Hare) treats moral judgements as universalisable prescriptions, allowing reasoning and disagreement within attitudes. Counter-response: prescriptions are not truth-apt either, and the fanatic who universalises consistently shows non-cognitivism cannot capture moral commitment as a stance towards facts. Weigh up and conclude consistently (e.g. the claim overstates: motivation and relativity support expressivism, but the logic of embedded contexts and the reason-giving character of moral disagreement show moral judgements are more than emotional expression — if cognitivism falls, error theory preserves the fact-stating purport better than emotivism).
practiceQuestions: Explain Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy. (5 marks)
Explain Hume's motivation argument and one cognitivist response. (12 marks)
Explain Mackie's argument from queerness. (5 marks)
Explain Hare's claim that moral judgements are universalisable prescriptions. (5 marks)
'Emotivism cannot account for how we use moral language.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)

topics.title: Metaphysics of God: Divine Attributes, Arguments and Religious Language
learningObjectives: Explain and evaluate the definitions of God as omnipotent, eternal and omniscient, including the paradox of the stone, Descartes vs Aquinas/Kenny, and Boethius vs Swinburne on eternality (Spec 3.3.1).
Explain and evaluate the ontological argument — Anselm (Proslogion 2 and 3), Descartes and Malcolm — with Gaunilo's perfect-island reply and Kant's 'existence is not a predicate' (Spec 3.3.2).
Explain and evaluate the teleological argument — Paley's watch, Swinburne's regularity — with Hume's critiques and Darwin's theory of evolution (Spec 3.3.2).
Explain and evaluate the cosmological argument — Aquinas' Three Ways, the Kalam argument, Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason — with Hume's and Russell's critiques (Spec 3.3.2).
Explain and evaluate the logical problem of evil (Mackie's inconsistent triad, Plantinga's free will defence) and the evidential problem (Rowe's fawn, Hick's vale of soul-making) (Spec 3.3.3).

Explain and evaluate religious experience (James, Swinburne's credulity and testimony, Flew's verification challenge) and religious language (via negativa, Aquinas' analogy, Ayer, Hare, Hick) (Specs 3.3.4–3.3.5).
Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; 'arguing with intent' and balanced evaluation only on 25-mark essays.
keyPoints: Omnipotence (Aquinas/Kenny): every power it is logically possible to have — the stone task is self-contradictory, not a genuine limit; Descartes: God can do the logically impossible, having created the eternal truths.
Boethius: God is timeless — 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life'; foreknowledge becomes timeless seeing, imposing only conditional necessity on free acts.
Ontological (Anselm Proslogion 2/3, Descartes, Malcolm) vs Kant: existence is not a real predicate (100 thalers) — the crucial debate is whether necessary existence escapes Kant.

Cosmological: Aquinas' Three Ways (per se regress), Kalam (no actual infinities), Leibniz (sufficient reason); Hume (fallacy of composition) and Russell ('the universe is just there, and that's all').

Evil: Mackie's triad answered by Plantinga (free will defence + transworld depravity); Rowe's fawn answered by theodicy (Hick) or sceptical theism. Flew's falsification challenge answered by Hare's bliks and Hick's eschatological verification.
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Kant is right: existence is not a predicate, and so the ontological argument fails.' Evaluate this claim. (25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 required: set out Anselm's Proslogion 2 (God = 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived'; exists in the understanding; greater to exist in reality; contradiction if God existed in the mind alone) and Proslogion 3 (necessary existence), Descartes' 'existence is a perfection' (triangle analogy) and Malcolm's version; explain Kant's critique — existence is not a real predicate ('is' adds no property; 100 real thalers and 100 imagined thalers share one concept). AO2 required: argue with intent, e.g. FOR the claim — (1) if 'is' adds nothing, defining God as existing, or counting existence among the perfections, begs the question: the argument analyses a concept and then asserts the concept is instantiated; (2) Malcolm's 'necessary existence' does not escape: treating a logical status as an attribute repeats exactly the error Kant identifies, so the argument still fails a priori. Consider the strongest objection AGAINST the claim: Kant targets ordinary, contingent existence; necessary existence — existence that cannot be lacked without incoherence — may be a genuine predicate, in which case Proslogion 3 survives, and Anselm's reply to Gaunilo (the argument's form applies to God alone) blocks the 'proves too much' objection; respond: even if necessary existence is a predicate, the move from coherence to instantiation needs defence — conceivability of a necessary being may not entail its instantiation. Weigh up (the crucial debate is Kant vs Malcolm on whether necessary existence is a predicate) and conclude consistently (e.g. the claim fails: Kant refutes arguments from contingent existence, but a modalised ontological argument treating necessary existence as a predicate remains live).
practiceQuestions: Explain the paradox of the stone and one response to it. (5 marks)
Explain Boethius' solution to the problem of God's foreknowledge and human free will. (12 marks)
Explain Aquinas' Third Way. (5 marks)
