practiceQuestions: State the AO2 assessment objective and describe what its top band (21-24 marks) looks like in a portfolio. (6 marks)
Explain the rule of 'fat over lean' in oil painting and the consequence of breaking it. (6 marks)
Distinguish relief and intaglio printmaking by where the ink sits, and name one method of each. (8 marks)
A student's sketchbook shows ten near-identical studies of the same subject in the same medium. Explain why this earns little AO2 credit and how the evidence could be rebuilt. (10 marks)
Explain how you would build AO2 evidence for the 15 supervised hours of Component 2 during the preparatory period. (12 marks)

topics.title: Annotation and Visual Language
learningObjectives: Explain what annotation is for in a coursework portfolio: recording ideas, observations and insights (AO3) while evidencing the reasoning behind AO1, AO2 and AO4 decisions.
Write annotations that move beyond description - intention, action, finding, next step - using appropriate specialist vocabulary, legibly and accurately.
Deploy the formal-elements vocabulary (line, tone, colour, texture, shape, form, space, composition, rhythm, scale) in analysis sentences, per the AQA 7202 skills list.
Record ideas systematically in sketchbooks, workbooks and journals: observations, gallery notes, media trials, critiques and critical reflection on progress.
Map annotation types to the assessment objectives so the moderator can find AO evidence without explanation.
Avoid the standard annotation failures: decorative notes, description without judgement, no links to artists or intentions, and loose unlabelled material.
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain how annotation in a coursework portfolio records ideas, observations and insights relevant to intentions, and show how the same annotations reflect critically on work and progress and evidence the other assessment objectives. (AO3 - 24 marks at A* level; assessed within AQA 7202/C and 7202/X)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO3: record + reflect critically; feeds AO1/AO2/AO4). Recording hits: primary observation (drawing and photography from the subject, on a variety of scales) annotated with findings; mind-maps generating artists, processes and imagery; gallery and museum notes recording what reproduction cannot show; media trials recorded as question - samples - comparison - decision; critique outcomes recorded. Reflection hits (the top-band differentiator): judgement notes in every session, dated so they read as reflection not hindsight; phase-transition review pages judging work against initial intentions and setting what the next phase must prove; reflection written as decisions - what failed, why, what changes. Feeds the other AOs: artist links in annotation evidence AO1; trials decisions and refinement notes evidence AO2; planning-study annotations and final-outcome evaluations evidence AO4. Language and format requirements stated: appropriate specialist vocabulary, legible, accurate language, notes attached to the work, supervised work clearly identified in Component 2. Top band: exceptional ability to record AND reflect critically - reflection at every phase, judgement in every note, and an audit trail the moderator can read cold.
practiceQuestions: State AO3 and explain the difference between its two halves. (6 marks)
Rewrite this annotation at the standard the top band expects: 'I used charcoal and it went quite well, I like the texture.' Explain each improvement. (8 marks)
Explain how the formal-elements vocabulary should be used in analysis, illustrating with two elements. (8 marks)
A student's portfolio shows strong final outcomes but almost no annotation on the pages between research and outcome. Explain the risk and the remedy. (10 marks)
Explain what should be recorded in a sketchbook during a gallery visit, and why first-hand study outweighs screen-based research. (8 marks)

topics.title: Western Classical Harmony
learningObjectives: Realise four-part SATB harmony in chorale style with secure voice leading: correct spacing, doubling, no parallel fifths or octaves, leading notes resolved and dissonances prepared (Edexcel 9MU0 Component 2, Bach chorale technique brief) (AO1/AO2).
Identify and use the four cadence types plus the cadential 6/4, and deploy secondary chords (ii, iii, IV, vi), dominant 7ths with inversions and secondary dominants such as V/V and V/vi (AO3/AO4).
Read and realise figured bass including 6, 6/4, 7, 6/5, 4/3 and 4/2, and explain suspensions as preparation-suspension-resolution (AO3).
Analyse modulations to closely related keys aurally and on skeleton scores using pivot-chord logic, as tested in Edexcel 9MU0/03 Section A (AO4).
Harmonise a given melody using an appropriate harmonic vocabulary, as demanded by the Edexcel chorale and arrangement briefs (AO2).
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain how the harmony at the close of a chorale phrase creates a perfect cadence, and how a suspension adds expressive tension. (5 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Marks land on five AO3/AO2 points: (1) identify Ic-V-I or V-I with both chords in root position; (2) leading note in V rises to the tonic, 7th of the chord falls by step; (3) soprano-bass contrary motion into the octave gives finality; (4) suspension described in three stages - note prepared as a consonance (4th above bass), held over as the bass changes to V creating dissonance, resolved down by step to the 3rd; (5) effect: the dissonance delays and intensifies the arrival on the tonic, typical of Bach's chorale cadences. Effect-based comments must accompany each label for full marks.
practiceQuestions: Name the four cadence types with their chord progressions, and state where each is typically used.
Explain how to modulate from C major to G major using a pivot chord, giving an example progression.
Distinguish a cadential 6/4 from a passing 6/4.
Explain how a 4-3 suspension is prepared, created and resolved, and why Bach uses it at cadences.
Describe your method for harmonising an unfamiliar 8-bar melody in the Bach chorale style.

topics.title: Sonata Form and Instrumental Genres
learningObjectives: Describe the tonal plan of a sonata-form exposition in a major key: first subject in tonic, transition modulating, second subject in dominant, codetta (AO1/AO3).
Explain how the development manipulates expository material through fragmentation, sequence and modulation, and how the recapitulation differs from the exposition (AO3/AO4).
Analyse first and second subject contrast (melody, rhythm, texture, key) in the set works: Berlioz, Symphonie Fantastique movement I and Wieck-Schumann, Piano Trio Op. 17 movement 1 (AO4).
Compare sonata form with related Classical structures: ternary, rondo, sonata-rondo, concerto double exposition and the four-movement symphonic cycle (AO3).
Use structural terminology with precision in Edexcel Section B essays, linking musical elements, context and language (AO3/AO4).
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the musical elements, context and language of Movement I of Berlioz's Symphonie Fantastique, with particular reference to how Berlioz adapts Classical sonata form. (30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO3 + AO4, Edexcel 9MU0/03 Section B essay two): (1) Knowledge - identify the form: long slow introduction (Réveries) then Allegro with first subject, transition, late lyrical second subject (idée fixe), development, climactic coda recall; key structure of C minor/major. (2) Analysis - how each element works: chromatic first subject, idée fixe's stepwise shape and orchestration, huge dynamic and register contrasts, expanded orchestra (four harps, added brass, divided strings). (3) Context and language - 1830 Paris, programme symphony, semi-autobiographical (Harriet Smithson), Romantic aesthetics vs the Classical symphonic model Berlioz knew from Beethoven. (4) Evaluation - judgement throughout: e.g. the idée fixe's late entry and coda return subvert Classical proportions to serve the programme; top answers argue a case rather than list features, using precise terminology (idée fixe, transition, coda, programmatic) anchored to the score.
practiceQuestions: Explain the tonal structure of the exposition in a Classical sonata form in a major key.
Describe four devices a composer uses in a sonata-form development and their effects.
How does the recapitulation differ from the exposition, and why?
Compare the treatment of sonata form in Wieck-Schumann's Piano Trio Op. 17 movement 1 with the Classical model.
Why does Berlioz place a long slow introduction before the allegro in movement I of Symphonie Fantastique, and how does the idée fixe alter sonata form?

topics.title: Set Works (Edexcel Areas of Study)
learningObjectives: Identify the key musical features, context and language of each set work across the six Edexcel areas of study (9MU0/03) (AO1/AO3).
Analyse set-work extracts from audio with skeleton scores, naming devices (leitmotif, ostinato, idée fixe, chorale) and their effects (AO4).
Place each set work in its genre and historical context - Lutheran cantata, programme symphony, film score, 1960s pop, acid jazz, gamelan influence, spectralism, primitivism (AO3).
Draw links between set works and unfamiliar music in the Section B essay one (20 marks) (AO4).
Evaluate the musical elements, context and language of one set work as a whole in essay two (Q6, 30 marks) (AO3/AO4).
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Elfman's Batman Returns shows that film music is built on leitmotif and harmonic colour rather than conventional melody.' With reference to the specified cues, evaluate this view. (10 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO3 + AO4): (1) Define leitmotif and apply: Penguin and Catwoman ideas recur and transform across 'Birth of a Penguin Parts I and II' and 'Batman vs the Circus'. (2) Harmonic colour: dark chromatic/minor harmony, tritone-related shifts, celesta and low-brass sonorities - cite moments. (3) Counter-evidence: Elfman's sweeping melodic writing (e.g. 'The Rise and Fall from Grace') shows memorable tunes do exist; Herrmann's Psycho by contrast abandons melody for ostinato and dissonance in 'The Murder', showing film music spans both poles. (4) Context: post-Wagnerian leitmotif tradition in Hollywood scoring; music's function is characterisation and cue-matching to picture. (5) Judgement: largely valid but overstated - leitmotif and colour dominate, yet melodic identity remains central to Elfman's idiom.
practiceQuestions: Describe how Bach presents the chorale melody in movement 1 of Ein feste Burg and explain the effect.
How does Herrmann create tension in the Psycho cues without conventional melody?
Compare the use of non-Western musical material in Debussy's Pagodes and Shankar's Breathing Under Water.
Explain the significance of the rhythm and harmony in 'The Augurs of Spring' from The Rite of Spring.
What makes Eleanor Rigby unusual as a 1960s pop recording, and how would you link it to another set work in the unfamiliar-music essay?

topics.title: Aural and Dictation
learningObjectives: Complete short melodic dictation exercises (pitch and rhythm) on staff notation from unfamiliar music related to the set works (Edexcel 9MU0/03 Section A) (AO4).
Identify aurally chords, keys, cadences and modulations, including inversions and dominant 7ths (AO3/AO4).
Answer skeleton-score listening questions on set works: locate devices, name keys and cadences, justify opinions (AO4).
Manage the individual audio player and extract timings to maximise marks per listen (AO4).
Apply set-work knowledge to unfamiliar extracts in the Section B essay one (20 marks) (AO3/AO4).
topics.exampleQuestion: You hear an unfamiliar extract in a popular style. Complete the melody on the staff provided, then identify the key and the cadence at the end of the phrase. (6 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO4): (1) Correct key signature and time signature written immediately (1 mark); (2) contour and phrase-ending pitch marked after first listen (1); (3) rhythm accurate - metre, bar lines, rests, syncopation (2); (4) pitches accurate - scale degrees onto the staff, intervals correct (1); (5) key named with evidence (tonic from final chord/opening harmony) and cadence identified by progression and type (e.g. imperfect, ?-V) (1). Partial credit applies: rhythm or pitch alone scores; a named key without evidence does not. Never leave blanks - plausible scale-degree guesses earn marks, silence does not.
practiceQuestions: Describe your complete method for a melody/rhythm dictation exercise with three plays.
How would you identify aurally whether a chord is in root position, first or second inversion?
Name the four cadences and how each sounds; how are they tested in 9MU0/03?
How do you spot a modulation in a listening question?
What does essay one (Q5, 20 marks) in Section B require, and what is the best method?

topics.title: Composition Briefs
learningObjectives: State the 9MU0/02 portfolio requirements: two compositions, 60 marks, 40-mark free choice/AoS brief (min 4 minutes) plus 20-mark technique brief (min 1 minute), combined minimum 6 minutes (AO1).
Distinguish the six briefs relating to areas of study (released 1 September) from the four technique briefs - Bach chorale, two-part counterpoint, arrangement, remix (released 1 April) (AO1).
Apply the assessment criteria: coherence (unity and variety), expressive control (response to brief, audience and occasion) and technical control (idiomatic writing, devices and conventions) (AO2).
Use development devices - repetition, sequence, fragmentation, variation - and manage texture and harmonic vocabulary to reach Level 5 bands (AO2).
Avoid self-penalising choices: excess length, unidiomatic writing, ignoring the brief's stated audience and occasion (AO2).
topics.exampleQuestion: 'To score well, a composition must be long and harmonically complex.' Evaluate this claim with reference to the Edexcel composing assessment criteria. (10 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO2 awareness applied analytically): (1) Length: minimum 4 minutes (free choice) + 1 minute (technique), combined 6 minutes; guided maximum 8 - submissions over the maximum are still marked but 'may be self-penalising', so length beyond the guide adds no reward. (2) Harmony: the musical language names inversions, dominant 7ths and extended chords, but the grids reward control and coherence, not complexity for its own sake - grid 3 caps unidiomatic or mishandled writing, and grid 1 rewards a 'mature balance of unity and variety'. (3) What actually earns Level 5: assured, imaginative development of ideas (grid 1), effective response to the brief's audience and occasion (grid 2), idiomatic command of style and convention (grid 3); the technique grid rewards 'fluency and creativity' with 'elegant, well shaped lines'. (4) Judgement: the claim is false - controlled development of modest material beats sprawling complexity; a fluent 6-minute portfolio with clear structure and idiomatic writing out-scores an overloaded 10-minute one.
practiceQuestions: State the full requirements of the Edexcel 9MU0/02 composing portfolio.
Outline the parameters of the four technique briefs and what each assesses.
Explain what the three assessment grids reward and what caps each one.
How would you develop an 8-bar idea into a Level 5 four-minute composition?
Why can a composition be 'self-penalising', and how do you avoid it?

topics.title: Performance and Repertoire
learningObjectives: State the 9MU0/01 requirements: 30%, 60 marks, a recorded recital of at least eight minutes of music, solo, ensemble, improvisation or music-technology realisation (AO1).
Apply the difficulty levels booklet: level 7 is 'standard', 8+ 'more difficult', levels 1-6 'less difficult' and potentially self-penalising (AO1).
Explain the marking: three grids (technical control; accuracy and fluency; expressive control, style and context) out of 48 plus 12 marks for difficulty (AO1).
Plan a recital programme balancing difficulty, duration and contrast, and manage the recording rules (recorded after 1 March, submitted by 15 May, whole re-records only) (AO1).
Compare Edexcel's approach with OCR H543 and Eduqas, including their programme-note requirements (AO1).
topics.exampleQuestion: 'Playing easier music perfectly gains more marks than playing harder music with minor errors.' Evaluate this claim with reference to the Edexcel performance assessment model. (10 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO1 awareness applied analytically): (1) The model: 60 marks = three grids out of 48 + 12 for difficulty; the raw grid mark maps through the difficulty level column, so identical technical quality earns more at higher difficulty. (2) Difficulty levels: level 7 is 'standard'; 8+ 'more difficult'; levels 1-6 'less difficult' and flagged as potentially self-penalising - they may restrict access to higher grid bands. (3) However, accuracy and fluency (grid 2) penalises errors: harder music invites more slips, and lost grid marks can outweigh difficulty gains - 'more than one or two' errors drops a band. (4) Judgement: the claim is false as stated - optimum is the hardest music playable securely; the specification's own warning is that easier pieces self-penalise, but so does insecure over-reaching. A balanced, secure Grade 7-8 programme is the mark-maximising choice.
practiceQuestions: State the full requirements of the Edexcel 9MU0/01 performing assessment.
Explain how the 60 marks are allocated and how difficulty affects the total.
How does Edexcel assess instruments with no graded exam tradition?
Compare the Edexcel and OCR/Eduqas performance assessments.
How would you plan a recital programme to maximise marks?

topics.title: Theatre Practitioners: Brecht, Stanislavski and Artaud
learningObjectives: Define the core terminology of Brecht, Stanislavski and Artaud precisely enough for AO1 credit (epic theatre, Verfremdungseffekt, gestus, given circumstances, magic if, objectives, emotional memory, Theatre of Cruelty).
Apply each practitioner's methods to specific moments of performance texts, justifying every decision by its intended effect on an audience (AO2).
Contrast the three practitioners' views of the actor-audience relationship in evaluative answers.
Use a practitioner lens to generate director, performer and designer decisions for AQA 7262 Component 1 Section B and Edexcel 9DR0 Component 3 Section C.
Avoid biography-led writing: every paragraph must move from method to staging decision to audience effect.
topics.exampleQuestion: As a director, explain how you would apply Brecht's ideas in a staging of Mother Courage and Her Children to communicate an anti-war message to a contemporary audience. (AQA 7262 Component 1 Section B style, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic for the top band:
  • AO1 accuracy: use terms correctly — epic theatre, episodic structure, Verfremdungseffekt, gestus, demonstration, historicification, didactic song, placards.
  • AO2 justified decisions tied to the text: open with a placard fixing scene 1 ('Spring 1624. Sweden fears no war...') to historicify; keep the cart as a mobile gestus pulled round the stage; visible rig and half-curtain; harsh white light instead of atmospheric wash.
  • Alienation choices at the key losses: each 'loss' of a son announced flatly, almost as an accounting entry; after Swiss Cheese's death Courage sings her trade song rather than grieving, denying catharsis.
  • Gestus specified: Yvette's hat and garters as costume semiotics of a body traded to the army; Courage biting the coin.
  • Audience effect throughout: every decision justified as preventing empathy long enough for the audience to judge war profiteering — the opposite of a tearful tragedy reading.
  • Conditions for the marks: decisions must be specific to cited moments (not a generic Brecht checklist), and the interpretation must thread consistently from opening placard to final scene, with the cart's final pull showing Courage unchanged.
practiceQuestions: Explain how Stanislavski's 'magic if' and 'given circumstances' work together to produce truthful performance.
As a director of Hedda Gabler, explain how you would use Stanislavski's System in rehearsal to develop the portrayal of Hedda in Act 1.
'Artaud's ideas are more visible in twenty-first-century theatre than Brecht's.' Evaluate this claim.
Explain how gestus communicates social meaning in Mother Courage and Her Children.
Compare how Brecht and Stanislavski each treat the actor-audience relationship.

topics.title: Devising Theatre
learningObjectives: State exactly what each board's devising component requires (AQA 7262 Component 2: devised performance + 3,000-word working notebook, 30%; Edexcel 9DR0 Component 1: devised piece from a set-play stimulus + 3,000-word portfolio, 40%).
Plan a devising process from stimulus to performance: research, practical exploration, selection, structuring, design integration and refinement.
Justify structural and stylistic choices (linear vs episodic, motifs, framing) by their intended effect on an audience.
Write notebook or portfolio entries that evidence development and collaboration rather than narrating the timetable.
Evaluate your own process analytically: intention vs outcome, problems solved, choices rejected.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate how your response to the stimulus influenced the structure of your devised piece, justifying two significant changes made during the development process. (Edexcel 9DR0 Component 1 portfolio style)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic for the top band:
  • AO1 creating and developing ideas: identify the stimulus element that anchored the work (a theme, image or character type from the set play) and the artistic intention that grew from it.
  • Justified decisions, not description: change 1 and change 2 each stated as a before/after (e.g. linear chronology replaced by montage of three images; a naturalistic kitchen scene cut and replaced by a physical-theatre sequence).
  • Evidence of testing: workshops, peer-audience response, or rehearsal observation that motivated each change.
  • Stimulus traced through: the response to the stimulus remains visible in the final structure — the marker can see the journey from source to stage.
  • Evaluation register: intention vs outcome ('the montage did communicate X, but the final image needed one more transformation, which time did not allow').
  • Conditions: changes must be significant (structural, not line-edits), connected to the stimulus, and the justification must reference intended audience effect, not personal preference alone.
practiceQuestions: How should you evidence a practitioner's methods in the AQA working notebook without it becoming a biography?
Evaluate the use of two workshop techniques in developing your devised material.
Your group received conflicting responses to the stimulus. Evaluate how you resolved this.
Explain how you structured your devised piece and justify why an episodic structure suited your stimulus.
What makes written evaluation band 5 rather than merely descriptive?

topics.title: Interpreting Set Texts
learningObjectives: Map your set plays to the correct component: AQA 7262 Section A (dramatic and stylistic study) and Section B (staging); Edexcel 9DR0 Component 3 Section B (page to stage) and Section C (interpreting texts).
Construct a coherent director's concept and derive concrete staging decisions from it.
Justify interpretation with textual evidence — dialogue, stage directions, subtext and structure — rather than personal preference.
Apply practitioner lenses (Stanislavski, Brecht, Artaud) to generate performer, director and designer decisions for set texts.
Evaluate alternative interpretations and defend your chosen one by its intended effect on a contemporary audience.
topics.exampleQuestion: As a director, explain how you would realise your interpretation of the final scene of Yerma to communicate meaning to a twenty-first-century audience. (AQA 7262 Component 1 Section B style, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic for the top band:
  • AO1 interpretive coherence: a stated concept governing the scene (e.g. 'Yerma's society as a locked room; the climax as the door breaking') with period/setting decision justified from the text's fertility ritual and chorus.
  • AO2 moment-specific staging: decisions for the specified scene only — the shepherd's arrival, the struggle at the bed, the killing, the Peasant Woman's final verdict — with blocking, levels and proxemics named.
  • Design integrated as meaning: e.g. the doorway of light through which the shepherd enters (the 'open door' motif literalised), cold sound design replacing the earlier water motifs, costume of Yerma unchanged so the audience reads accumulated damage.
  • Practitioner-informed option credited: e.g. Artaudian chant and percussive sound in the struggle, or a Brechtian placard before the verdict — each justified by audience effect.
  • Audience effect as the verdict of every paragraph: contemporary relevance stated and earned (fertility, coercion, honour culture made legible to a modern house).
  • Conditions: scene-specific detail is mandatory; generalised whole-play staging caps the mark; an alternative considered strengthens evaluation.
practiceQuestions: As a director, explain how you would stage the opening of Road by Jim Cartwright to establish the world of the play for the audience.
As a director, explain how you would use the ensemble to stage Christopher's overwhelmed moments in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time.
As a director, explain how you would stage the opening scene of That Face to present Martha and Mia's relationship for a contemporary audience.
As a director, justify a Brechtian interpretation of Woyzeck for a contemporary audience. (Edexcel 9DR0 Component 3 Section C style)
As a performer, explain how you would apply Stanislavski's System to play Hedda Gabler in the burning of the manuscript.

topics.title: Live Theatre Review
learningObjectives: State the conditions of each board's live theatre question (AQA 7262 C1 Section C: extract provided, 25 marks; Edexcel 9DR0 C3 Section A: 20 marks, 500 words of notes allowed in).
Analyse performance, design and directing through specific, named moments rather than general impressions.
Convert description into evaluation: every technique linked to its effect on the audience and judged against the production's intention.
Deploy precise vocabulary (semiotics, proxemics, kinaesthetic response, soundscape, staging configuration) accurately under timed conditions.
Structure a top-band answer: production facts, thematic paragraphs, evaluative conclusion.
topics.exampleQuestion: Analyse and evaluate how effectively the acting and design of the live production you have seen communicated meaning to its audience. Refer to the extract provided. (AQA 7262 Component 1 Section C style, 25 marks)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic for the top band:
  • AO2 analysis of specific realisation: named moments from the extract staged in detail — vocal/physical skills, proxemics, lighting states, sound cues — never generalised praise.
  • Evaluation running throughout: each moment judged for effectiveness on the audience, using the audience's own response as evidence where possible.
  • Integration of acting and design: the two must be connected (e.g. how the isolation special forced intimacy onto a duologue) rather than covered in separate lists.
  • Intention referenced: the production's interpretive stance identified early and used as the criterion for the final judgement.
  • Vocabulary deployed accurately: semiotics, proxemics, tempo-rhythm, configuration — precise terms attached to precise observations.
  • Conditions: the extract anchors the answer (whole-production wanderings lose the AO2 focus); description without verdict caps below top band; balanced judgement (one admitted weakness) strengthens rather than weakens evaluation.
practiceQuestions: Evaluate how successfully one performer communicated their character in the production you have seen.
Analyse how design elements created meaning in a key moment of the production you have seen.
Evaluate the director's interpretation in the production you have seen.
Using your notes, explain how one moment of the production created impact on the audience. (Edexcel 9DR0 C3 Section A style)
'The most effective productions manipulate their audience's behaviour.' How far did the production you have seen do this?

topics.title: Design Elements: Set, Costume, Lighting and Sound
learningObjectives: Analyse set and costume as semiotic systems: colour, texture, period, status and transformation carrying meaning to the audience.
Use lighting vocabulary accurately — states, angles, colour, cues — and justify each state by its function (visibility, focus, mood, time, place).
Distinguish diegetic and non-diegetic sound and analyse soundscape, underscoring and silence as designed meaning.
Apply practitioner principles to design: Brecht's non-illusionism, Stanislavski's authentic detail, Artaud's sensory overload.
Structure designer-perspective answers: design decision → how it is realised → intended audience meaning, evidenced from the text.
topics.exampleQuestion: As a designer, explain how you would use lighting and sound in the final scene of Yerma to communicate the collapse of the play's world to a contemporary audience. (AQA 7262 Component 1 style, 30 marks)
topics.modelAnswer:
Mark-scheme logic for the top band:
  • AO2 concrete design decisions: named states and cues for the specified scene — e.g. the warm domestic wash that served the opening world extinguished scene by scene until a single cold special isolates Yerma at the bed.
  • Cue placement analysed: the blackout on the killing rather than after the verdict; the six-second hold of silence before the Peasant Woman speaks.
  • Sound design specified: diegetic water motif (present since scene 1) cut to silence — its absence the meaning; non-diegetic low drone rising as the chorus gathers; the women's chanted keening placed behind the audience so sound encircles the house.
  • Function vocabulary used accurately: isolation special, crossfade, snap, soundscape, diegetic/non-diegetic — each attached to an effect, not name-dropped.
  • Audience meaning justified: collapse communicated as the withdrawal of every warm design language the production built, so the audience experiences the world leaving before the words say it.
  • Conditions: scene-specific (not whole-play design); lighting and sound integrated rather than listed; a considered alternative strengthens evaluation.
practiceQuestions: As a designer, explain your set design for The Glass Menagerie and justify how it serves the play's memory structure.
Explain how you would use costume semiotics in a staging of The Importance of Being Earnest to communicate class and performance to a modern audience.
As a designer, explain how you would use lighting to stage the overwhelms and overload of Christopher in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time.
Explain how a Brechtian designer would stage Mother Courage and Her Children, justifying the design against a naturalistic alternative.
As a sound designer, explain how you would use sound in Yerma to track the protagonist's psychological deterioration.

topics.title: Media Language
learningObjectives: Analyse how technical, symbolic and written codes construct meaning and response in any set product (AO2)
Apply Neale's genre theory to explain how products balance repetition and difference for industries and audiences (AO2)
Use Todorov, Propp and Barthes' narrative codes to map narrative structure and audience engagement (AO2)
Denote then connote: apply Barthes' order of signification and anchorage to print and audiovisual texts (AO2)
Evaluate how multimodal texts (websites, video games, vlogs) use the affordances of different modes (AO2)
Deploy precise media language vocabulary under timed exam conditions (AO1)
keyPoints: Nothing is accidental: every technical and aesthetic choice is a meaning-making decision you must be able to justify (AO2).
Neale: genres are 'instances of repetition and difference' - familiarity sells, novelty sustains.
Todorov: equilibrium, disruption, recognition, repair, new equilibrium - changed, not restored, in complex texts.
Barthes: denote first, then connote; ask how anchorage steers the reading.
Structure every analysis: convention named, example located, meaning explained, audience response inferred.
topics.exampleQuestion: Explore how media language is used to construct meanings and responses in the set newspaper front pages of the Daily Mirror and The Times. [12]
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO2 analysis of media language in the set products, with AO1 terminology): (1) Identify the form conventions of each front page - masthead, lead story, image, typography, price, promo straps. (2) The Mirror: red masthead and bold sans-serif headline connote urgency and populism; colloquial written code ('one of us' register) constructs a preferred reading aligned with its centre-left, ordinary-Briton news values; image choice dramatises emotion and anchors the story to human interest. (3) The Times: blue masthead, serif typography, restrained headline and multi-story layout connote authority, tradition and measured judgement; the anchorage of images with formal captions constructs the reader as informed citizen rather than entertained consumer. (4) Responses sought: Mirror seeks emotional identification and indignation; The Times seeks trust and deliberation - two constructed positions for two segmented audiences. (5) Top band: evaluate via Levi-Strauss (binary oppositions of elite/ordinary, tradition/modernity) and note that the same day's events are re-presented differently, proving constructedness.
practiceQuestions: Explain how genre conventions create audience pleasure in the set television product you have studied. [8]
Explore how narrative is used in the set advertising and marketing products you have studied. [12]
How useful is Todorov's narratology for understanding the set products you have studied? [25]
Explain how Barthes' concepts of denotation, connotation and myth can be applied to the set products you have studied. [12]
Explore how multimodality shapes audience response in the set online media products you have studied. [12]

topics.title: Representation
learningObjectives: Explain Hall's claim that representation is constitutive - media do not reflect reality but construct it (AO1)
Apply Dyer's account of stereotypes and their functions to analyse set products past and present (AO2)
Deploy Mulvey, van Zoonen, Butler and bell hooks to evaluate gendered representation, including counter-arguments (AO2)
Analyse representations of ethnicity, age, disability, sexuality and class with precise terminology (AO2)
Evaluate how far representation has changed over time, using historical vs contemporary set products (AO3)
Structure P-E-A analytical chains that link choices to ideology to audience positioning (AO2)
keyPoints: Hall: representation is constitutive, not reflective - the media help construct the realities they claim to describe.
Dyer: stereotypes order the world, shortcut identification and can project the dominant group's fears onto the Other.
Mulvey: the male gaze codes women as image, men as bearer of the look - test it against Tide, GQ and music video.
Butler: gender is performed through repetition, so representation participates in constructing gender norms.
Always historicise: what was conventional at production is not what is conventional now.
topics.exampleQuestion: Discuss the ways in which gender is represented in the set advertising and marketing products you have studied. In your answer you should refer to feminist theories. [WJEC/Eduqas A680 Component 1 style]
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO2 application of feminist theory to set products, with AO1 knowledge and historical context): (1) Tide: housewife stereotype - domestic competence as the whole of femininity, anchored by typography to the 1950s domestic settlement; apply Mulvey (woman as spectacle for the approving consumer gaze) and van Zoonen (gender as discourse of the period). (2) WaterAid: Claudia constructed as agent - singing, moving - a countertype resisting the passive-victim script; apply hooks (empowerment vs charity-commodification of the female subject). (3) McCain: inclusive family construction - gender roles broadened, but family still defined through mealtime care labour. (4) Evaluate: historicise (conventional then vs now); Gauntlett's counter (audiences pick 'n' mix, read ironically); conclusion - representations construct, not reflect, gender (Hall/Butler), and change tracks shifts in who controls production and what sells.
practiceQuestions: Explain how Hall's theory of representation can be applied to the set newspaper products you have studied. [12]
How useful are Dyer's ideas about stereotypes for understanding representation in the set products you have studied? [25]
Explore how the male gaze is used and/or challenged in the set products you have studied. [12]
Explain how Butler's theory of gender performativity can be applied to the set products you have studied. [12]
How far is representation of marginalised groups in the media improving? In your answer refer to the set products you have studied. [25]

topics.title: Media Industries
learningObjectives: Explain vertical and horizontal integration, conglomeration and synergy with named examples (AO1)
Compare funding models (licence fee, advertising, subscription, tax relief, microtransactions) and their consequences for content (AO2)
Evaluate the BBC's public service remit, charter framework and funding under political and market pressure (AO2)
Map the UK regulatory landscape (Ofcom, BBFC, IPSO, ASA, PEGI/VSC) and its difficulties in the digital age (AO2)
Apply Curran and Seaton, Hesmondhalgh and Livingstone and Lunt to the set products and current industries (AO2)
Assess how digital disruption has transformed production, distribution, funding and regulation (AO3)
keyPoints: Curran and Seaton: concentrated ownership prioritises profit over pluralism - less diversity, weaker democracy.
Hesmondhalgh: cultural industries are risk-averse; 'independent' labels are often brands owned by majors.
Livingstone and Lunt: regulators face a dilemma - protect or enable choice - sharpened by digital convergence.
BBC: Reith's inform, educate, entertain; charter-funded licence fee; Ofcom-regulated since 2017.
Digital disruption: streaming, piracy and Web 2.0 dismantled the vertical, stable, analogue industry model.
topics.exampleQuestion: Discuss the relevance of Curran and Seaton's ideas about ownership and control to the media industries you have studied. [OCR H409 Component 02 style]
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO2 application of theory to industries, with AO1 knowledge and AO3 evaluation): (1) State the theory: concentrated ownership driven by profit motive produces limited variety, creativity and pluralism - media serve capital before citizens. (2) Apply to set products: Mirror/Reach and Times/News UK press concentration and shared news values; Straight Outta Compton as Universal-packaged counter-cultural content; Submarine/Warp as the subsidised indie alternative. (3) Evidence beyond set products: Big Five studio conglomeration, Disney's vertical integration, press ownership and political alignment. (4) Evaluate: digital distribution has lowered barriers (diversified voices despite concentrated ownership) - but platform gatekeepers (Google, Meta, Netflix) re-concentrate power through algorithms, so Curran and Seaton's logic migrates rather than expires. (5) Conclude: their claim remains a powerful lens on ownership-concentration, updated for the platform age.
practiceQuestions: Explain how vertical and horizontal integration shape the media industries you have studied. [12]
Is the licence fee still the best way to fund public service broadcasting? In your answer refer to the BBC. [25]
How useful is Livingstone and Lunt's theory of regulation for understanding the media today? [25]
Explain how digital disruption has changed the newspaper industry. Refer to the set newspaper products you have studied. [12]
How far do Hesmondhalgh's ideas about cultural industries explain the success of the set film products you have studied? [25]

topics.title: Audiences
learningObjectives: Apply Hall's encoding/decoding model to explain preferred, negotiated and oppositional readings of set products (AO2)
Apply Blumler and Katz's four gratifications to explain why audiences consume named products (AO2)
Use Jenkins to analyse fandom, participatory culture and transmedia behaviour (AO2)
Evaluate the effects debate: hypodermic syringe, Bandura's social learning and Gerbner's cultivation against active-audience evidence (AO2/AO3)
Analyse audience segmentation (demographic, psychographic) and its industrial logic (AO2)
Assess how and why audiences are regulated: BBFC, PEGI, watershed, Online Safety Act (AO2)
keyPoints: Hall: producers cannot guarantee readings - decoding is a social act, positioned by age, culture and politics.
Blumler and Katz: audiences actively use media for surveillance, identity, relationships and diversion.
Jenkins: fandom is participatory - 'textual poachers' rework texts; convergence enables transmedia storytelling.
Bandura (social learning) vs Gauntlett (audiences as reflexive): the effects debate is the exam's classic dialectic.
Audience regulation is protection logic: BBFC, PEGI, watershed, Online Safety Act - test it with Livingstone and Lunt.
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain how audiences can respond differently to the same media product. In your answer refer to Hall's encoding/decoding model and to the set products you have studied. [OCR H409 Component 02 style]
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO2 application of reception theory, AO1 terminology, AO3 evaluation): (1) State the model: producers encode a preferred meaning; audiences decode from social positions as preferred, negotiated or oppositional. (2) Apply with set products: Tide's encoded housewife ideal decoded with irony/opposition by contemporary audiences (historical distance); Mirror vs Times front pages decoded along political identity lines; WaterAid's empowerment encoding met by negotiated readings questioning the charity gaze; The Returned's artful restraint decoded as prestige by niche audiences and as dull by mass audiences (cultural capital). (3) Explain the mechanism: decoding is socially positioned (age, class, culture, politics), not random; anchorage steers but cannot compel (Barthes). (4) Evaluate: producers cannot guarantee readings; hegemony requires consent which can be withheld (Gramsci). (5) Conclude: divergent reception is the norm - 'distortion' between encoding and decoding is structured, not accidental.
practiceQuestions: Explain why the hypodermic syringe model is considered discredited, using the set products where relevant. [8]
How far do Bandura's and Gerbner's theories explain the effects of media violence on audiences? [25]
Explain how uses and gratifications can be applied to the set radio or online media products you have studied. [12]
How useful is Jenkins' theory of fandom for understanding contemporary audiences? [25]
Explain how and why audiences are regulated. Refer to the set products where relevant. [12]

topics.title: Media Theories
learningObjectives: Recall the full set of required theorists and locate each in the correct framework area (AO1)
Apply each theory to named set products with precise, specific claims (AO2)
Evaluate each theory's relevance and limitations against contemporary media (AO3)
Pair theories dialectically (effects vs activity, determinism vs agency) in extended answers (AO2/AO3)
Avoid name-dropping: use theory to drive analysis rather than decorate it (AO2)
Synthesise across the framework - representation, industries, audiences - in 25-mark essays (AO3)
keyPoints: The set list is an argument, not a syllabus: effects (Bandura, Gerbner) vs activity (Gauntlett, Jenkins, Shirky); determinism (Mulvey) vs agency (Gauntlett).
Apply theory to set products, not in a vacuum: every theory in this topic is examinable as 'apply to the set products you have studied'.
Evaluate relevance: pre-digital theories need updating (cultivation and the feed; reception and the algorithm).
Pair theories dialectically for 25-mark structure: thesis, antithesis, synthesis.
One theorist applied in depth beats four name-dropped.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the relevance of two of the theories you have studied to understanding media products today. You should refer to the set products you have studied. [OCR H409 Component 02 style, 25]
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic (AO2 application, AO3 evaluation of relevance, set-product specificity): (1) Choose a productive pairing - e.g. Bandura (effects) vs Gauntlett (activity). (2) Apply Bandura: social learning (imitation with identification/reward) underwrites video-game violence panics and PEGI's age logic; Luther's vigilante violence raises the copycat question. (3) Apply Gauntlett: audiences are reflexive users of media-as-resource - Zoella's audience picks 'n' mix identity; the Bobo doll's leap from lab imitation to real-world harm fails Gauntlett's methodological critique. (4) Evaluate relevance today: effects anxieties remain live (Online Safety Act 2023 as policy built on them), but activity evidence is stronger for contemporary behaviour - with the algorithmic feed as the genuine test case (personalised cultivation?). (5) Conclude with calibrated judgment: Bandura remains relevant where regulation and children are concerned; Gauntlett better explains everyday contemporary audience behaviour - relevance depends on the question asked.
practiceQuestions: How useful is Barthes' semiotics for understanding the set advertising and newspaper products you have studied? [25]
How far do Curran and Seaton's ideas about media power apply to the media industries today? [25]
Compare Bandura's and Gauntlett's theories of audience. Which better explains contemporary audience behaviour? [25]
How useful are Butler's and hooks' theories for understanding representation of gender and ethnicity in the set products you have studied? [25]
Evaluate the usefulness of Livingstone and Lunt's theory of regulation in the digital age. Refer to media products you have studied. [25]

topics.title: Media Production (NEA)
learningObjectives: Decode a NEA brief and choose the option that best matches your skills and concept control (AO3)
Write a statement of intent or aims that justifies language, representation and audience decisions with theory (AO3)
Plan and produce a cross-media production with genuine synergy between linked products (AO3)
Target a specified audience through gratification-led, segmentation-aware choices (AO3)
Apply representation decisions that construct rather than stereotype, citing Hall, Butler or Gauntlett (AO3)
Avoid the standard NEA pitfalls: genre blur, weak synergy, missed brief requirements, broken realism
keyPoints: The NEA is 30% of the A Level and marked against the same theoretical framework as the exams - production is theory applied.
Brief requirements are binary: met or missed. Read the brief twice, then highlight every noun.
The statement of intent (approximately 500 words) is where marks are won or lost: justify every choice with language, representation, industry and audience reasoning.
Synergy must be visible: shared world, identity, typography and call-to-action across all products.
Plan everything (storyboards, mock-ups), shoot tightly, edit ruthlessly - technical quality is a named strand.
topics.exampleQuestion: NEA brief (Eduqas A680 Component 3 style): Produce a cross-media production for a new television drama targeting a 16-25 audience, comprising a title sequence, a website homepage and a print-based marketing product. Write your statement of aims and objectives (approximately 500 words).
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic for a high-band statement of aims (AO3 across all strands): (1) Concept: name the drama, its genre (e.g. crime/psychological thriller hybrid), the three required products and the brief's stated 16-25 audience. (2) Media language: conventions named and deployed - low-key lighting, shallow focus, contrapuntal score coding genre threat; narrative enigma set up in the title sequence; Neale's repetition/difference stated (procedural conventions subverted by a legible hybridity). (3) Representation: protagonist constructed against the genre's default (e.g. a young female detective as countertype to the maverick-male detective - justified with Hall's constructedness and Dyer's countertype); structural not tokenistic - she holds narrative power. (4) Audience: 16-25 profiled demographically (age, ABC1/C2DE) and psychographically (explorers); gratifications by product (diversion in the sequence, identity and community on the website); platform and distribution logic (broadcast or streaming, with the website as engagement hub); synergy declared - shared world, typography, calls-to-action. (5) Technical: the production meets the promise - continuity editing, mixed sound, functional navigation, print-quality imagery.
practiceQuestions: Explain what a cross-media production is and why the NEA requires one. [8]
Write the media language paragraph of a statement of intent for a thriller title sequence. [12]
Write the representation paragraph of a statement of intent for a product representing a group historically stereotyped in the media. [12]
Explain how you would target a stated 16-25 audience across a cross-media production. [12]
Evaluate the most common reasons candidates lose marks in the NEA, and how to avoid them. [25]

topics.title: Applied Anatomy and Exercise Physiology
learningObjectives: Describe the cardiovascular responses to exercise: heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, Starling's law, venous return mechanisms and the vascular shunt (AQA 3.1.1; OCR 1.1; Edexcel Topic 1)
Explain respiratory mechanics, minute ventilation, gaseous exchange and the neural and chemical regulation of breathing at rest and during exercise (AQA 3.1.2; OCR 1.1)
Describe motor units, the all-or-nothing law, the three muscle fibre types, proprioceptors and PNF stretching (AQA 3.1.3; OCR 1.1)
Explain the ATP-PC, glycolytic and aerobic energy systems and apply the energy continuum to sporting examples (AQA 3.1.4; OCR 1.2)
Explain EPOC, its fast and slow components, and the value of an active cool-down (AQA 3.2; OCR 1.2)
Evaluate training methods and their cardiovascular, respiratory, neuromuscular and metabolic adaptations, including periodisation (AQA 3.2.2; OCR 1.2)
keyPoints: Q = SV x HR; trained athletes increase Q mainly through a larger stroke volume (160-200 ml) rather than a higher max heart rate
Venous return: skeletal muscle pump, respiratory pump, pocket valves, smooth muscle (venoconstriction), gravity; feeds Starling's law
Cardiac regulation via the CCC: chemoreceptors (CO2/pH), proprioceptors (muscle activity), baroreceptors (pressure); sympathetic accelerates, vagus (parasympathetic) slows
Vascular shunt redistributes blood: 15-20% to muscles at rest, 80-85% in maximal exercise, via arterioles and pre-capillary sphincters
Energy systems: ATP-PC (0-10 s, alactic), glycolytic (10 s-2 min, lactate produced), aerobic (dominant in sustained exercise); systems work as a continuum
EPOC: fast component restores PC, ATP and myoglobin O2 (2-3 min); slow component clears lactate, restores glycogen, temperature, ventilation and heart rate
topics.exampleQuestion: A 400 m runner relies heavily on anaerobic metabolism. Explain how the ATP-PC and glycolytic systems provide energy for her race, and how the recovery process following the race removes the resulting lactate. (8 marks, AQA Paper 1 style extended question)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic - the answer must hit four AO1 strands with AO2 application: (1) ATP-PC system: phosphocreatine stored in the sarcoplasm is split by creatine kinase into creatine + phosphate; the released energy resynthesises ATP from ADP + P (coupled reaction); no oxygen required (alactic); fuels the explosive start, dominant for the first ~10 s; yield small (~1 ATP per PC) but very high power. (2) Glycolytic system: anaerobic glycolysis of glucose/glycogen via PFK produces pyruvate, which becomes lactic acid without sufficient oxygen; net 2-3 ATP per molecule; dominant for the remaining ~35-45 s of the race; moderate power, moderate capacity. (3) Fatigue link (AO2): lactate dissociates to lactate + H+; H+ lowers pH, inhibits PFK and calcium release and cross-bridge cycling, explaining late-race deceleration. (4) Recovery/EPOC: fast (alactacid) component 2-3 min restores PC and ATP and reloads myoglobin; slow (lactacid) component removes lactate - oxidised as fuel in active muscle or converted to glucose/glycogen in the liver (Cori cycle) - replenishes glycogen, while elevated ventilation, heart rate and temperature return to rest; an active cool-down maintains the muscle pump and speeds lactate removal. Full marks require the sequence, the enzyme/terminology precision (creatine kinase, PFK, coupled reaction, alactacid/lactacid), and the application to 400 m pacing throughout.
practiceQuestions: Explain how venous return is maintained during exercise and how Starling's law increases stroke volume. (6 marks)
Identify the characteristics of the three muscle fibre types and justify their differing proportions in a marathon runner and a 100 m sprinter. (6 marks)
Explain the two components of EPOC and how an active cool-down aids recovery after a hockey match. (5 marks)
A coach uses PNF stretching to improve a gymnast's flexibility. Explain how the proprioceptors and the PNF technique produce this improvement. (5 marks)
Evaluate the physiological adaptations six months of aerobic training would produce for a 10,000 m runner. (10 marks)

topics.title: Biomechanics
learningObjectives: Apply Newton's three laws of motion to sporting examples and calculate force using F = ma (AQA 3.3.1; OCR 1.3; Edexcel Topic 2)
Identify the components and classes of lever, calculate mechanical advantage and explain why most limbs operate at a mechanical disadvantage (AQA 3.3.2; OCR 1.3)
Define and apply linear motion quantities: distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, momentum and impulse, including force-time graphs (AQA 3.3.3; OCR 1.3)
Explain angular motion: torque, moment of inertia, angular momentum and its conservation, applied to somersaulting and twisting (AQA 3.3.4; OCR 1.3)
Analyse projectile motion: release angle, speed and height, the 45 degree optimum and its modification (AQA 3.3.5; OCR 1.3)
Explain fluid mechanics - drag, the Bernoulli principle and the Magnus effect - and centre of mass and stability factors (AQA 3.3.6; OCR 1.3)
keyPoints: Newton's laws: inertia (first), F = ma (second), equal and opposite reaction (third); sprinter in blocks demonstrates all three

Lever classes: 1st (fulcrum between - nodding), 2nd (load between - heel raise, always mechanical advantage), 3rd (effort between - biceps curl, most limbs, mechanical disadvantage for force but greater speed and range)
Impulse = force x time; area under a force-time graph = impulse = change in momentum; longer contact time reduces peak force (cushioned catch)
Airborne angular momentum is conserved: tucking reduces moment of inertia so angular velocity rises (somersaults); extending slows rotation for landing
Projectile: release speed matters most, then angle (45 degrees optimal on level ground; less when released above landing height) and relative height
Bernoulli: faster airflow = lower pressure; Magnus effect on spinning balls - topspin dips, backspin floats, sidespin swerves
topics.exampleQuestion: A trampolinist wants to increase the number of somersaults completed in a single bounce and then land safely. Using principles of angular motion, explain how this is achieved. (8 marks, AQA Paper 1 style extended question)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic - four AO1 principles with AO2 application: (1) Angular motion is produced by torque (force x perpendicular distance from the axis) - the trampolinist generates torque at take-off by contacting the bed with a body lean/arm action so rotational momentum is created. (2) Angular momentum = moment of inertia x angular velocity, and while airborne (no external torque) it is conserved - it can only be redistributed. (3) Tucking the knees and arms to the chest reduces the moment of inertia (mass distribution moved towards the axis; I = sum mr squared), so angular velocity must increase - the somersault rotates faster, allowing more rotations per bounce. (4) Extending the body before contact increases the moment of inertia, so angular velocity decreases - rotation slows for a controlled, safe landing. Full marks require the conservation statement (cannot add angular momentum airborne), the I-angular velocity inverse trade, the mr squared reasoning for why tucking works, and the application to both the extra somersaults and the landing phase.
practiceQuestions: Explain how a sprinter leaving the blocks demonstrates Newton's three laws of motion. (6 marks)
During plantar flexion the foot acts as a second-class lever. Identify its components and explain the mechanical advantage this gives. (4 marks)
Use the concept of impulse to explain how a netball player catches a fast pass safely and how a thrower maximises the speed of a chest pass. (4 marks)
Explain how the Magnus effect causes a tennis ball hit with topspin to dip into the court. (4 marks)
Analyse how a gymnast maximises stability when landing a vault. (4 marks)

topics.title: Skill Acquisition
learningObjectives: Classify skills on the continua: open-closed, gross-fine, discrete-serial-continuous, self-externally paced, and justify the classification (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1; Edexcel Topic 3)
Justify types and methods of practice (part, whole, whole-part-whole, progressive part, massed, distributed, variable) and explain positive, negative and bilateral transfer (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1)
Compare theories of learning: operant conditioning (Skinner), cognitive theory, social learning theory (Bandura) and constructivism, with coaching applications (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1)
Describe information processing models (Whiting, Welford), selective attention and memory (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1)
Explain reaction time: simple and choice, Hick's law, the single-channel hypothesis and the psychological refractory period (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1)
Evaluate types of guidance (visual, verbal, manual, mechanical) and feedback (intrinsic/extrinsic, positive/negative, KR/KP, concurrent/terminal) (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1)
keyPoints: Skill classification is a continuum, not a category: open-closed (environment), gross-fine (muscle size), discrete-serial-continuous (structure), self-externally paced (control)
Methods of practice: whole/part/whole-part-whole/progressive part (structure), massed vs distributed (time), variable practice for open skills

Theories of learning: operant (reinforcement shapes S-R bonds), cognitive (insight, whole learning), social learning (Bandura ARMD - attention, retention, motor reproduction, motivation), constructivist (learner builds understanding, guided discovery)
Information processing: input - STSS - perception - STM/LTM - decision - effector - output - feedback (Welford); Whiting simplified it to receptor, translatory and effector mechanisms
Hick's law: reaction time rises with choice number; psychological refractory period = single-channel delay after a feint; anticipation shortens RT
Guidance: visual/verbal for most, manual/mechanical for safety and shaping; feedback: intrinsic vs extrinsic, positive vs negative, KR vs KP, concurrent vs terminal
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the use of operant conditioning and social learning theory when teaching a complex gymnastics skill to a beginner. (10 marks, AQA Paper 2 style)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic - AO1: accurate description of both theories with theorists; AO2: application to a beginner and a complex gymnastics skill; AO3: evaluation with strengths and weaknesses and a conclusion. Operant conditioning (Skinner): trial and error learning strengthens the stimulus-response bond; positive reinforcement (praise, rewards) and negative reinforcement (removing an unpleasant stimulus) strengthen correct responses; punishment weakens wrong ones; shaping reinforces successive approximations - the coach could reward a partial somersault before the full skill. Strengths for this context: builds correct technique through reward, motivates beginners, suits closed skills drilled in a stable environment. Weaknesses: trial and error is slow and risky for a dangerous, complex skill; a beginner may learn incorrect responses before reinforcement corrects them; punishment risks demotivation; it does not develop understanding. Social learning theory (Bandura): learning through observation and copying models, via the four ARMD stages - attention (accurate, safe demonstration from a significant other), retention (cues and mental rehearsal), motor reproduction (beginner must be physically capable - mechanical guidance helps), motivation (praise and success drive copying). Strengths: fast, safe - the beginner copies correct technique rather than discovering it by trial and error; demonstrations suit closed skills. Weaknesses: copying is only as good as the model; the beginner may reproduce the shape without understanding; motivation may not transfer without reinforcement. Balanced conclusion: for a complex, potentially dangerous skill, social learning theory provides the safe, fast template (demonstration plus guidance), and operant conditioning then consolidates the correct S-R bond through reinforcement and shaping - the two are complementary rather than competing.
practiceQuestions: Classify a penalty kick in football using three skill classification continua and justify your choices. (4 marks)
Explain Hick's law and the psychological refractory period, using a netball example. (5 marks)
A coach teaches a trampoline somersault to a beginner. Explain when visual, verbal, manual and mechanical guidance would each be appropriate. (6 marks)
Explain positive, negative and bilateral transfer, and give two strategies a coach uses to optimise positive transfer. (4 marks)
Explain intrinsic and extrinsic feedback and knowledge of results and knowledge of performance, with an example of each, and state when each is most effective. (6 marks)

topics.title: Sport Psychology
learningObjectives: Compare trait and interactionist theories of personality and apply the triadic model of attitudes, including changing attitudes via cognitive dissonance (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2; Edexcel Topic 4)
Explain intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and achievement motivation theory (Atkinson and McClelland: NACH/NAF) and achievement goal theory (Nicholls) (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2)
Evaluate arousal theories - drive theory (Hull), inverted U (Yerkes-Dodson), catastrophe model (Fazey and Hardy) and peak flow - and apply anxiety management techniques (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2)
Distinguish trait and state anxiety, their measurement, and explain theories and control of aggression (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2)
Explain social facilitation (Zajonc, evaluation apprehension) and group dynamics: Steiner's model, the Ringelmann effect and social loafing (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2)
Apply goal setting (outcome/performance/process, SMART), Weiner's attribution theory with retraining, and Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2)
keyPoints: Personality: trait theory (stable, innate) vs interactionist (Lewin B = f(P,E)); Hollander's layers - psychological core, typical responses, role-related behaviour
Attitudes: triadic model (cognitive, affective, behavioural); changed by cognitive dissonance (Festinger) and persuasive communication (source, message, situation, recipient)

Arousal: drive theory (linear, dominant response), inverted U (optimal point, lower for complex skills), catastrophe (Fazey and Hardy - high cognitive anxiety plus arousal = sudden collapse), peak flow (complete absorption)
Anxiety: trait (stable, Spielberger/SCAT) vs state (situational); cognitive vs somatic; measured by questionnaires, observation, physiological measures
Groups: Steiner - actual = potential - losses (faulty processes: motivation, coordination); Ringelmann effect and social loafing countered by identifiable contributions and roles

Attribution (Weiner): locus (internal/external), stability (stable/unstable), control; retrain failure to internal unstable controllable (effort); Bandura self-efficacy: performance accomplishments, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, physiological states
topics.exampleQuestion: A footballer converts penalties reliably in training but his performance collapses suddenly in a cup shoot-out. Explain the catastrophe model of arousal and evaluate strategies he could use to prevent the collapse. (10 marks, AQA Paper 2 style)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic - AO1: accurate description of the catastrophe model and strategies; AO2: application to the shoot-out scenario; AO3: evaluation with strengths, limitations and a conclusion. AO1: Fazey and Hardy's catastrophe model holds that performance depends on the interaction of physiological arousal and cognitive anxiety; when cognitive anxiety (worry) is low, the inverted U relationship holds, but when cognitive anxiety is high, further increases in physiological arousal cause a sudden, catastrophic drop in performance rather than a gradual decline; recovery requires arousal to fall well below the original optimal point. AO2: the shoot-out raises cognitive anxiety (high stakes, importance of outcome) and physiological arousal (crowd, fatigue) - crossing the threshold produces the sudden collapse, explaining why reliable training performance fails in competition. AO3 strategies: cognitive techniques lower cognitive anxiety - imagery/mental rehearsal of successful penalties, positive self-talk, outcome-independent process goals (strike technique), mindfulness; somatic techniques lower physiological arousal - progressive muscle relaxation, slow breathing, biofeedback, a consistent pre-shot routine. Evaluation: cognitive techniques target the model's key variable (cognitive anxiety) so are most relevant; routines and overlearned technique make the dominant response correct (link to drive theory - expertise protects against arousal); overconfidence is a risk if arousal falls too low (inverted U left side); conclusion - combining cognitive anxiety management with a rehearsed routine gives the best protection because it addresses both variables of the model.
practiceQuestions: Explain the drive theory and the inverted U hypothesis of arousal, including one limitation of each. (5 marks)
Distinguish trait and state anxiety and identify three ways anxiety can be measured. (5 marks)
Explain Steiner's model, the Ringelmann effect and social loafing, and give three strategies a coach uses to reduce losses in a team. (8 marks)
Explain Weiner's attribution dimensions and how a coach should retrain attributions after a losing run. (6 marks)
Explain Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy with a sporting example of each. (6 marks)

topics.title: Socio-cultural Issues in Sport
learningObjectives: Describe the characteristics of pre-industrial popular recreations and contrast them with rationalised post-industrial sport, including the role of the public schools (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1; Edexcel Topic 5)
Explain rationalisation and codification: governing bodies, leagues, respectability and the spread of sport through universities, the army and the railways (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1)
Evaluate globalisation, commercialisation and the media, including the golden triangle and the effects on performers, sport and spectators (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1)
Explain ethics and deviance: sportsmanship, gamesmanship, contract to win, drug use and the role of WADA, and match fixing (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1)
Explain causes and control of player and crowd violence, and forms of discrimination (sexism, racism, disability) with initiatives (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1)
Outline routes to sporting excellence: talent identification, the performance pyramid, and the roles of UK Sport, TASS and national governing bodies (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1)
keyPoints: Popular recreations: natural/simple, local, occasional, severe, ritual, wagering; caused by poor transport, illiteracy, rural life
Post-industrial sport: urbanisation initially damaged sport, then railways, Factory Acts (Saturday half-day) and middle-class leadership enabled rational recreation
Public schools: muscular Christianity (playing sport builds character), codification, the melting pot, spread via universities, church, army and railways (old boys)
Golden triangle: sport - sponsorship - media interdependence; positives (money, profile, participation) and negatives (scheduling, advertising control, win-at-all-costs)
Deviance: sportsmanship vs gamesmanship vs contract to win; drugs explained by pressure/money, controlled by WADA/UKAD testing and the prohibited list
Routes to excellence: grassroots - club - county - regional - national; UK Sport funds elite (lottery), TASS supports dual-career athletes, NGBs run talent identification
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the impact of commercialisation and the media on modern sport. (20 marks, OCR H555 style extended response)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic - AO1: knowledge of commercialisation, the golden triangle and media types; AO2: application to named sports/events; AO3: evaluation weighing benefits against costs with a justified conclusion. AO1/AO2: Commercialisation treats sport as a business - income from sponsorship, advertising, broadcasting rights, gate receipts and merchandising. The golden triangle shows the interdependence of sport, sponsorship and the media: media pay for rights because sponsors pay for the audience; sport reinvests the money in facilities, wages and grass-roots funding. Apply with examples: Premier League broadcast deals fund academy and community programmes; the Olympics' sponsorship programme (TOP) funds the Games; VAR and Hawk-Eye improve fairness; women's sport coverage has grown participation. AO3 positives: massive investment, raised profile and participation, global audiences, technological improvement of officiating and viewing, performer incomes. AO3 negatives: scheduling moved for TV and breaks in play for advertising; advertiser control (naming rights, kit rules); media money concentrated on few sports, starving minority and disability sport; club finances fragile - dependent on rights income; win-at-all-costs pressure from the stakes feeding deviance (doping, match fixing); spectator costs rising (subscription channels, ticket inflation). Conclusion: commercialisation and the media have transformed sport's quality, reach and fairness, but benefits are unevenly distributed and financial pressure feeds ethical problems - the strongest answers judge that the gains outweigh the costs only where governing bodies regulate the balance (listed events, integrity monitoring, equity funding).
practiceQuestions: Describe the characteristics of pre-industrial popular recreations and explain how they contrast with rationalised post-industrial sport. (6 marks)
Explain the role of the public schools in the codification and spread of sport in 19th-century Britain. (6 marks)
Explain why performers use drugs in sport and the role of WADA in controlling doping. (8 marks)
Explain the causes of player violence in sport and how it can be controlled. (6 marks)
Outline the route from talent identification to national sporting excellence, naming the key organisations and their roles. (6 marks)

topics.title: Performance Data and NEA
learningObjectives: Distinguish quantitative and qualitative analysis of performance and explain notational analysis (AQA NEA; OCR EAPI; Edexcel Topic analysis)
Explain validity, reliability, normative data and standardised protocols in performance measurement
Describe the NEA structure for each board: practical performance plus analysis and evaluation (AQA 3.7; OCR Component 04; Edexcel Components 3-4) and the mark scheme logic
Outline the structure of a written/oral performance analysis: strengths, weaknesses, prioritised weakness, theory explanation, development programme
Describe fitness testing protocols (aerobic, speed, power, strength, flexibility, agility, body composition) with advantages and limitations (AQA 3.2; OCR 1.2)
Explain data collection methods: primary/secondary data, laboratory versus field testing, recording procedures and pre-test safety
keyPoints: Quantitative = numerical and objective (times, counts); qualitative = observed quality judged against a technical model - the NEA needs both
Validity = measures what it claims; reliability = repeatable results; both require standardised protocols, calibrated equipment and normative comparison

NEA weightings: AQA 7582 - practical 15% + analysis and evaluation 15%; OCR H555 - practical 15% + EAPI oral 15%; Edexcel 9PE0 - practical performance and performance analysis/development programme together 30%

Performance analysis structure: overview - strengths justified with data - weaknesses - prioritise the main weakness - explain with theory (physiology, skill acquisition, psychology) - periodised development programme with re-test

Fitness tests: multi-stage fitness test/Cooper (aerobic), 30 m sprint (speed), vertical jump (power), 1RM/grip dynamometer (strength), sit-and-reach (flexibility), Illinois (agility), skinfolds/BIA (body composition)
Laboratory tests: accurate, controlled, standardised but expensive and less sport-specific; field tests: cheap, accessible, specific but less valid - estimated results
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate and suggest improvements to the weak technical component of a performer in your chosen sport. (20 marks, OCR H555 EAPI style oral response)
topics.modelAnswer: Mark-scheme logic - AO1: accurate knowledge of the technical model and development practices; AO2: application to the performer observed in the video; AO3: analysis (identify and prioritise the weakness with justification) and evaluation (development plan linked to theory and measurable re-test). Structure the oral response: (1) Overview (brief): performer, sport, position, level. (2) Strengths: two or three, each justified with evidence from the video plus a technical model reference. (3) Weaknesses: two or three, identified from video observation against the technical model, with theory explanation - e.g. inconsistent contact point caused by information processing under pressure (selective attention, anticipation) and high state anxiety raising arousal beyond the optimum (inverted U/catastrophe). (4) Prioritisation: state which weakness limits performance most and why it is the most improvable and measurable - this justification is where AO3 marks concentrate. (5) Development plan: a periodised programme with specific corrective practices targeting the cause (e.g. variable practice with defensive pressure for the technique; progressive muscle relaxation and imagery for the anxiety; linking practice methods - whole-part-whole, distributed practice), SMART targets, and a re-test/video re-analysis to evaluate improvement. (6) Close by linking the plan back to the theory: the practices correct the identified cause, and the measurable re-test demonstrates whether the programme worked. Full marks require timing discipline (roughly 2 min strengths, 3 min weaknesses, 1 min prioritisation, 4 min plan), data-justified claims throughout, and theory that is applied rather than listed.
practiceQuestions: Distinguish between validity and reliability, using a fitness test example of each. (4 marks)
Describe the protocol for the multi-stage fitness test and identify two limitations. (5 marks)
Compare laboratory and field fitness tests, giving one advantage and one limitation of each. (6 marks)
Explain how notational analysis produces quantitative data and how a coach would use it to improve a team's performance. (4 marks)
Outline the structure of the AQA NEA analysis and evaluation task, including the theory links required. (6 marks)

topics.title: Double Entry and the Ledger
learningObjectives: Apply the accounting equation and the dual effect of every transaction to decide the correct debit and credit entries for any transaction (AQA 7127, 3.3) (AO1/AO2).
Select the correct book of prime entry for each transaction type and post accurately to the ledger using folio references (3.3) (AO2).
Prepare and interpret a trial balance, naming the six error types it fails to detect and justifying why it is not proof of accuracy (3.4) (AO1/AO3).
Open, use and clear a suspense account through the journal, and assess the effect of each correction on profit for the year (3.4) (AO2/AO3).
Prepare sales and purchases ledger control accounts, reconcile them to lists of balances, and reconcile the cash book to the bank statement (3.4) (AO2).
Evaluate the benefits and costs of operating a double entry bookkeeping system, using business examples (3.1/3.3) (AO3).
keyPoints: Debit: expenses, assets, drawings increase. Credit: liabilities, capital/equity, income increase. Revenue received in advance is a liability, not income.
Balanced errors (complete omission, same wrong amount both sides, wrong account, reversal, principle, compensating) never break the trial balance; only one-sided errors do.
Only one-sided errors need a suspense account. A correction made with equal debit and credit via suspense never changes profit; corrections touching income or expense accounts do.
Prepare control accounts from day books and the cash book only - never from the personal ledgers - so the reconciliation actually tests them.

Bank reconciliation: update the cash book first (charges, interest, standing orders, direct debits and credits, dishonoured cheques), then adjust for timing: subtract unpresented cheques, add outstanding lodgements.
topics.exampleQuestion: Explain the purpose of a trial balance, and discuss whether a trial balance that agrees proves that the ledger accounts are free from errors. Support your answer with named error types and examples. (12 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1 (knowledge, ~4 marks): the trial balance lists every ledger balance at a date in debit and credit columns; because each transaction carries equal debits and credits, the columns should agree, so it tests the arithmetic accuracy of the double entry system. AO2 (application, ~2 marks): reference to what happens when it fails - the difference is placed in a suspense account until corrected by journal. AO3 (analysis/evaluation, ~6 marks): a balanced trial balance does NOT prove accuracy because balanced errors never disturb it. Must name and illustrate at least four of: complete omission (transaction never recorded); error of commission (correct amounts, wrong account of the same class); error of principle (correct amounts, wrong class of account, e.g. capital expenditure to purchases); original entry error (wrong figure on both sides); reversal of entries; compensating errors. Conclude with judgement: the trial balance is a necessary but insufficient check; assurance requires control account reconciliations, bank reconciliation, stock counts and internal check (segregation of duties). Top answers structure as argument, not list, and end with a supported conclusion.
