practiceQuestions: Prepare journal entries with narrations for each of the following transactions of a sole trader: (i) bought goods on credit from Pell Ltd £2,400; (ii) sold goods on credit to Kaur £3,100; (iii) returned goods to Pell Ltd £180; (iv) Kaur paid the amount due by cheque; (v) the owner took goods costing £150 for personal use. (10 marks)

A trial balance shows debit balances totalling £96,000 and credit balances totalling £95,900. (a) Open the suspense account. (b) The following errors are then found: a cheque for £100 received from a credit customer was debited to bank but never credited to the customer's account; a credit sale of £400 to D Fell was completely omitted; motor expenses of £600 were debited to motor vehicles. Show the journal entries to correct each error and clear the suspense account, and state the effect of each correction on profit for the year. (12 marks)

From the following, prepare the sales ledger control account for March: opening balance of trade receivables £18,400; credit sales £96,500; cash and cheques received from customers £88,200; discounts allowed £1,300; irrecoverable debts written off £950; returns inwards £1,150; contra with the purchases ledger £700. State the closing balance. (8 marks)

The cash book shows a debit balance of £4,320 but the bank statement shows £4,880. The statement shows bank charges of £50, a direct credit from a customer of £200, unpresented cheques of £1,150 and an outstanding lodgement of £740. Prepare the adjusted cash book and reconcile it to the bank statement. (8 marks)
Evaluate the benefits and costs to a growing sole trader of introducing a full double entry bookkeeping system with control accounts, instead of continuing with incomplete records. (12 marks)

topics.title: Financial Statements
learningObjectives: Prepare a statement of profit or loss and a statement of financial position for a sole trader from a trial balance, correctly classifying cost of sales, expenses and other income (AQA 7127, 3.6) (AO2).
Apply the accounting concepts - accruals/matching, prudence, going concern, consistency, business entity, materiality, realisation - and explain their effect on reported figures (3.5) (AO1/AO2).
Record year-end adjustments: accruals, prepayments, straight-line and reducing-balance depreciation, disposals, irrecoverable debts and the allowance for trade receivables (3.6) (AO2).
Prepare the financial statements of a limited company including share capital, share premium, retained earnings, dividends and the taxation and finance cost lines (3.7/3.16) (AO2).
Prepare partnership appropriation accounts, capital and current accounts applying the terms of the partnership agreement (3.15) (AO2).
Evaluate the effect on profit and the statement of financial position of omitted or misstated adjustments, and discuss the limitations of historical cost reporting (AO3).
keyPoints: Cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases + carriage inwards - closing inventory. Carriage outwards is a selling expense, never in cost of sales.
Depreciation is never a cash flow; the cash left at purchase and at disposal. Straight line = (cost - residual)/useful life; reducing balance = % × net book value each year.
The MOVEMENT in the allowance for receivables goes to the statement of profit or loss, not the total; a write-off goes straight to receivables and to expense.
Company statement of profit or loss: operating profit - finance costs = profit before tax - tax = profit for the year. Dividends are appropriations of profit, not expenses.
Partnership: capital accounts usually stay fixed; interest on capital, salaries and residual shares flow through the current accounts; interest on drawings is added back before the residual split.
topics.exampleQuestion: The draft profit for the year of a sole trader is £41,800 before any year-end adjustments. Adjustments outstanding: rent of £1,000 accrued; insurance prepaid £400; depreciation of equipment £6,000 (straight line); irrecoverable debt written off £1,500; increase in the allowance for doubtful debts £400. Calculate the adjusted profit for the year and explain, with reference to the accruals concept, why each adjustment is necessary. (12 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO2 calculation: adjusted profit = 41,800 − 1,000 (accrual) − 6,000 (depreciation) − 1,500 (irrecoverable debt) − 400 (allowance increase) + 400 (prepayment: deducting £400 from the insurance expense RAISES profit relative to the draft) = £33,300. Adjusted profit = 41,800 − 1,000 + 400 − 6,000 − 1,500 − 400 = £33,300. AO1/AO2 explanation per adjustment: accrual - the accruals concept requires the expense of the period to be charged whether or not paid, so profit falls and a current liability arises; prepayment - the £400 relates to next period, so it is excluded from this period's expense and shown as a current asset; depreciation - allocation of the asset's cost over its useful life under the matching concept, a non-cash expense; irrecoverable debt - the receivable is no longer an asset (realisation/prudence), so revenue effectively earned is reversed; allowance increase - prudence: provide for the estimated doubtful proportion, charging only the movement. Conclusion: adjustments convert cash-based draft figures into period-matched profit, and each also moves the statement of financial position (accruals in current liabilities, prepayments in current assets, lower NBV, lower net receivables).
practiceQuestions: From the following, prepare a statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December: revenue £240,000; opening inventory £22,000; purchases £121,400; carriage inwards £3,600; closing inventory £25,000; carriage outwards £4,800; wages £38,000; rent £12,000 plus accrual £1,000; insurance £2,400 less prepayment £400; irrecoverable debts written off £1,500; increase in allowance for receivables £400; depreciation of equipment £6,000. State gross profit and profit for the year. (10 marks)

A machine was bought on 1 October Year 1 for £54,000 (residual value £6,000, useful life 8 years, straight line, monthly pro-rata). It was sold on 30 June Year 5 for £28,000. Calculate the depreciation charge for each year to disposal, the accumulated depreciation and net book value at disposal, and the profit or loss on disposal. Show the disposal account. (10 marks)

A company's equity at 1 January: ordinary share capital (400,000 £1 shares) £400,000; share premium £60,000; retained earnings £320,000. During the year: profit for the year £95,000; dividends paid £40,000; a 1-for-10 bonus issue was made using share premium. Prepare the equity section of the statement of financial position at 31 December. (8 marks)

Partners Ash and Birch share residual profits 3:2. Capitals: Ash £60,000, Birch £40,000; interest on capital 5%. Birch is entitled to a salary of £12,000. Interest on drawings: Ash £600, Birch £400. Profit for the year before appropriations is £98,000, and drawings were Ash £30,000, Birch £35,000. Prepare the appropriation account and each partner's current account. (12 marks)
Evaluate whether the use of historical cost, with the prudence concept, provides financial statements that are useful to decision-makers. (12 marks)

topics.title: Ratio Analysis
learningObjectives: Calculate the full AQA ratio set from financial statements: gross and operating margins, mark-up, ROCE, current and acid test, receivables, payables and inventory days, gearing and interest cover (AQA 7127, 3.8 with appendix) (AO2).
Select valid comparatives - prior year, industry norm, plan - and interpret movements with plausible business causes (3.8) (AO2/AO3).
Analyse profitability, liquidity and gearing together, recognising trade-offs such as liquidity versus profitability and risk versus return (3.8) (AO3).
Evaluate the limitations of ratio analysis: historical cost, estimates, window dressing, single-year data, inflation and non-financial factors (3.17) (AO3).
Communicate a justified recommendation for a named stakeholder, integrating calculations with qualitative evidence (3.17) (AO3).
keyPoints: ROCE = operating profit ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities). Using profit for the year or total assets is the most common formula error.
Current ratio benchmark ~1.5-2:1, acid test ~1:1 - but benchmarks are starting points for investigation, not verdicts.
Working capital cycle = inventory days + receivables days − payables days: the gap the business must finance.
Gearing above 50% is high by convention, but judge it with interest cover and cash flow stability, never alone.
Every interpretation answer: calculate, compare (prior year/industry), identify cause, state consequence, then conclude with limitations.
topics.exampleQuestion: Using the data below, calculate for 2025 and 2024 the gross profit margin, ROCE, current ratio and gearing, and analyse the performance and financial position of the company. (20 marks) 2025: revenue £900,000; gross profit £315,000; operating profit £90,000; equity £600,000; non-current liabilities £300,000; inventory £75,000; receivables £110,000; cash £15,000; current liabilities £150,000. 2024: revenue £800,000; gross profit £280,000; operating profit £72,000; equity £550,000; non-current liabilities £300,000; inventory £60,000; receivables £80,000; cash £60,000; current liabilities £160,000.
topics.modelAnswer: Calculations (AO2, ~8 marks): GPM 35.0% both years. ROCE: 90,000/900,000 = 10.0%; 72,000/850,000 = 8.5%. Current ratio: 200,000/150,000 = 1.33:1; 200,000/160,000 = 1.25:1. Gearing: 300,000/900,000 = 33%; 300,000/850,000 = 35%. Analysis (AO3, ~12 marks): performance - flat gross margin with revenue up 12.5% suggests stable pricing against costs; operating margin up 9.0% to 10.0% shows overhead control; ROCE up 1.5 points despite capital employed rising only 6% - efficiency of asset use improved (link: ROCE = margin × capital turnover). Position - current ratio and gearing stable, but composition deteriorated: cash fell from £60,000 to £15,000 while receivables rose from £80,000 to £110,000 (days up from 37 to 45), so liquidity quality worsened; acid test 0.83:1 against 0.88:1. Judgement: performance improving, position adequate but increasingly dependent on collecting receivables; recommend credit control review. Limitations: single company, historical cost, no cash flow statement; two-year trend only.
practiceQuestions: Using the two-year data in the example question, calculate for both years: operating profit margin, ROCE, current ratio, acid test, receivables days, payables days and inventory days (cost of sales 2025 £585,000; 2024 £520,000; payables 2025 £120,000; 2024 £115,000). (14 marks)
Interpret the movement in each of the seven ratios from question 1 and identify one plausible business cause and one consequence for each. (12 marks)

Company Y has non-current liabilities of £480,000, equity of £320,000, operating profit of £96,000 and debenture interest at 12%. Calculate gearing and interest cover and evaluate whether a bank should lend Y a further £100,000. (12 marks)
A supplier is deciding whether to sell goods worth £40,000 to the company in the example data (2025) on 30-day credit. Using the 2025 ratios, advise the supplier. (10 marks)
Explain what window dressing is and evaluate how far ratio analysis can be trusted when management may window dress the accounts. Support your answer with a calculation. (12 marks)

topics.title: Costing and Budgeting
learningObjectives: Classify costs as fixed, variable, semi-variable or stepped, and direct or indirect, and split semi-variable costs using the high-low method (AQA 7127, 3.10/3.12) (AO2).
Calculate contribution, break-even output and revenue, margin of safety and target-profit output, and evaluate the uses and limitations of break-even analysis (3.10) (AO2/AO3).
Calculate overhead absorption rates, absorbed overhead and under/over absorption, and reconcile marginal and absorption costing profits when inventory levels change (3.12) (AO2/AO3).
Prepare cash budgets with receipts and payments timed correctly, and evaluate the purposes of budgeting including behavioural effects such as budgetary slack (3.9) (AO2/AO3).
Calculate materials, labour and overhead variances against a flexed budget, and explain plausible causes and interdependence (3.11) (AO2/AO3).
keyPoints: Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit; margin of safety = actual − break-even; target-profit units = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit.

Marginal costing values inventory at variable production cost and writes off fixed overheads as period costs; absorption costing carries fixed overhead in inventory - profits differ when inventory levels change.
OAR always uses BUDGETED overhead ÷ BUDGETED activity. Under-absorption = actual overhead > absorbed overhead.
Cash budgets forecast cash, not profit: sales on credit become receipts next month; purchases are paid a month after buying; depreciation never appears.
Variances compare ACTUAL with FLEXED budget. Materials: price (paid vs standard price) and usage (used vs standard for actual output). Labour: rate and efficiency.
topics.exampleQuestion: A company makes a single product. Fixed costs are £84,000 per year, selling price £24 per unit, variable cost £14 per unit. Budgeted output is 11,000 units. (a) Calculate the break-even output, the margin of safety (units and %), and the output needed for a target profit of £36,000. (b) Evaluate the usefulness of break-even analysis to the managers of this business. (12 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: (a) AO2: contribution = 24 − 14 = £10; break-even = 84,000 ÷ 10 = 8,400 units; margin of safety = 11,000 − 8,400 = 2,600 units = 2,600 ÷ 11,000 × 100 = 23.6% of budgeted sales; target profit output = (84,000 + 36,000) ÷ 10 = 12,000 units. (b) AO3 evaluation: usefulness - simple and transparent; quantifies risk via the 23.6% margin of safety (sales can fall 23.6% before losses); supports pricing decisions (a £2 price cut raises break-even from 8,400 to 10,500 units); provides a target (12,000 units) for capacity and sales planning; the break-even chart communicates the cost/revenue structure to non-specialists. Limitations - assumes linearity (no economies of scale or bulk discounts), constant fixed costs at all outputs (they step), all output sold at one price, a single product or constant mix, and a static demand environment; it is short-run because fixed costs must eventually be covered. Judgement: useful as a first-pass planning and risk tool, particularly for the margin of safety, but should be stress-tested for price and cost changes and supported by market evidence before committing to the 12,000-unit target.
practiceQuestions: Fixed costs are £84,000. Selling price £24, variable cost £14, budgeted output 11,000 units. Calculate: contribution per unit; break-even in units and in revenue; margin of safety in units and as a percentage; output required for a target profit of £36,000. (8 marks)

Total costs at 4,000 units were £38,000; at 9,000 units they were £78,000. Using the high-low method, calculate the variable cost per unit and the fixed cost, and predict total cost at 7,000 units. (6 marks)

Budgeted overhead £180,000; budgeted machine hours 24,000. Actual overhead £176,000; actual machine hours 22,000. Calculate the OAR, the overhead absorbed, and the under/over absorption, explaining its causes. (6 marks)

Standard: 3 kg at £5 per kg and 1.5 labour hours at £12 per hour per unit. Actual output 4,000 units; materials used 12,400 kg costing £59,520; labour 6,200 hours costing £74,400. Calculate the materials price and usage variances and the labour rate and efficiency variances, and suggest one consistent explanation. (10 marks)

Prepare the cash budget for January and February. Opening cash 1 January £5,000. Sales: December £40,000, January £50,000, February £60,000 - half cash, half collected one month later. Purchases: December £24,000, January £30,000, February £32,000 - paid one month later. Wages £10,000 and overheads £6,000 per month paid when incurred. Equipment £15,000 paid in February. State each closing balance. (10 marks)

topics.title: Ethics, Technology and Society
learningObjectives: Explain the five fundamental ethical principles - integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour - and apply them to scenarios (AQA 7127, 3.18) (AO1/AO2).
Identify ethical threats (self-interest, self-review, familiarity, intimidation, advocacy) and evaluate appropriate safeguards (3.18) (AO2/AO3).
Analyse techniques of creative accounting and window dressing and evaluate their impact on the business, the accounting function and stakeholders (3.18) (AO2/AO3).
Evaluate the benefits and costs of computerised accounting systems and the strengths and risks of spreadsheet modelling (3.1) (AO2/AO3).
Assess data security threats and safeguards, including UK GDPR duties, and communicate justified recommendations (3.1/3.18) (AO3).
keyPoints: The five principles come as a package: a technically perfect but dishonest computation breaches integrity and objectivity even if it is arithmetically correct.

Threats: self-interest (financial stake), self-review (checking your own work), familiarity (long relationships), intimidation (pressure from client or employer), advocacy (promoting the client's position).
Creative accounting distorts every ratio built on profit or assets - margins, ROCE, gearing - so users inherit the distortion; auditors and governance exist to detect it.
Accounting software automates double entry and reporting but concentrates risk: one database error or breach multiplies; backups, access controls and audit trails are not optional.
Spreadsheets are powerful modelling tools but weak controls: no audit trail, formula rot, version chaos - validate inputs, protect cells, document versions.
topics.exampleQuestion: Evaluate the impact on stakeholders of a business overstating its profits through creative accounting techniques. (12 marks)
topics.modelAnswer: AO1: define creative accounting - manipulation of reported results within or beyond the rules to mislead (techniques: early revenue recognition, capitalising expenses, understating provisions or allowances, overstating inventory); distinguish from legal window dressing. AO2 application: overstatement flows through statements - cost of sales understated or income overstated raises profit and equity; ratios (ROCE, margins, EPS) inherit the distortion; bonuses and dividends may be paid from fictitious profit. AO3 stakeholder analysis: shareholders and potential investors misprice shares - on discovery wealth collapses; lenders over-lend on understated risk and understated gearing; employees hold pensions in the employer's equity and lose jobs in the aftermath; suppliers extend credit to a hollow business; HMRC collects the wrong tax; the profession and auditors suffer reputational and regulatory consequences (Enron and WorldCom as named illustrations - debt hidden off balance sheet; expenses capitalised). Balanced elements: regulation, audit, governance and ratio cross-checks reduce but do not eliminate the risk; incentives (bonuses, covenant compliance, share prices) explain why it recurs. Judgement: the damage is systemic - misallocation of society's capital - and falls hardest on the least-informed stakeholders; ethical principles exist because markets only work on trustworthy information.
